# PART 512 — BASIS VECTORS

Now we have two important concepts:

A set can **span** a vector space.

A set can be **linearly independent**.

A basis is where both properties hold simultaneously.

---

# 512.1 Why basis exists

Suppose we want to describe every vector in a space using some reference vectors.

If our reference vectors do not span the whole space, some vectors cannot be represented.

If they are dependent, representations may not be unique.

So we need:

\[
\boxed{
\text{enough vectors to reach everything}
}
\]

but also:

\[
\boxed{
\text{no redundant vectors}
}
\]

That gives the basis definition.

---

# 512.2 Formal definition

A set

\[
B=
\{
\vec b_1,\ldots,\vec b_n
\}
\]

is a **basis** of vector space \(V\) if:

\[
\operatorname{span}(B)=V
\]

and the vectors in \(B\) are linearly independent.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{basis}
=
\text{independent spanning set}
}
\]

This is one of the fundamental definitions of linear algebra.

---

# 512.3 Why both conditions are necessary

Consider:

\[
\{(1,0)\}.
\]

This set is independent.

But it does not span \(\mathbb R^2\).

Therefore it is not a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).

Now consider:

\[
\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}.
\]

It spans \(\mathbb R^2\).

But it is dependent because:

\[
(1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1).
\]

Therefore it is also not a basis.

Only something that is simultaneously spanning and independent qualifies.

---

# 512.4 Standard basis of \(\mathbb R^2\)

The familiar basis is:

\[
\vec e_1=(1,0)
\]

and

\[
\vec e_2=(0,1).
\]

They are independent and span every vector:

\[
(x,y)
=
x\vec e_1+y\vec e_2.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\{(1,0),(0,1)\}
}
\]

is a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).

This particular one is called the **standard basis**.

Part 516 later gives it its dedicated treatment.

---

# 512.5 Standard basis of \(\mathbb R^3\)

Similarly:

\[
\vec e_1=(1,0,0)
\]

\[
\vec e_2=(0,1,0)
\]

\[
\vec e_3=(0,0,1).
\]

Every:

\[
(x,y,z)
\]

can be written:

\[
x\vec e_1+y\vec e_2+z\vec e_3.
\]

They are independent.

Therefore they form a basis.

Again, detailed treatment belongs to Part 517.

---

# 512.6 Basis vectors do not have to be unit length

Consider:

\[
\vec b_1=(2,0)
\]

and:

\[
\vec b_2=(0,3).
\]

These vectors are independent.

Can they span \(\mathbb R^2\)?

For arbitrary target:

\[
(x,y),
\]

we need:

\[
a(2,0)+b(0,3)=(x,y).
\]

That means:

\[
2a=x
\]

and:

\[
3b=y.
\]

So:

\[
a=\frac{x}{2}
\]

and:

\[
b=\frac{y}{3}.
\]

Every target has a solution.

Therefore they form a basis.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{basis vectors need not be normalized}
}
\]

---

# 512.7 Basis vectors do not have to be perpendicular

Take:

\[
\vec b_1=(1,0)
\]

and:

\[
\vec b_2=(1,1).
\]

They are independent.

Any target:

\[
(x,y)
\]

must satisfy:

\[
a(1,0)+b(1,1)
=
(x,y).
\]

Expanding:

\[
(a+b,b)=(x,y).
\]

Thus:

\[
b=y
\]

and:

\[
a=x-y.
\]

Always solvable.

Therefore these two vectors form a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).

Geometrically:

```text
     b2
    /
   /
  /
 •────────→ b1
```

The coordinate grid is now slanted.

That is perfectly legal.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{basis}\neq\text{orthonormal basis}
}
\]

Orthonormal bases come later in Part 559.

---

# 512.8 Basis as a coordinate measuring system

A basis tells us which directions count as our coordinate directions.

If:

\[
B=
\{\vec b_1,\vec b_2\},
\]

then instead of describing vectors using the standard X/Y directions, we describe them using amounts along:

\[
\vec b_1
\]

and:

\[
\vec b_2.
\]

So basis vectors are not merely "important vectors."

They define a **coordinate language**.

This is the bridge into Part 514.

---

# 512.9 Basis and uniqueness

Because basis vectors are independent, the representation

\[
\vec v
=
a_1\vec b_1+\cdots+a_n\vec b_n
\]

has unique coefficients.

Because they span \(V\), such coefficients exist for every \(\vec v\in V\).

Thus a basis gives both:

\[
\boxed{\text{existence}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\text{uniqueness}}
\]

of coordinates.

That is the real reason basis is so important.

---

# 512.10 Removing redundant generators until a basis remains

Suppose:

\[
S=
\{
(1,0),
(0,1),
(1,1)
\}.
\]

This spans \(\mathbb R^2\), but it is dependent.

Because:

\[
(1,1)
=
(1,0)+(0,1),
\]

we can remove the third vector without changing the span.

We are left with:

\[
\{
(1,0),(0,1)
\}.
\]

That is independent and still spans.

Thus it is a basis.

Conceptually:

```text
spanning set
    ↓ remove redundant generators
independent spanning set
    ↓
basis
```

Later algorithms such as Gaussian elimination, QR and SVD provide systematic ways of discovering this structure.

---

# PART 513 — DIMENSION OF A VECTOR SPACE

Now a striking fact appears.

Different bases of the same finite-dimensional vector space always contain the same number of vectors.

That number is called the **dimension**.

---

# 513.1 The motivating question

Suppose one basis of \(\mathbb R^2\) is:

\[
\{(1,0),(0,1)\}.
\]

Another is:

\[
\{(1,1),(1,-1)\}.
\]

Another is:

\[
\{(2,0),(1,7)\}.
\]

The actual basis vectors differ.

Yet all bases contain exactly two vectors.

Why?

Because the space has two independent directions of freedom.

That count is the dimension.

---

# 513.2 Formal definition

If \(V\) has a finite basis containing \(n\) vectors, then:

\[
\boxed{
\dim V=n.
}
\]

For example:

\[
\dim\mathbb R^2=2
\]

and:

\[
\dim\mathbb R^3=3.
\]

The number is not tied to one particular basis.

It is an invariant of the vector space itself.

---

# 513.3 Why "number of components" is not the deepest definition

For \(\mathbb R^3\), vectors happen to be represented using three real coordinates.

So it is tempting to define dimension as:

> number of components.

That is not the fundamental definition.

The deeper statement is:

\[
\boxed{
\dim V
=
\text{number of vectors in any basis of }V.
}
\]

Component count follows after a basis is chosen.

This matters because vector spaces can consist of objects that are not initially coordinate tuples.

---

# 513.4 Example: a plane inside \(\mathbb R^3\)

Consider:

\[
W=
\{
(x,y,0)
\}.
\]

This is a subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\).

A basis is:

\[
(1,0,0),\qquad(0,1,0).
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\dim W=2.
}
\]

Notice that every vector is physically stored using three coordinates:

\[
(x,y,0),
\]

but the subspace has dimension only \(2\).

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{storage component count}
\neq
\text{intrinsic dimension}
}
\]

in general.

That distinction becomes extremely important in graphics and geometry.

---

# 513.5 Example: a line in \(\mathbb R^3\)

Let:

\[
W=
\{
t(1,2,3)\mid t\in\mathbb R
\}.
\]

A basis is simply:

\[
\{(1,2,3)\}.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\dim W=1.
}
\]

Yet every vector still uses three ambient coordinates.

Again:

```text
ambient storage:
3 numbers

intrinsic freedom:
1 coefficient
```

---

# 513.6 Zero subspace dimension

The zero subspace is:

\[
\{\vec0\}.
\]

It has no nonzero independent vectors.

Its basis is the empty set:

\[
\varnothing.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\dim\{\vec0\}=0.
}
\]

This is mathematically consistent with:

\[
\operatorname{span}(\varnothing)=\{\vec0\}.
\]

---

# 513.7 Degrees of freedom intuition

Dimension is often interpreted as the number of independent scalar choices required to identify a vector once a basis is fixed.

In a line:

\[
t\vec b_1
\]

we choose one scalar \(t\).

Dimension:

\[
1.
\]

In a plane:

\[
a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2
\]

we choose two scalars.

Dimension:

\[
2.
\]

In \(\mathbb R^3\):

\[
a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2+c\vec b_3.
\]

Three independent scalar choices.

Dimension:

\[
3.
\]

This "degrees of freedom" interpretation is extremely useful.

---

# 513.8 Why three vectors cannot be independent in a 2D space

Suppose:

\[
\dim V=2.
\]

A basis already contains two independent vectors and spans everything.

Any third vector \(\vec w\) is already inside the span of those two.

Therefore:

\[
\vec w=a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2.
\]

So:

\[
a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2-\vec w=\vec0.
\]

That is a nontrivial zero combination.

Thus the three vectors are dependent.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{no independent set in an }n\text{-dimensional space can contain more than }n\text{ vectors}.
}
\]

---

# 513.9 Why fewer than \(n\) vectors cannot span an \(n\)-dimensional space

If fewer than \(n\) vectors spanned an \(n\)-dimensional space, we could remove all remaining basis directions while still reaching everything.

That would contradict the fact that a basis requires \(n\) independent directions.

More formally, the key theorem is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{any spanning set has at least }n\text{ vectors}
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
\text{any independent set has at most }n\text{ vectors}.
}
\]

When both equality conditions are satisfied, the set is a basis.

---

# 513.10 Dimension is not physical spatial dimension only

Graphics programmers often hear dimension and immediately think:

```text
2D
3D
4D homogeneous coordinates
```

But vector-space dimension is much broader.

For example, real polynomials of degree at most two:

\[
p(x)=a+bx+cx^2
\]

can be generated by:

\[
1,\quad x,\quad x^2.
\]

Those three are independent.

So the polynomial space has dimension:

\[
3.
\]

Yet nobody is claiming the polynomial physically exists in 3D space.

Dimension means:

\[
\boxed{
\text{number of independent basis directions in the abstract vector space}.
}
\]

---

# 513.11 Dimension and memory

Suppose a plane is embedded in \(\mathbb R^3\).

You might store a point in the plane as:

```cpp
struct Vec3 {
    float x, y, z;
};
```

which uses three scalar slots.

But if you know the plane basis:

\[
\vec b_1,\vec b_2,
\]

you could represent the same plane vector using only two coefficients:

```cpp
struct PlaneCoordinates {
    float u;
    float v;
};
```

and reconstruct:

\[
\vec x=u\vec b_1+v\vec b_2.
\]

Thus intrinsic dimension can enable more compact representations.

Whether that is worthwhile depends on runtime costs, storage, transformations and API complexity.

---

# PART 514 — COORDINATE REPRESENTATION RELATIVE TO A BASIS

This is where Part 506 becomes fully formal.

We previously said:

\[
\vec v
\neq
(v_x,v_y,v_z)
\]

as concepts.

Now we can say precisely what the tuple is.

It is the list of coefficients needed to reconstruct \(\vec v\) from a chosen basis.

---

# 514.1 Formal coordinate definition

Let:

\[
B=
(\vec b_1,\ldots,\vec b_n)
\]

be an ordered basis of \(V\).

Because \(B\) spans \(V\), every vector \(\vec v\in V\) can be written:

\[
\vec v
=
c_1\vec b_1+\cdots+c_n\vec b_n.
\]

Because \(B\) is independent, those coefficients are unique.

We define:

\[
\boxed{
[\vec v]_B
=
(c_1,\ldots,c_n).
}
\]

Read:

> coordinates of \(\vec v\) relative to basis \(B\).

This is the precise mathematical meaning of coordinates.

---

# 514.2 Why the basis must be ordered

Consider basis:

\[
B=(\vec b_1,\vec b_2).
\]

Coordinates:

\[
(3,5)
\]

mean:

\[
3\vec b_1+5\vec b_2.
\]

If we reverse basis order:

\[
B'=(\vec b_2,\vec b_1),
\]

then the same vector has coordinates:

\[
(5,3).
\]

So although a basis is often informally described as a set, coordinate representation requires an **ordered basis**.

The component positions correspond to particular basis vectors.

---

# 514.3 Standard coordinates

Take standard basis:

\[
E=
\left(
(1,0),
(0,1)
\right).
\]

For vector:

\[
\vec v=(3,2)
\]

geometrically, we have:

\[
\vec v
=
3(1,0)+2(0,1).
\]

Therefore:

\[
[\vec v]_E=(3,2).
\]

This is why ordinary Cartesian coordinates feel like the vector itself.

We use the standard basis so constantly that the basis is often omitted.

But strictly:

\[
(3,2)
\]

means:

\[
[\vec v]_E=(3,2)
\]

relative to that chosen basis.

---

# 514.4 Nonstandard basis example

Let:

\[
B=
(\vec b_1,\vec b_2)
\]

where:

\[
\vec b_1=(1,1)
\]

and:

\[
\vec b_2=(1,-1).
\]

Take geometric vector whose standard coordinates are:

\[
(4,2).
\]

We seek:

\[
c_1,c_2
\]

such that:

\[
c_1(1,1)+c_2(1,-1)=(4,2).
\]

Component equations:

\[
c_1+c_2=4
\]

\[
c_1-c_2=2.
\]

Add:

\[
2c_1=6.
\]

Therefore:

\[
c_1=3.
\]

Then:

\[
c_2=1.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
[\vec v]_B=(3,1).
}
\]

But in the standard basis:

\[
\boxed{
[\vec v]_E=(4,2).
}
\]

Same vector.

Different coordinates.

This is Part 506 made mathematically precise.

---

# 514.5 Coordinates are not physical measurements in universal axes

The tuple

\[
(3,1)_B
\]

means:

\[
3\vec b_1+1\vec b_2.
\]

It does not necessarily mean:

```text
3 metres world X
1 metre world Y
```

unless the basis vectors actually correspond to those directions and units.

This is exactly why graphics APIs must track coordinate spaces.

---

# 514.6 Reconstructing the vector from coordinates

Given:

\[
[\vec v]_B=(c_1,\ldots,c_n),
\]

reconstruction is:

\[
\boxed{
\vec v
=
c_1\vec b_1+\cdots+c_n\vec b_n.
}
\]

This process takes coefficients and turns them back into the underlying vector.

In code for a 2D basis:

```cpp
struct Vec2 {
    float x;
    float y;
};

struct Basis2 {
    Vec2 b1;
    Vec2 b2;
};

Vec2 reconstruct(
    const Basis2& basis,
    float c1,
    float c2) noexcept
{
    return {
        c1 * basis.b1.x + c2 * basis.b2.x,
        c1 * basis.b1.y + c2 * basis.b2.y
    };
}
```

Mathematically:

```cpp
c1 * basis.b1
```

is:

\[
c_1\vec b_1.
\]

Then adding the second term performs the linear combination.

---

# 514.7 Why coordinates are unique

Suppose:

\[
\vec v
=
a_1\vec b_1+\cdots+a_n\vec b_n
\]

and also:

\[
\vec v
=
c_1\vec b_1+\cdots+c_n\vec b_n.
\]

Subtract:

\[
\vec0
=
(a_1-c_1)\vec b_1+\cdots+(a_n-c_n)\vec b_n.
\]

Since basis vectors are independent:

\[
a_i-c_i=0
\]

for every \(i\).

Thus:

\[
a_i=c_i.
\]

So each vector has exactly one coordinate tuple relative to a chosen basis.

Without independence, coordinates would not be unique.

Without spanning, some vectors would have no coordinates at all.

This is why basis requires both.

---

# 514.8 Coordinate arithmetic

Suppose:

\[
[\vec u]_B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)
\]

and:

\[
[\vec v]_B=(v_1,\ldots,v_n).
\]

Then:

\[
\vec u+\vec v
=
\sum_i u_i\vec b_i+\sum_i v_i\vec b_i.
\]

Regroup:

\[
=
\sum_i(u_i+v_i)\vec b_i.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
[\vec u+\vec v]_B
=
[\vec u]_B+[\vec v]_B
}
\]

component-wise.

Likewise:

\[
\boxed{
[a\vec v]_B
=
a[\vec v]_B.
}
\]

This is why coordinate tuples faithfully reproduce vector-space operations.

The coordinate map preserves linear structure.

---

# 514.9 Mathematical vector versus machine coordinate structure

You now have four layers:

```text
abstract vector
      ↓ choose ordered basis
coordinate tuple
      ↓ choose scalar representation
floating-point components
      ↓ choose physical layout
bytes in memory
```

For example:

\[
\vec v
\]

might become:

\[
[\vec v]_B=(3,1)
\]

then:

```cpp
Vec2 coords{3.0f, 1.0f};
```

then bytes representing two IEEE-754 floats.

Each layer answers a different question.

---

# PART 515 — CHANGING BASIS CONCEPTUALLY

Now suppose we have two different coordinate languages.

The vector does not change.

The numbers used to describe it do.

A **change of basis** converts one coordinate representation of the same vector into another.

---

# 515.1 The central picture

Suppose:

\[
B=(\vec b_1,\vec b_2)
\]

and:

\[
C=(\vec c_1,\vec c_2)
\]

are two bases of the same vector space.

A vector \(\vec v\) may have:

\[
[\vec v]_B=(a,b)
\]

and:

\[
[\vec v]_C=(p,q).
\]

But there is still only one geometric/abstract vector:

\[
\boxed{
\vec v
}
\]

So:

\[
a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2
=
p\vec c_1+q\vec c_2.
\]

Change of basis means solving for the new coefficients.

---

# 515.2 The conceptual algorithm

To change from basis \(B\) coordinates to basis \(C\) coordinates:

```text
coordinates in B
      ↓
reconstruct the underlying vector
      ↓
express that same vector using C
      ↓
coordinates in C
```

That is the deepest concept.

Later matrices will make this efficient.

But you should understand the operation before learning the matrix shortcut.

---

# 515.3 Concrete example

Let standard basis be:

\[
E=
((1,0),(0,1)).
\]

Let alternative basis:

\[
B=
((1,1),(1,-1)).
\]

Suppose:

\[
[\vec v]_B=(3,1).
\]

First reconstruct the vector.

\[
\vec v
=
3(1,1)+1(1,-1).
\]

Compute:

\[
3(1,1)=(3,3).
\]

Then:

\[
(3,3)+(1,-1)
=
(4,2).
\]

Therefore:

\[
[\vec v]_E=(4,2).
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
(3,1)_B
\longrightarrow
(4,2)_E.
}
\]

Nothing physically moved.

Only our coordinate description changed.

---

# 515.4 Reverse conversion

Now start with:

\[
[\vec v]_E=(4,2).
\]

We want coordinates in \(B\).

Solve:

\[
a(1,1)+b(1,-1)=(4,2).
\]

As before:

\[
a+b=4
\]

\[
a-b=2.
\]

Therefore:

\[
a=3,\qquad b=1.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
(4,2)_E
\longrightarrow
(3,1)_B.
}
\]

The two conversions are inverses.

---

# 515.5 Why basis changes can alter component magnitudes dramatically

Consider basis:

\[
B=
((100,0),(0,100)).
\]

A vector with standard coordinates:

\[
(50,200)
\]

has basis-\(B\) coordinates:

\[
\left(
\frac{50}{100},
\frac{200}{100}
\right)
=
(0.5,2).
\]

So the same vector may have coordinates:

\[
(50,200)
\]

or:

\[
(0.5,2).
\]

Coordinate magnitudes alone do not tell you physical vector size unless you know the basis.

This is another reason coordinate metadata matters.

---

# 515.6 Rotation of basis versus rotation of vector

This distinction is critical.

Suppose a physical vector remains fixed.

You rotate the coordinate axes.

Its coordinates change.

That is a **passive** viewpoint.

Alternatively, keep axes fixed and rotate the physical vector.

That changes the actual vector.

That is an **active** viewpoint.

These can lead to formulas that look like inverses of each other.

Full active/passive transformation treatment is Part 654, but you should already know:

\[
\boxed{
\text{rotate vector}
\neq
\text{rotate coordinate system}.
}
\]

---

# 515.7 Graphics interpretation: object space and world space

Imagine an object's local basis is rotated relative to world basis.

A local vector may be:

\[
(1,0,0)_{\text{local}}.
\]

That means:

> one unit along the object's local first basis direction.

In world coordinates, that same geometric direction might be:

\[
(0.707,0,0.707)_{\text{world}}.
\]

The vector is the same geometric direction.

The coordinate tuple changed because the basis changed.

This is exactly what local-to-world transformations formalize later.

---

# 515.8 Camera-space interpretation

Suppose a world-space direction is:

\[
(0,0,-1)_{\text{world}}.
\]

If the camera rotates, the same world direction may have very different camera-space coordinates.

Nothing about the world direction itself changed.

Only its representation in the camera basis changed.

This is why graphics debugging must always ask:

\[
\boxed{
\text{coordinates relative to which basis?}
}
\]

---

# 515.9 Why change-of-basis requires an invertible relationship

If \(B\) and \(C\) are both bases of the same finite-dimensional space, then every vector has:

- exactly one coordinate representation in \(B\),
- exactly one coordinate representation in \(C\).

So converting:

\[
[\vec v]_B
\rightarrow
[\vec v]_C
\]

must be reversible.

If you could not recover the original coordinates, one of the representations would have lost information.

This is why the eventual change-of-basis transformation is invertible.

Later matrix language will express this much more compactly.

---

# 515.10 What if the "basis" vectors are dependent?

Suppose someone attempts to use:

\[
(1,0)
\]

and:

\[
(2,0)
\]

as a coordinate basis for \(\mathbb R^2\).

They are dependent.

They cannot represent vectors such as:

\[
(0,1).
\]

Even for vectors they can represent, coefficients are not unique.

For:

\[
(4,0),
\]

you could use:

\[
4(1,0)+0(2,0)
\]

or:

\[
0(1,0)+2(2,0).
\]

So no unique coordinate conversion exists.

This is exactly why basis requires independence.

---

# 515.11 What if the "basis" does not span?

Take only:

\[
\{(1,0)\}
\]

for \(\mathbb R^2\).

It is independent but cannot represent:

\[
(0,1).
\]

So some vectors have no coordinate representation.

Again, not a valid basis for the whole space.

---

# 515.12 Basis change as solving equations

In 2D, suppose:

\[
\vec c_1=(c_{11},c_{21})
\]

and:

\[
\vec c_2=(c_{12},c_{22}).
\]

Given target vector:

\[
\vec v=(x,y),
\]

coordinates \((p,q)\) in basis \(C\) satisfy:

\[
p\vec c_1+q\vec c_2=\vec v.
\]

Component-wise:

\[
pc_{11}+qc_{12}=x
\]

\[
pc_{21}+qc_{22}=y.
\]

So basis conversion is fundamentally a small **system of linear equations**.

Phase 8 eventually teaches how to solve such systems robustly.

Matrices later package the basis vectors and these equations elegantly.

But conceptually:

\[
\boxed{
\text{change of basis}
=
\text{solve for new coefficients of the same vector}.
}
\]

---

# 515.13 Canonical C++ representation

Without yet introducing a full matrix library:

```cpp
struct Vec2 {
    double x;
    double y;
};

struct Basis2 {
    Vec2 b1;
    Vec2 b2;
};
```

Reconstruction:

```cpp
Vec2 fromBasisCoordinates(
    const Basis2& basis,
    Vec2 coordinates) noexcept
{
    const double a = coordinates.x;
    const double b = coordinates.y;

    return {
        a * basis.b1.x + b * basis.b2.x,
        a * basis.b1.y + b * basis.b2.y
    };
}
```

To resolve a vector into a general 2D basis, solve:

\[
a b_{1x}+b b_{2x}=v_x
\]

\[
a b_{1y}+b b_{2y}=v_y.
\]

For the 2D case, eliminating variables gives the denominator:

\[
D
=
b_{1x}b_{2y}
-
b_{2x}b_{1y}.
\]

Then:

\[
a
=
\frac
{v_xb_{2y}-b_{2x}v_y}
{D}
\]

and:

\[
b
=
\frac
{b_{1x}v_y-v_xb_{1y}}
{D}.
\]

So:

```cpp
Vec2 toBasisCoordinates(
    const Basis2& basis,
    Vec2 v)
{
    const double D =
        basis.b1.x * basis.b2.y
      - basis.b2.x * basis.b1.y;

    if (std::abs(D) < 1e-12) {
        throw std::runtime_error("Basis is singular or nearly singular");
    }

    const double a =
        (v.x * basis.b2.y - basis.b2.x * v.y) / D;

    const double b =
        (basis.b1.x * v.y - v.x * basis.b1.y) / D;

    return {a, b};
}
```

Do **not** memorize that formula as the essence of basis conversion.

The essence is:

\[
a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2=\vec v.
\]

The formula is merely one algebraic solution of that equation.

Later matrices and Gaussian elimination provide the general machinery.

---

# 515.14 Why the denominator matters

The denominator

\[
D
=
b_{1x}b_{2y}
-
b_{2x}b_{1y}
\]

becomes zero exactly when the two 2D vectors are linearly dependent.

Example:

\[
\vec b_1=(1,2)
\]

and:

\[
\vec b_2=(2,4).
\]

Then:

\[
D
=
1\cdot4-2\cdot2
=
4-4
=
0.
\]

So the coordinate-solving equations do not have a unique solution.

That connects three ideas:

\[
\boxed{
\text{basis}
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{independence}
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{unique coordinate solve}
}
\]

In Part 626 you will recognize \(D\) as the 2D determinant.

---

# 515.15 Near-dependent bases and numerical instability

Suppose:

\[
\vec b_1=(1,0)
\]

and:

\[
\vec b_2=(1,10^{-10}).
\]

Mathematically they are independent.

Therefore they form a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).

But:

\[
D=10^{-10}.
\]

The denominator is tiny.

That means small errors in the input coordinates can produce huge changes in solved coefficients.

This basis is mathematically valid but numerically poor.

Geometrically, its axes are almost parallel.

A good coordinate system should usually avoid such near-degeneracy.

This previews the idea of conditioning.

---

# 511–515: THE ENTIRE CHAIN

Start with generators:

\[
\vec v_1,\ldots,\vec v_k.
\]

Their span tells us everything they can produce.

But perhaps some vectors are redundant.

Test:

\[
a_1\vec v_1+\cdots+a_k\vec v_k=\vec0.
\]

If only the trivial coefficient solution exists, they are:

\[
\boxed{\text{linearly independent}}.
\]

If they are also able to span the entire space, they form a:

\[
\boxed{\text{basis}}.
\]

Every basis of a finite-dimensional space contains the same number of vectors.

That number is:

\[
\boxed{\dim V}.
\]

Given ordered basis:

\[
B=(\vec b_1,\ldots,\vec b_n),
\]

every vector has unique coordinates:

\[
[\vec v]_B
=
(c_1,\ldots,c_n)
\]

meaning:

\[
\vec v
=
c_1\vec b_1+\cdots+c_n\vec b_n.
\]

Pick another basis \(C\), and the same vector receives another tuple:

\[
[\vec v]_C.
\]

Converting between them is:

\[
\boxed{\text{change of basis}}.
\]

So:

```text
generators
   ↓
span
   ↓
ask whether generators are redundant
   ↓
linear independence
   ↓
independent + spanning
   ↓
basis
   ↓
number of basis vectors
   ↓
dimension
   ↓
coefficients relative to basis
   ↓
coordinates
   ↓
replace basis, preserve vector
   ↓
change of basis
```

---

# A COMPLETE WORKED EXAMPLE

Consider the plane:

\[
W=
\{
(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3
\mid
x+y-z=0
\}.
\]

From Part 510:

\[
z=x+y.
\]

Therefore:

\[
(x,y,z)
=
(x,y,x+y)
\]

which can be written:

\[
x(1,0,1)+y(0,1,1).
\]

Define:

\[
\vec b_1=(1,0,1),
\qquad
\vec b_2=(0,1,1).
\]

They span \(W\).

Now test independence:

\[
a\vec b_1+b\vec b_2=\vec0.
\]

Expand:

\[
a(1,0,1)+b(0,1,1)
=
(a,b,a+b).
\]

Set equal to:

\[
(0,0,0).
\]

Therefore:

\[
a=0
\]

and:

\[
b=0.
\]

So they are independent.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
B=(\vec b_1,\vec b_2)
}
\]

is a basis of \(W\).

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
\dim W=2.
}
\]

Now consider:

\[
\vec v=(3,4,7).
\]

Check the plane constraint:

\[
3+4-7=0.
\]

So \(\vec v\in W\).

Relative to basis \(B\):

\[
\vec v
=
3\vec b_1+4\vec b_2.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
[\vec v]_B=(3,4).
}
\]

Notice the transformation in representation:

```text
ambient ℝ³ coordinates:
(3,4,7)

intrinsic coordinates in W:
(3,4)
```

Same vector inside the subspace.

Different coordinate representation.

The plane is 2-dimensional even though it is embedded in three-dimensional ambient space.

That one example unifies Parts 508–515.

---

# ENGINE / GRAPHICS INTERPRETATION

Suppose an object's local frame is described by three independent directions:

\[
\vec r,\quad\vec u,\quad\vec f
\]

for right, up and forward.

If they span 3D space and are independent, they form a basis.

A local direction:

\[
(2,1,-4)_{\text{local}}
\]

means:

\[
2\vec r+1\vec u-4\vec f.
\]

That resulting geometric vector can then be expressed in world coordinates.

Changing local coordinates to world coordinates is fundamentally a basis-conversion problem.

Later matrices make this:

\[
\text{coordinate vector}
\rightarrow
\text{matrix multiply}
\rightarrow
\text{new coordinate vector}.
\]

But the matrix is not the underlying idea.

The underlying idea is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{same vector, different basis coefficients}.
}
\]

---

# NUMERICAL REALITY

Mathematically, basis vectors are either independent or dependent.

Computationally, you often encounter a third practical category:

\[
\text{nearly dependent}.
\]

Suppose:

\[
\vec b_1=(1,0,0)
\]

\[
\vec b_2=(0,1,0)
\]

\[
\vec b_3=(1,1,10^{-9}).
\]

Mathematically, the third vector has a tiny but nonzero out-of-plane component, so all three are independent.

But resolving arbitrary vectors into that basis may require large cancelling coefficients.

Floating-point noise can be amplified drastically.

So production numerical code does not merely ask:

> Is the determinant exactly zero?

It asks questions about:

- scale,
- relative tolerance,
- condition number,
- singular values,
- numerical rank.

Those advanced concepts come later, but this is why they exist.

---

# INTERVIEW ATTACK TREE

**Level 1 — What is linear independence?**

A set is linearly independent if:

\[
a_1\vec v_1+\cdots+a_k\vec v_k=\vec0
\]

implies:

\[
a_1=\cdots=a_k=0.
\]

**Level 2 — Why does a nontrivial zero combination imply redundancy?**

Because if \(a_j\neq0\), we can solve:

\[
\vec v_j
=
-\sum_{i\neq j}\frac{a_i}{a_j}\vec v_i,
\]

so \(\vec v_j\) lies in the span of the others.

**Level 3 — What is a basis?**

An independent spanning set.

**Level 4 — Why does a basis give unique coordinates?**

Spanning guarantees existence of coefficients; independence guarantees uniqueness.

**Level 5 — What is dimension?**

The number of vectors in any basis of a finite-dimensional vector space.

**Level 6 — Can a 2D subspace live in \(\mathbb R^3\)?**

Yes. Example:

\[
\{(x,y,0)\}.
\]

Its ambient representation uses three coordinates, but a basis has two vectors, so its intrinsic dimension is two.

**Level 7 — What exactly are coordinates?**

Coefficients of a vector's unique linear combination with respect to an ordered basis.

**Level 8 — What is change of basis?**

Replacing one coordinate representation with another while keeping the underlying vector fixed.

**Level 9 — Why must a basis change be invertible?**

Because each basis gives a one-to-one coordinate representation of the same space.

**Level 10 — Why can a mathematically valid basis still be bad numerically?**

If the basis vectors are nearly dependent, small input errors can require large changes in coefficients. The representation is ill-conditioned.

a_1\vec v_1+\cdots+a_k\vec v_k=\vec0
\]

with a nonzero coefficient means one vector is reconstructible from the others.

You should be able to prove that independent generators give unique coefficients.

You should be able to distinguish immediately between:

\quad

You should take a basis such as:

B=

and manually find:

\]

Then reverse the process.

Most importantly, you should be able to state the full conceptual separation:

\[
\boxed{
\text{vector}
\neq
\text{basis}
\neq
\text{coordinates}
}
\]

The vector is the mathematical/geometric object.

The basis is the reference system used to describe it.

The coordinates are the coefficients relative to that basis.

Changing the basis changes the coordinates, **not necessarily the vector**.

# PART 571 — AFFINE COMBINATIONS VERSUS LINEAR COMBINATIONS

This distinction is fundamental because vectors and points do **not** obey exactly the same algebra.

---

## 571.1 Linear combination

Given vectors:

\[
v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n
\]

and arbitrary scalars:

\[
a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n,
\]

a linear combination is:

\[
\boxed{
a_1v_1+a_2v_2+\cdots+a_nv_n.
}
\]

There is **no restriction** on:

\[
a_1+\cdots+a_n.
\]

Example:

\[
v_1=(1,0),
\qquad
v_2=(0,1).
\]

Then:

\[
3v_1-7v_2
=
(3,-7).
\]

Perfectly valid.

Linear combinations belong naturally to vector spaces.

---

# 571.2 Why vectors allow this

Vectors are free displacements.

If:

\[
v
\]

is a displacement, then:

\[
2v
\]

means twice the displacement.

And:

\[
-v
\]

means the opposite displacement.

The zero vector exists naturally:

\[
0v=0.
\]

So unrestricted scaling makes sense.

---

# 571.3 Points are different

Suppose:

\[
A,B
\]

are points.

What does:

\[
2A
\]

mean geometrically?

Without choosing an origin, nothing intrinsic.

Likewise:

\[
A+B
\]

has no natural meaning as a point in ordinary affine geometry.

But this does make sense:

\[
B-A.
\]

Why?

Point minus point produces a displacement vector.

And:

\[
A+v
\]

makes sense:

point plus displacement gives point.

That was Parts 521–522.

---

# 571.4 Affine combination

An affine combination of points:

\[
P_1,\ldots,P_n
\]

has form:

\[
\boxed{
a_1P_1+\cdots+a_nP_n
}
\]

subject to:

\[
\boxed{
a_1+\cdots+a_n=1.
}
\]

The sum-to-one constraint is what makes the result independent of the arbitrary origin.

---

# 571.5 Derive translation invariance

Translate all points by \(t\):

\[
P_i'=P_i+t.
\]

Then:

\[
\sum_i a_iP_i'
=
\sum_i a_i(P_i+t).
\]

Expand:

\[
=
\sum_i a_iP_i+
\left(
\sum_i a_i
\right)t.
\]

If:

\[
\sum_i a_i=1,
\]

then:

\[
=
\sum_i a_iP_i+t.
\]

Exactly what a point should do under translation.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{sum of weights}=1
}
\]

is the mathematical condition that makes the combination affine.

---

# 571.6 If weights sum to zero

Something interesting happens.

Suppose:

\[
\sum_i a_i=0.
\]

Then under translation:

\[
\sum_i a_i(P_i+t)
=
\sum_i a_iP_i.
\]

The translation disappears.

So a weighted point combination whose coefficients sum to zero behaves like a **vector**, not a point.

Example:

\[
B-A.
\]

Weights:

\[
(-1,+1).
\]

Sum:

\[
0.
\]

And indeed:

\[
B-A
\]

is a displacement vector.

This is a deep unification:

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_i=1
\Rightarrow
\text{point-like affine result}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_i=0
\Rightarrow
\text{vector-like translation-invariant result}.
}
\]

---

# 571.7 Midpoint as affine combination

Midpoint:

\[
M=\frac12A+\frac12B.
\]

Weights sum:

\[
\frac12+\frac12=1.
\]

So midpoint is affine.

Translate A and B together and M translates with them.

---

# 571.8 Extrapolation is still affine

Consider:

\[
P=2B-A.
\]

Weights:

\[
-1+2=1.
\]

So this is still an affine combination.

Geometrically:

```text
A -------- B -------- P
```

P lies beyond B.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{affine does not imply inside}.
}
\]

Negative weights are allowed.

That distinction becomes Part 572.

---

# 571.9 Linear vs affine in one sentence

Linear combination:

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_iv_i
}
\]

with arbitrary coefficients.

Affine combination:

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_iP_i,
\qquad
\sum a_i=1.
}
\]

Linear combination answers:

> What vector can I construct from these vectors?

Affine combination answers:

> What point can I construct relative to these points without caring where the global origin is?

---

# 571.10 C++ semantic design

This is why a strong math API might distinguish:

```cpp
struct Point3;
struct Vec3;
```

and permit:

```cpp
Point3 + Vec3 -> Point3
Point3 - Point3 -> Vec3
Vec3 + Vec3   -> Vec3
```

while deliberately not defining arbitrary:

```cpp
Point3 + Point3
```

except through named operations such as:

```cpp
midpoint(a, b)
```

or barycentric interpolation.

The type system can protect affine semantics.

---

# PART 572 — CONVEX COMBINATIONS

An affine combination allows negative coefficients.

A **convex combination** adds one more restriction:

\[
\boxed{
a_i\ge0.
}
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\sum_i a_iP_i,
\qquad
a_i\ge0,
\qquad
\sum_i a_i=1.
}
\]

---

# 572.1 Why nonnegative matters

Take two points:

\[
A,B.
\]

Any affine combination is:

\[
P=(1-t)A+tB.
\]

Because weights sum to one.

If:

\[
0\le t\le1,
\]

both weights are nonnegative.

Then P lies on the line segment between A and B.

If:

\[
t>1,
\]

then:

\[
1-t<0.
\]

P moves beyond B.

If:

\[
t<0,
\]

P moves beyond A.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{nonnegative affine weights keep you inside the endpoints}.
}
\]

---

# 572.2 Triangle case

For triangle:

\[
A,B,C,
\]

a convex combination is:

\[
P=\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C
\]

where:

\[
\alpha,\beta,\gamma\ge0
\]

and:

\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1.
\]

Exactly the barycentric inside-triangle condition from Part 568.

Thus barycentric coordinates inside a triangle are convex weights.

---

# 572.3 Convex versus affine

Example:

\[
P=-A+B+C.
\]

Weights:

\[
-1+1+1=1.
\]

So it is affine.

But:

\[
-1<0.
\]

Therefore not convex.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{every convex combination is affine}
}
\]

but:

\[
\boxed{
\text{not every affine combination is convex}.
}
\]

---

# 572.4 Physical intuition: mixing

Suppose three paints have colors:

\[
C_1,C_2,C_3.
\]

You mix:

\[
20\%,30\%,50\%.
\]

Weights:

\[
0.2,0.3,0.5
\]

sum to one and are nonnegative.

Result:

\[
C=0.2C_1+0.3C_2+0.5C_3.
\]

That is a convex combination.

Negative paint quantity would not make physical sense.

This "weighted average" intuition is excellent for convex combinations.

---

# 572.5 Convex combinations are weighted averages

Because weights are nonnegative and sum to 1, no term can push the result past all inputs in an affine sense.

For real scalars:

\[
x=\sum_i a_ix_i
\]

satisfies:

\[
\min_i x_i
\le x\le
\max_i x_i.
\]

For vectors/points, the analogous geometric statement is that the result stays within the convex region generated by the inputs.

That leads directly to convex sets.

---

# PART 573 — CONVEX SETS

A set \(C\) is convex if taking any two points inside it and connecting them with a straight segment never leaves the set.

Formal definition:

\[
\boxed{
x,y\in C,\quad
t\in[0,1]
\Rightarrow
(1-t)x+ty\in C.
}
\]

That expression is exactly a two-point convex combination.

---

# 573.1 Circle disk versus circle boundary

Be careful.

A **filled disk**:

```text
   *****
 *********
***********
***********
 *********
   *****
```

is convex.

Take any two points inside. The connecting line segment remains inside.

But the **circle boundary alone** is not convex.

Take opposite boundary points:

```text
A ●-----------● B
```

The line segment between them runs through the interior, which is not part of the boundary-only set.

Therefore the set fails the definition.

---

# 573.2 Rectangle

A filled rectangle is convex.

Any line segment connecting two interior points stays inside.

---

# 573.3 Crescent / concave polygon

Consider:

```text
********
*      *
*   ****
*   *
*   ****
*      *
********
```

Take points on opposite sides of an indentation.

The segment can pass outside the shape.

Therefore the set is nonconvex.

---

# 573.4 Why engines love convex objects

Convex geometry has strong properties.

For example:

- a line intersects a convex set in at most one continuous interval;
- local extrema are easier to reason about;
- separating directions behave cleanly;
- support points are meaningful;
- collision algorithms such as GJK operate naturally on convex shapes.

Nonconvex shapes are often decomposed into convex pieces because convex collision questions are dramatically easier.

---

# 573.5 Convexity can be defined using any finite convex combination

The two-point definition implies a stronger statement.

If:

\[
x_1,\ldots,x_n\in C
\]

and:

\[
a_i\ge0,
\qquad
\sum_i a_i=1,
\]

then:

\[
\boxed{
\sum_i a_ix_i\in C.
}
\]

We can prove this recursively.

For three points:

\[
a+b+c=1.
\]

Assume:

\[
a+b>0.
\]

Define:

\[
q=
\frac{a}{a+b}x+
\frac{b}{a+b}y.
\]

Those normalized weights sum to one, so:

\[
q\in C.
\]

Then:

\[
ax+by+cz
=
(a+b)q+cz.
\]

Since:

\[
(a+b)+c=1,
\]

this is a convex combination of \(q\) and \(z\).

Therefore it lies in C.

So convex sets contain all convex mixtures of their points.

---

# 573.6 Convexity is affine-invariant

Apply an affine transform:

\[
F(x)=Lx+t.
\]

Take points:

\[
x,y\in C.
\]

Their transformed convex combination:

\[
F((1-s)x+sy).
\]

Because F is affine:

\[
=
(1-s)F(x)+sF(y).
\]

Therefore affine transformations preserve convexity.

So:

- translation;
- rotation;
- scale;
- shear;
- reflection

all preserve convexity as long as the affine transform is applied consistently.

A cube can become a sheared parallelepiped and remain convex.

---

# PART 574 — CONVEX HULL INTUITION

Suppose you have arbitrary points:

```text
       ●

 ●          ●

       ●

   ●             ●
```

You want the **smallest convex set containing all of them**.

That is the convex hull.

---

# 574.1 Rubber-band intuition

Hammer nails into a board at the sample points.

Stretch a rubber band around all nails.

Release it.

The rubber band contracts until it touches the outermost nails.

The enclosed region is the convex hull.

```text
        ●
      /   \
   ●       ●
   |   ●   |
   ●       ●
      \   /
        ●
```

Interior points do not affect the hull boundary.

---

# 574.2 Formal definition through convex combinations

Given points:

\[
p_1,\ldots,p_n,
\]

their convex hull is:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{conv}\{p_i\}
=
\left\{
\sum_i a_ip_i
\mid
a_i\ge0,\;
\sum_i a_i=1
\right\}.
}
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{convex hull = set of every possible convex combination of the input points}.
}
\]

This connects directly to Parts 572–573.

---

# 574.3 Why it is the smallest convex set

Let H be all convex combinations of the points.

First, every original point belongs to H because choose one weight 1 and the rest 0.

Second, H is convex because a convex combination of convex combinations is again a convex combination.

Third, any convex set containing all original points must contain every convex combination of those points.

Therefore it must contain H.

So H is the smallest possible convex container.

---

# 574.4 Why hulls matter in engines

Suppose a complicated model:

```text
spiky robot mesh
thousands of triangles
```

needs broad collision approximation.

A convex hull can produce a simpler outer shell.

It loses concavities but preserves containment.

This can drastically simplify collision queries.

Other uses include:

- collision proxies;
- mesh simplification;
- bounding geometry;
- computational geometry;
- navigation;
- separating-axis reasoning.

---

# 574.5 Hull vertices versus interior points

Suppose point:

\[
P
\]

can be written as a convex combination of other points.

Then P does not need to be a hull vertex.

Example:

\[
P=\frac13A+\frac13B+\frac13C.
\]

P lies inside triangle ABC.

It cannot push the convex hull outward.

This is why hull algorithms throw away most interior data.

---

# PART 575 — MINKOWSKI SUM INTUITION

Now we move from convex geometry to one of the central constructions in collision detection.

Given two sets:

\[
A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n,
\]

their Minkowski sum is:

\[
\boxed{
A+B
=
\{a+b\mid a\in A,\;b\in B\}.
}
\]

Every point of A is added to every point of B.

---

# 575.1 Point + shape intuition

Let:

\[
A=\{p\}
\]

contain a single point.

Then:

\[
A+B
=
p+B.
\]

This simply translates B by p.

So Minkowski sum generalizes translation from a single offset to an entire set of offsets.

---

# 575.2 Segment + segment

Take horizontal segment:

\[
A=[-1,1]\times\{0\}.
\]

Take vertical segment:

\[
B=\{0\}\times[-1,1].
\]

Every point:

\[
(x,0)\in A
\]

plus every:

\[
(0,y)\in B
\]

produces:

\[
(x,y)
\]

with:

\[
-1\le x\le1,
\qquad
-1\le y\le1.
\]

Therefore their Minkowski sum is a square.

So:

```text
horizontal segment
+
vertical segment
=
rectangle
```

Set addition can create a higher-dimensional shape.

---

# 575.3 Shape sweeping intuition

Suppose A represents all positions of an object's center and B represents the shape around that center.

Then:

\[
A+B
\]

represents all space occupied while B's reference point travels through A.

Example:

A = line segment path.

B = disk.

Then:

\[
A+B
\]

is a capsule-like swept region:

```text
   ___________
 /             \
|               |
 \_____________/
```

This makes Minkowski sums extremely useful for:

- swept volumes;
- configuration spaces;
- motion planning;
- collision expansion.

---

# 575.4 Disk + polygon

If B is a disk of radius r, then:

\[
A+B
\]

is conceptually A expanded outward by radius r.

Corners become rounded.

This appears in robot path planning:

Instead of moving a circular robot around obstacles, you can enlarge obstacles by the robot radius and treat the robot as a point.

That is a configuration-space trick.

---

# 575.5 Minkowski sums preserve convexity

Suppose A and B are convex.

Take:

\[
x=a_1+b_1
\]

and:

\[
y=a_2+b_2
\]

from \(A+B\).

For:

\[
t\in[0,1],
\]

consider:

\[
(1-t)x+ty.
\]

Substitute:

\[
=
(1-t)(a_1+b_1)
+
t(a_2+b_2).
\]

Group:

\[
=
[(1-t)a_1+ta_2]
+
[(1-t)b_1+tb_2].
\]

Because A is convex:

\[
(1-t)a_1+ta_2\in A.
\]

Because B is convex:

\[
(1-t)b_1+tb_2\in B.
\]

Thus the sum belongs to:

\[
A+B.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
A,B\text{ convex}
\Rightarrow
A+B\text{ convex}.
}
\]

This fact is crucial for GJK-style collision algorithms.

---

# 575.6 Complexity if done naively for point sets

Suppose polygon A has:

\[
m
\]

vertices and B has:

\[
n.
\]

Naively adding every pair creates:

\[
mn
\]

candidate points:

\[
a_i+b_j.
\]

Then one could compute their convex hull.

That is often wasteful.

For convex polygons arranged in angular order, Minkowski sums can be generated much more efficiently by merging edge directions.

That algorithm belongs later; current concern is the geometric operation itself.

---

# PART 576 — MINKOWSKI DIFFERENCE INTUITION

The collision version of Minkowski difference is usually:

\[
\boxed{
A-B
=
\{a-b\mid a\in A,\;b\in B\}.
}
\]

This is equivalent to:

\[
\boxed{
A+(-B)
}
\]

where:

\[
-B=\{-b\mid b\in B\}.
\]

So Minkowski difference means:

```text
reflect B through origin
then Minkowski-add it to A
```

---

# 576.1 Why collision detection loves this

Suppose shapes A and B intersect.

Then there exists some point:

\[
p
\]

such that:

\[
p\in A
\]

and:

\[
p\in B.
\]

Therefore choose:

\[
a=p,
\qquad
b=p.
\]

Then:

\[
a-b=0.
\]

Thus:

\[
0\in A-B.
\]

Conversely, if:

\[
0\in A-B,
\]

then there exist:

\[
a\in A,\quad b\in B
\]

such that:

\[
a-b=0.
\]

Therefore:

\[
a=b.
\]

So the shapes share a point.

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
A\cap B\neq\emptyset
\iff
0\in A-B.
}
\]

That is a spectacular transformation.

We changed:

> Do two complicated shapes overlap?

into:

> Does one derived shape contain the origin?

That is the core insight behind GJK collision detection.

---

# 576.2 Simple 1D example

Let:

\[
A=[2,4]
\]

and:

\[
B=[3,5].
\]

Then:

\[
A-B
\]

contains values:

\[
a-b.
\]

Minimum:

\[
2-5=-3.
\]

Maximum:

\[
4-3=1.
\]

So:

\[
A-B=[-3,1].
\]

It contains:

\[
0.
\]

Therefore A and B overlap.

Correct.

---

# 576.3 Non-overlap case

Let:

\[
A=[0,1]
\]

and:

\[
B=[3,4].
\]

Then:

\[
A-B
=
[-4,-2].
\]

Zero is not inside.

Thus shapes do not overlap.

---

# 576.4 Why relative position appears naturally

A difference:

\[
a-b
\]

is a relative displacement between a point of B and a point of A.

So Minkowski difference converts pairwise relative geometry into one origin-centered shape.

The origin represents:

\[
a=b.
\]

That is exactly collision/contact.

---

# 576.5 Terminology warning

Some mathematical morphology literature uses "Minkowski difference" or erosion-related notation differently.

In collision detection, when engineers say Minkowski difference for GJK, they usually mean:

\[
\boxed{
A+(-B)
=
\{a-b\}.
}
\]

Always inspect the definition in a specific source rather than trusting the name alone.

---

# PART 577 — SUPPORT FUNCTIONS OF CONVEX SHAPES

Now imagine a convex shape.

Pick some direction:

\[
d.
\]

Ask:

> Which point of the shape lies farthest in direction d?

That operation is the **support mapping**.

---

# 577.1 Support function

For set C:

\[
\boxed{
h_C(d)
=
\max_{x\in C}
d\cdot x.
}
\]

The result:

\[
h_C(d)
\]

is a scalar.

It tells how far C extends in direction d, measured as a dot-product coordinate.

A **support point** is some:

\[
x^*
\]

where that maximum is attained:

\[
\boxed{
x^*\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C}
d\cdot x.
}
\]

There may be more than one support point.

---

# 577.2 Why dot product selects "farthest"

If d is unit:

\[
d\cdot x
\]

is the signed scalar projection of x onto d.

So maximizing it literally means:

> choose the point whose projection along d is largest.

If d is not unit, the ordering is unchanged for positive scaling.

Thus support direction does not need normalization merely to find the maximizing point.

---

# 577.3 Square example

Square:

\[
[-1,1]^2.
\]

Take:

\[
d=(1,0).
\]

Maximize:

\[
d\cdot(x,y)=x.
\]

Maximum is:

\[
1.
\]

Any point on right edge:

\[
(1,y)
\]

is a support point.

So support points need not be unique.

---

# 577.4 Diagonal direction

Take:

\[
d=(1,1).
\]

Dot at square corners:

\[
(-1,-1)\rightarrow -2,
\]

\[
(1,-1)\rightarrow0,
\]

\[
(-1,1)\rightarrow0,
\]

\[
(1,1)\rightarrow2.
\]

So support point:

\[
\boxed{(1,1)}.
\]

---

# 577.5 Sphere support point

Sphere centered at c, radius r.

We want maximize:

\[
d\cdot x.
\]

Every sphere point can be written:

\[
x=c+ru
\]

where:

\[
\|u\|=1.
\]

Then:

\[
d\cdot x
=
d\cdot c+r(d\cdot u).
\]

Maximum of:

\[
d\cdot u
\]

for unit u occurs when:

\[
u=\frac d{\|d\|}.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
support_C(d)
=
c+r\frac d{\|d\|}
}
\]

for nonzero d.

And scalar support value:

\[
\boxed{
h_C(d)
=
d\cdot c+r\|d\|.
}
\]

---

# 577.6 Box support point

For axis-aligned box with min/max coordinates, maximize:

\[
d_xx+d_yy+d_zz.
\]

Each coordinate can be chosen independently.

If:

\[
d_x>0,
\]

choose maximum X.

If:

\[
d_x<0,
\]

choose minimum X.

Thus support point can be found with a few sign tests.

No iteration over the entire surface is needed.

---

# 577.7 Convex hull support

If C is the convex hull of vertices:

\[
v_1,\ldots,v_n,
\]

the maximum linear functional occurs at an extreme point.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
h_C(d)
=
\max_i d\cdot v_i.
}
\]

So for a convex polygon/polyhedron represented by vertices, a simple support implementation scans vertices.

Complexity:

\[
O(n)
\]

per query.

More specialized representations can accelerate this.

---

# 577.8 The crucial Minkowski support identity

For:

\[
C=A+B,
\]

compute:

\[
h_C(d).
\]

By definition:

\[
h_{A+B}(d)
=
\max_{a\in A,b\in B}
d\cdot(a+b).
\]

Distribute:

\[
=
\max_{a,b}
[d\cdot a+d\cdot b].
\]

Because a and b are independent choices:

\[
=
\max_a d\cdot a
+
\max_b d\cdot b.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
h_{A+B}(d)
=
h_A(d)+h_B(d).
}
\]

And support points can be combined:

\[
\boxed{
support_{A+B}(d)
=
support_A(d)
+
support_B(d)
}
\]

choosing compatible maximizers.

---

# 577.9 Minkowski difference support mapping

Recall:

\[
A-B=A+(-B).
\]

Support of reflected B:

\[
support_{-B}(d)
=
-support_B(-d).
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
support_{A-B}(d)
=
support_A(d)
-
support_B(-d).
}
\]

This formula is one of the core reasons GJK does **not need to explicitly construct the Minkowski difference**.

You ask A and B independently for support points.

Then subtract.

That can be dramatically cheaper than constructing a new polyhedron.

---

# 577.10 GJK preview

GJK conceptually asks whether:

\[
0\in A-B.
\]

But instead of building:

\[
A-B
\]

explicitly, it repeatedly queries support points in strategically chosen directions.

The support function lets the algorithm explore the boundary of the Minkowski difference on demand.

That is a major engine connection.

# PART 578 — HOMOGENEOUS COORDINATES AS PROJECTIVE REPRESENTATIVES

Now we switch domains.

This Part begins one of the most important representation tricks in graphics.

Suppose we have ordinary 3D point:

\[
p=(x,y,z).
\]

Homogeneous coordinates represent it with four numbers:

\[
\boxed{
(X,Y,Z,W).
}
\]

But these four numbers are **not simply a normal 4D point**.

They are a representative of a projective equivalence class.

---

# 578.1 Multiple quadruples represent the same point

For any nonzero scalar:

\[
\lambda\neq0,
\]

the homogeneous tuples:

\[
(X,Y,Z,W)
\]

and:

\[
(\lambda X,\lambda Y,\lambda Z,\lambda W)
\]

represent the same projective point.

We write conceptually:

\[
\boxed{
(X,Y,Z,W)
\sim
(\lambda X,\lambda Y,\lambda Z,\lambda W).
}
\]

Example:

\[
(2,4,6,2)
\]

and:

\[
(1,2,3,1)
\]

represent the same Euclidean point.

Why?

Divide by W.

---

# 578.2 Dehomogenization

If:

\[
W\neq0,
\]

recover ordinary coordinates:

\[
\boxed{
x=\frac XW,
\qquad
y=\frac YW,
\qquad
z=\frac ZW.
}
\]

For:

\[
(2,4,6,2),
\]

we get:

\[
(1,2,3).
\]

For:

\[
(10,20,30,10),
\]

same:

\[
(1,2,3).
\]

So homogeneous coordinates contain scale redundancy.

---

# 578.3 Why deliberately introduce redundancy?

Because that redundancy makes transformations that were awkward in ordinary coordinates become expressible uniformly in a higher-dimensional representation.

Most importantly:

- translation;
- perspective/projective operations;
- points at infinity;
- projective intersections.

The later matrix Parts will exploit this heavily.

For now, understand the representation itself.

---

# 578.4 Canonical representative

For an ordinary Euclidean point:

\[
p=(x,y,z),
\]

the simplest homogeneous representative is:

\[
\boxed{
(x,y,z,1).
}
\]

But it is not the only one.

Equivalent:

\[
(2x,2y,2z,2),
\]

\[
(-3x,-3y,-3z,-3),
\]

etc.

As long as W is nonzero and the scale is shared across all four components.

---

# 578.5 Homogeneous coordinates as rays through a higher-dimensional origin

This gives strong intuition.

Consider 2D Euclidean point:

\[
(x,y).
\]

Represent it in 3D homogeneous space:

\[
(x,y,1).
\]

All equivalent representatives lie on the line:

\[
\lambda(x,y,1).
\]

So one projective point corresponds to a **line through the origin** in homogeneous space.

Example:

```text
          • (2x,2y,2)
         /
        • (x,y,1)
       /
      /
     O
```

All nonzero points on that line represent the same projective point.

That's why homogeneous coordinates are called **representatives** rather than ordinary unique coordinates.

---

# 578.6 Why the plane W=1 is special

Ordinary Euclidean points can be visualized as intersections of homogeneous rays with:

\[
W=1.
\]

Given representative:

\[
(X,Y,Z,W),
\]

move along the same homogeneous ray until W becomes 1.

Scale by:

\[
\frac1W.
\]

Then:

\[
\left(
\frac XW,
\frac YW,
\frac ZW,
1
\right).
\]

That is exactly dehomogenization.

---

# 578.7 What happens at W=0?

You cannot divide by zero.

So:

\[
(X,Y,Z,0)
\]

does not represent a finite Euclidean point.

Instead these represent **directions / points at infinity** in projective geometry.

That is exactly Part 579.

---

# 578.8 Projective representatives and numeric scale

Because:

\[
H\sim\lambda H,
\]

a homogeneous vector can grow or shrink in magnitude without changing the represented projective point.

This means comparing raw homogeneous tuples componentwise is often wrong.

For example:

\[
(1,2,3,1)
\]

and:

\[
(2,4,6,2)
\]

are not numerically equal as `Vec4`s but represent the same projective point.

This semantic distinction matters later when debugging clip-space/projective code.

---

# PART 579 — POINTS AND DIRECTIONS THROUGH HOMOGENEOUS \(w\)

Now we connect homogeneous coordinates to the point/vector distinction from Parts 521–524.

This is one of the nicest pieces of graphics mathematics.

---

# 579.1 Point

An ordinary Euclidean point:

\[
P=(x,y,z)
\]

is represented canonically as:

\[
\boxed{
P_h=(x,y,z,1).
}
\]

Direction vector:

\[
V=(v_x,v_y,v_z)
\]

is represented as:

\[
\boxed{
V_h=(v_x,v_y,v_z,0).
}
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
w=1
\Rightarrow
\text{point}
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
w=0
\Rightarrow
\text{direction}
}
\]

for canonical affine homogeneous representatives.

But there is a deeper reason than "that's the convention."

---

# 579.2 Translation is the key

A point should respond to translation:

\[
P' = P+t.
\]

A direction should not:

\[
V'=V.
\]

Homogeneous \(w\) lets one representation distinguish these two behaviors.

Conceptually define affine transformation:

\[
x\mapsto Ax+t.
\]

For homogeneous pair:

\[
(x,w),
\]

the corresponding rule can be written:

\[
\boxed{
(x,w)
\mapsto
(Ax+wt,\;w).
}
\]

Look what happens.

For a point:

\[
w=1.
\]

Then:

\[
Ax+1t
=
Ax+t.
\]

Translation applies.

For a direction:

\[
w=0.
\]

Then:

\[
Ax+0t
=
Ax.
\]

Translation disappears.

That is the reason \(w\) works.

---

# 579.3 This reproduces affine point/vector algebra

Take two homogeneous points:

\[
P_h=(P,1),
\]

\[
Q_h=(Q,1).
\]

Subtract:

\[
Q_h-P_h
=
(Q-P,0).
\]

The result has:

\[
w=0.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{point} - \text{point}
=
\text{direction}.
}
\]

Exactly as affine geometry demanded.

---

# 579.4 Point + direction

\[
(P,1)+(V,0)
=
(P+V,1).
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{point}+\text{direction}
=
\text{point}.
}
\]

Again perfect.

---

# 579.5 Direction + direction

\[
(V,0)+(W,0)
=
(V+W,0).
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{direction}+\text{direction}
=
\text{direction}.
}
\]

Again correct.

---

# 579.6 Point + point exposes why affine semantics matter

\[
(P,1)+(Q,1)
=
(P+Q,2).
\]

This has:

\[
w=2.
\]

If you dehomogenize:

\[
\left(
\frac{P+Q}{2},1
\right),
\]

you get the midpoint.

This is interesting, but it does **not** mean ordinary point addition should suddenly be interpreted as a fundamental geometric operation.

Homogeneous scale equivalence changed the semantics.

You must know whether you're doing vector arithmetic on representatives or meaningful affine/projective operations.

---

# 579.7 Difference between w=0 and "the zero vector"

A direction:

\[
(v_x,v_y,v_z,0)
\]

can be nonzero.

The w component being zero does not mean the whole homogeneous vector is zero.

Example:

\[
(1,0,0,0)
\]

means the X direction / a projective point at infinity along X.

The actual all-zero homogeneous vector:

\[
(0,0,0,0)
\]

is invalid as a projective representative because scaling it never produces a meaningful nonzero representative.

Projective homogeneous coordinates exclude the all-zero tuple.

---

# 579.8 Why directions are points at infinity

Take ordinary point:

\[
P_\lambda
=
(\lambda v_x,\lambda v_y,\lambda v_z).
\]

Its homogeneous form:

\[
(\lambda v_x,\lambda v_y,\lambda v_z,1).
\]

Scale the homogeneous representative by:

\[
\frac1\lambda:
\]

\[
(v_x,v_y,v_z,1/\lambda).
\]

Now let:

\[
\lambda\rightarrow\infty.
\]

Then:

\[
1/\lambda\rightarrow0.
\]

So the limiting projective representative is:

\[
\boxed{
(v_x,v_y,v_z,0).
}
\]

That is why \(w=0\) is interpreted as a point infinitely far away in direction v.

This is not merely poetic terminology.

It falls naturally out of homogeneous scaling.

---

# 579.9 Parallel lines and points at infinity

In Euclidean geometry, parallel lines never meet.

Projective geometry extends the plane/space so parallel lines meet at a point at infinity corresponding to their common direction.

For example, railway tracks:

```text
\                    /
 \                  /
  \                /
   \              /
    \            /
     \          /
      \        /
       \      /
        \    /
         \  /
```

In perspective vision they appear to meet at a **vanishing point**.

Projective geometry treats that vanishing direction as a legitimate projective point.

Homogeneous \(w=0\) is the algebraic representation of that idea.

---

# 579.10 Why graphics needs this distinction

Later, transformations use one unified representation:

```cpp
Vec4 point     {x, y, z, 1};
Vec4 direction {x, y, z, 0};
```

Then translation naturally affects the first but not the second.

That becomes especially valuable when using one transformation representation for:

- positions;
- directions;
- tangent vectors;
- camera coordinates;
- projective operations.

However, surface normals later require additional care because normals are not ordinary direction vectors under general affine transformations. That is exactly why Part 582 exists.

---

# 579.11 C++ representation

Conceptually:

```cpp
struct HPoint3 {
    double x;
    double y;
    double z;
    double w;
};

[[nodiscard]]
HPoint3 fromPoint(Point3 p)
{
    return {p.x, p.y, p.z, 1.0};
}

[[nodiscard]]
HPoint3 fromDirection(Vec3 v)
{
    return {v.x, v.y, v.z, 0.0};
}
```

But a production API may prefer distinct semantic types instead of allowing arbitrary misuse of raw `Vec4`.

Why?

Because:

```cpp
Vec4
```

does not tell you whether:

- it is a homogeneous point;
- a direction;
- a color;
- a quaternion;
- arbitrary four-component data.

Same storage shape, different mathematics.

---

# 579.12 Dehomogenizing only points

If:

\[
w\neq0,
\]

you can produce Euclidean point:

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\frac{x}{w},
\frac{y}{w},
\frac{z}{w}
\right).
}
\]

If:

\[
w=0,
\]

that division is invalid.

So this code:

```cpp
Vec3 euclidean = {
    h.x / h.w,
    h.y / h.w,
    h.z / h.w
};
```

requires the explicit precondition:

\[
h.w\neq0.
\]

Later perspective pipelines depend heavily on exactly when this division is valid and meaningful.

---

# THE ENTIRE CONVEXITY BLOCK IN ONE ONGOING EXAMPLE

Suppose a game has a player represented by a convex capsule and a wall represented by a convex box.

## Affine combination

The player's center can be described relative to reference points without depending on the world origin.

## Convex combination

Any convex mixture of points inside the capsule remains inside the capsule.

## Convex set

The capsule is convex: segment between any two internal points remains inside.

## Convex hull

If we start with sample points from a coarse collision mesh, their convex hull forms the smallest convex shell containing them.

## Minkowski sum

Expand the wall by the player's collision shape.

Now instead of moving a fat player around the wall, conceptually move a point around an expanded obstacle.

## Minkowski difference

For two convex collision shapes A and B:

\[
A-B
\]

turns overlap into an origin-containment question:

\[
\boxed{
A\cap B\neq\emptyset
\iff
0\in A-B.
}
\]

## Support function

Instead of explicitly building:

\[
A-B,
\]

ask:

\[
support_A(d)-support_B(-d).
\]

That gives an extreme point of the Minkowski difference.

That chain is basically the mathematical foundation underneath GJK.

---

# THE ENTIRE HOMOGENEOUS BLOCK IN ONE ONGOING EXAMPLE

Suppose a sword model contains:

position:

\[
P=(2,1,5)
\]

and forward direction:

\[
F=(0,0,-1).
\]

Homogeneous form:

\[
P_h=(2,1,5,1)
\]

and:

\[
F_h=(0,0,-1,0).
\]

Move sword by:

\[
t=(10,0,0).
\]

Point should move:

\[
P'=(12,1,5).
\]

Direction should remain:

\[
F'=(0,0,-1).
\]

The homogeneous rule:

\[
(x,w)\mapsto(Ax+wt,w)
\]

automatically does this.

For point:

\[
w=1
\Rightarrow
+t.
\]

For direction:

\[
w=0
\Rightarrow
+0t.
\]

That one bit of affine information carried by \(w\) is why homogeneous coordinates are so powerful.

---

# DEEP CONNECTION: AFFINE WEIGHTS AND HOMOGENEOUS \(w\)

There is a beautiful relationship between Part 571 and Part 579.

Suppose homogeneous points:

\[
P_i=(p_i,1).
\]

Take weighted combination:

\[
\sum_i a_iP_i.
\]

Its resulting w component is:

\[
\boxed{
w=\sum_i a_i.
}
\]

Therefore:

### If weights sum to 1

\[
w=1.
\]

The result is point-like.

That is an affine combination.

### If weights sum to 0

\[
w=0.
\]

The result is direction-like.

That is a translation-invariant vector combination.

So homogeneous coordinates encode the exact distinction we developed abstractly in affine geometry:

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_i=1
\leftrightarrow
\text{point}
\leftrightarrow
w=1
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_i=0
\leftrightarrow
\text{direction}
\leftrightarrow
w=0.
}
\]

This is not coincidence.

It is the same affine structure written in a different representation.

---

# DEEP CONNECTION: CONVEX HULL AND SUPPORT FUNCTIONS

The convex hull of points:

\[
p_1,\ldots,p_n
\]

contains infinitely many points.

Yet to find its extreme position in direction d:

\[
h(d)
=
\max_{x\in hull} d\cdot x,
\]

you only need to inspect the extreme input vertices.

Why?

Any point in the hull is:

\[
x=\sum_i a_ip_i
\]

with convex weights.

Then:

\[
d\cdot x
=
\sum_i a_i(d\cdot p_i).
\]

Because the coefficients are a convex mixture, this value can never exceed the maximum individual:

\[
\max_i d\cdot p_i.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
h_{\operatorname{conv}(P)}(d)
=
\max_i d\cdot p_i.
}
\]

This is why support mappings work so cleanly for convex hulls.

---

# NUMERICAL AND ENGINE FAILURE MODES

### Affine/convex weights

Floating-point weights may sum to:

\[
0.99999994
\]

instead of 1.

For interpolation this may be harmless or can be renormalized if required.

But blindly renormalizing can hide a deeper bug if the error is large.

---

### Convex-set assumptions

A collision algorithm designed only for convex shapes can fail catastrophically if fed a concave mesh.

A support function alone is not enough to magically make a nonconvex object behave like a convex one; support queries expose the convex hull of the set for linear maximization purposes.

---

### Minkowski operations

Explicitly constructing a Minkowski difference can explode combinatorially for large polyhedra.

Support-based algorithms avoid materializing the entire shape.

---

### Support directions

Direction:

\[
d=0
\]

has no unique "farthest direction."

For a support function:

\[
d\cdot x=0
\]

for every x.

Any point is a maximizer.

A support mapping should have a documented zero-direction policy.

---

### Homogeneous points

Never dehomogenize with:

\[
w=0.
\]

And for tiny:

\[
|w|\ll1,
\]

division can generate huge coordinates and amplify numerical error.

That has a real projective interpretation: the point is very far away in Euclidean coordinates.

---

# HARDWARE / COMPLEXITY

Parts 571–574 are primarily mathematical structures.

For a finite convex combination of \(n\) vectors of dimension d:

\[
O(nd)
\]

arithmetic.

Testing convexity of an arbitrary polyhedron is a broader geometry problem; the definition itself is not an algorithm.

A naive support point for an n-vertex convex mesh costs:

\[
\boxed{O(n)}
\]

dots.

For analytic primitives such as sphere, AABB or capsule, support can often be:

\[
\boxed{O(1)}.
\]

This is one reason collision systems often provide shape-specific support functions.

Homogeneous point/direction representation adds one scalar component. For a float vector:

```text
Vec3 = 3 floats
Vec4 = 4 floats
```

The additional component may actually align naturally with SIMD widths and later matrix operations, though storage/performance depends on layout and architecture.

# THE FINAL 571–579 MENTAL MODEL

The whole block is really one giant progression.

First:

\[
\boxed{
\text{linear combination}
}
\]

lets vectors combine freely.

Restrict coefficients so they sum to one:

\[
\boxed{
\text{affine combination}.
}
\]

Then require them also to be nonnegative:

\[
\boxed{
\text{convex combination}.
}
\]

All points obtainable this way form:

\[
\boxed{
\text{convex hull}.
}
\]

Convex shapes can then be combined:

\[
\boxed{
A+B
}
\]

or compared through relative geometry:

\[
\boxed{
A-B.
}
\]

Instead of constructing those shapes explicitly, ask only for their farthest point:

\[
\boxed{
support(d).
}
\]

That becomes the foundation of convex collision detection.

Then we revisit affine point/vector semantics from a new representation angle.

Homogeneous coordinates add:

\[
\boxed{w}
\]

so that one higher-dimensional representation can distinguish:

\[
\boxed{
\text{points}
}
\]

from:

\[
\boxed{
\text{directions}.
}
\]

And the deepest connection is:

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_i=1
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{point-like}
\Longleftrightarrow
w=1
}
\]

versus:

\[
\boxed{
\sum a_i=0
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{direction-like}
\Longleftrightarrow
w=0.
}
\]

That connection is going to make later matrices and transforms far less mysterious.
