# Part 600 — Reconstructing a Production-Ready `Vec3` Library from First Principles

This is the capstone of **Phase 6: Scalars, Vectors, Vector Spaces, Norms, and Geometric Algebra Foundations**. The curriculum deliberately ends the phase by forcing us to reconstruct the object we have been using for almost 100 Parts rather than merely recognizing formulas. Project_Sheldon_Master_Curricul…

The target is not:

```cpp
struct Vec3 {
    float x, y, z;
};
```

with 40 random operators attached.

The target is understanding the entire chain:

\[
\boxed{
\text{geometry}
\rightarrow
\text{mathematical contract}
\rightarrow
\text{API}
\rightarrow
\text{floating point}
\rightarrow
\text{memory}
\rightarrow
\text{CPU execution}
}
\]

so that if every math library disappeared tomorrow, you could rebuild the essential vector layer yourself.

---

# 600.1 Start with the problem, not the class

Imagine we are implementing a game engine.

A character has:

\[
P=(10,3,-5)
\]

as a position.

Its velocity is:

\[
V=(2,0,1).
\]

A surface has normal:

\[
N=(0,1,0).
\]

A light direction might be:

\[
L=(0.3,0.8,-0.5).
\]

A triangle supplies edges:

\[
E_1=B-A,
\qquad
E_2=C-A.
\]

Every subsystem repeatedly needs:

\[
a+b,
\]

\[
a-b,
\]

\[
\lambda a,
\]

\[
a\cdot b,
\]

\[
a\times b,
\]

\[
\|a\|,
\]

\[
\hat a,
\]

projection, rejection, reflection, angles, finite checks, and so on.

Without a reusable vector abstraction, every system starts writing:

```cpp
float dx = bx - ax;
float dy = by - ay;
float dz = bz - az;
```

over and over.

Then one system computes magnitude correctly.

Another forgets Z.

Another normalizes zero.

Another mixes local and world coordinates.

Another treats a normal as a position.

The purpose of the vector library is therefore not merely code reuse.

It creates a **central mathematical contract** for the engine.

---

# 600.2 First establish what the core type represents

We need a numeric carrier for coordinates:

\[
v=(x,y,z).
\]

The most basic representation is:

```cpp
template<class T>
struct Vec3T
{
    T x{};
    T y{};
    T z{};
};
```

For graphics:

```cpp
using Vec3f = Vec3T<float>;
using Vec3d = Vec3T<double>;
```

But unrestricted `T` is questionable.

What would this mean?

```cpp
Vec3T<std::string>
```

Nothing useful.

So constrain it.

With C++20:

```cpp
#include <concepts>

template<std::floating_point T>
struct Vec3T
{
    T x{};
    T y{};
    T z{};
};
```

Now our base type explicitly models floating-point Euclidean coordinates.

We could separately create integer vector types if needed.

---

# 600.3 Why not make only `Vec3f`?

Because the scalar type is an independent engineering decision.

A renderer may use:

```cpp
Vec3f
```

for normals, local positions, colors and GPU-bound data.

A large-world simulation might use:

```cpp
Vec3d
```

for authoritative world positions.

The same algebra applies.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{dimension}
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
\text{scalar precision}
}
\]

should not necessarily be welded together.

---

# 600.4 Our first complete object

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
struct Vec3T
{
    T x{};
    T y{};
    T z{};

    constexpr Vec3T() noexcept = default;

    constexpr Vec3T(
        T x_,
        T y_,
        T z_) noexcept
        : x{x_},
          y{y_},
          z{z_}
    {
    }

    explicit constexpr Vec3T(T s) noexcept
        : x{s},
          y{s},
          z{s}
    {
    }
};
```

Now:

```cpp
Vec3f a{1.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f};
```

means:

\[
a=(1,2,3).
\]

And explicit broadcast:

```cpp
Vec3f ones{1.0f};
```

means:

\[
(1,1,1).
\]

Because the scalar constructor is `explicit`, this does not silently happen:

```cpp
void foo(Vec3f);

foo(5.0f); // should not implicitly become (5,5,5)
```

That is deliberate API hygiene.

---

# 600.5 Memory representation

Assume the common case:

\[
sizeof(float)=4.
\]

Then mathematical payload:

\[
3\times4=12\text{ bytes}.
\]

Conceptually:

```text
Vec3f

address +0
┌──────────────┐
│      x       │ 4 bytes
├──────────────┤
│      y       │ 4 bytes
├──────────────┤
│      z       │ 4 bytes
└──────────────┘
```

We do **not** force:

```cpp
alignas(16)
```

on the fundamental type.

Why?

Because Part 594 showed that the best storage representation is workload dependent.

A million 12-byte vectors:

\[
12\text{ MB}.
\]

A million 16-byte vectors:

\[
16\text{ MB}.
\]

A 33% increase.

So our canonical numeric type begins compact.

If a SIMD subsystem wants another layout, it can use one.

---

# 600.6 Verify assumptions rather than imagining them

Tests/build assertions can inspect properties:

```cpp
#include <type_traits>

using Vec3f = Vec3T<float>;

static_assert(
    std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Vec3f>
);

static_assert(
    std::is_standard_layout_v<Vec3f>
);
```

On a target where your engine contract requires 12-byte packed storage:

```cpp
static_assert(sizeof(Vec3f) == 12);
```

But only make that assertion if it is genuinely an engine ABI requirement.

Do not turn incidental platform behavior into a universal mathematical requirement.

---

# 600.7 Why trivial copyability is desirable

Our vector owns no resources.

No heap allocation.

No file handles.

No pointer ownership.

No custom destruction.

So:

```cpp
Vec3f b = a;
```

should simply copy the scalar values.

A vector is a canonical **value type**.

Its lifetime should be boring.

That is a feature.

---

# 600.8 Component indexing

Named access is great:

```cpp
v.x
v.y
v.z
```

Generic algorithms also need:

```cpp
v[i]
```

Implement explicitly:

```cpp
constexpr T& operator[](
    std::size_t i) noexcept
{
    assert(i < 3);

    switch (i)
    {
        case 0: return x;
        case 1: return y;
        default: return z;
    }
}

constexpr T const& operator[](
    std::size_t i) const noexcept
{
    assert(i < 3);

    switch (i)
    {
        case 0: return x;
        case 1: return y;
        default: return z;
    }
}
```

We avoid clever object-layout tricks merely to save a three-case switch that the compiler will typically optimize aggressively.

---

# 600.9 Constants

Useful named constructors:

```cpp
static constexpr Vec3T zero() noexcept
{
    return {T(0), T(0), T(0)};
}

static constexpr Vec3T one() noexcept
{
    return {T(1), T(1), T(1)};
}

static constexpr Vec3T xAxis() noexcept
{
    return {T(1), T(0), T(0)};
}

static constexpr Vec3T yAxis() noexcept
{
    return {T(0), T(1), T(0)};
}

static constexpr Vec3T zAxis() noexcept
{
    return {T(0), T(0), T(1)};
}
```

But note:

\[
(0,1,0)
\]

is the second coordinate axis.

It is not intrinsically:

> world up.

That convention belongs above the generic math layer.

---

# 600.10 Arithmetic begins from vector-space axioms

We need componentwise addition because:

\[
(a_x,a_y,a_z)
+
(b_x,b_y,b_z)
=
(a_x+b_x,a_y+b_y,a_z+b_z).
\]

Implement compound assignment first:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>& operator+=(
    Vec3T<T>& a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a.x += b.x;
    a.y += b.y;
    a.z += b.z;
    return a;
}
```

Then:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator+(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a += b;
    return a;
}
```

Subtraction similarly:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>& operator-=(
    Vec3T<T>& a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a.x -= b.x;
    a.y -= b.y;
    a.z -= b.z;
    return a;
}
```

---

# 600.11 Scalar multiplication

Vector-space scalar multiplication:

\[
\lambda(x,y,z)
=
(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z).
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator*(
    Vec3T<T> v,
    T s) noexcept
{
    return {
        v.x * s,
        v.y * s,
        v.z * s
    };
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator*(
    T s,
    Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return v * s;
}
```

Division:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator/(
    Vec3T<T> v,
    T s) noexcept
{
    return {
        v.x / s,
        v.y / s,
        v.z / s
    };
}
```

The primitive operator follows floating-point arithmetic.

Higher-level functions enforce geometric preconditions.

---

# 600.12 What we deliberately do NOT define

We do not define:

```cpp
Vec3 * Vec3
```

because there are too many plausible meanings:

\[
\text{dot product},
\]

\[
\text{Hadamard product}.
\]

Use explicit operations:

```cpp
dot(a, b);
hadamard(a, b);
cross(a, b);
```

When mathematics contains multiple multiplication concepts, the code should say which one.

---

# 600.13 Dot product

From Parts 534–536:

\[
\boxed{
a\cdot b
=
a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z.
}
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr T dot(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return
        a.x * b.x +
        a.y * b.y +
        a.z * b.z;
}
```

Its meaning depends on context.

For Euclidean vectors in the same orthonormal coordinate space it measures:

\[
\|a\|\|b\|\cos\theta.
\]

If coordinate spaces differ, the numeric operation still runs but the geometry is meaningless.

We will address that semantic layer shortly.

---

# 600.14 Cross product

\[
\boxed{
a\times b
=
(
a_yb_z-a_zb_y,\;
a_zb_x-a_xb_z,\;
a_xb_y-a_yb_x
).
}
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> cross(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return {
        a.y * b.z - a.z * b.y,
        a.z * b.x - a.x * b.z,
        a.x * b.y - a.y * b.x
    };
}
```

Properties we can test:

\[
a\cdot(a\times b)\approx0
\]

and:

\[
b\cdot(a\times b)\approx0.
\]

Also:

\[
a\times b=-(b\times a).
\]

---

# 600.15 Squared length

Do not invoke `sqrt` unless needed.

\[
\boxed{
\|v\|^2=v\cdot v.
}
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr T lengthSquared(
    Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return dot(v, v);
}
```

Useful for:

```cpp
if (lengthSquared(delta)
    < radius * radius)
{
    ...
}
```

instead of:

```cpp
if (length(delta) < radius)
```

when only comparison is needed.

---

# 600.16 Length deserves more thought

The naïve implementation:

```cpp
return std::sqrt(dot(v, v));
```

can overflow during intermediate squaring even if we want a numerically careful norm.

Example with very large components:

\[
v=(10^{30},10^{30},0).
\]

Binary32 can represent approximately \(10^{30}\).

But:

\[
10^{60}
\]

cannot fit in binary32.

So:

\[
v\cdot v
\]

may overflow to infinity even though the actual length:

\[
\sqrt2\times10^{30}
\]

is still within float's exponent range.

This is why robust norm implementations scale.

---

# 600.17 Robust length derivation

Let:

\[
m=
\max(|x|,|y|,|z|).
\]

If:

\[
m=0,
\]

length is zero.

Otherwise write:

\[
v=m\,u
\]

where:

\[
u=
\left(
\frac{x}{m},
\frac{y}{m},
\frac{z}{m}
\right).
\]

Every component of \(u\) has magnitude at most 1.

Then:

\[
\|v\|
=
m\|u\|.
\]

And:

\[
1\le\|u\|\le\sqrt3
\]

for nonzero v with max component normalized to magnitude one.

Intermediate squaring is now safe from the original huge dynamic range.

Implementation:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
T length(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    const T ax = std::abs(v.x);
    const T ay = std::abs(v.y);
    const T az = std::abs(v.z);

    const T m =
        std::max({ax, ay, az});

    if (m == T(0))
        return T(0);

    const Vec3T<T> u = v / m;

    return m *
        std::sqrt(dot(u, u));
}
```

Alternatively, standard-library `hypot` implementations are designed specifically for robust Euclidean norms.

---

# 600.18 Finite-state validation

Geometry generally expects finite coordinates.

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
bool isFinite(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return
        std::isfinite(v.x) &&
        std::isfinite(v.y) &&
        std::isfinite(v.z);
}
```

Also useful:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
bool hasNaN(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return
        std::isnan(v.x) ||
        std::isnan(v.y) ||
        std::isnan(v.z);
}
```

Do not wait until rendering explodes.

Validate at important subsystem boundaries.

---

# 600.19 Normalization: the textbook version

Mathematically:

\[
\hat v=
\frac{v}{\|v\|}.
\]

The naïve implementation:

```cpp
return v / length(v);
```

fails for:

\[
v=0.
\]

And a poorly implemented length can underflow/overflow.

So normalization should represent failure.

---

# 600.20 Robust normalization without giant/small intermediate values

Again define:

\[
m=\max(|x|,|y|,|z|).
\]

If:

\[
m=0
\]

there is no direction.

If any component is nonfinite, reject it.

Otherwise:

\[
u=\frac vm.
\]

Then normalize u:

\[
\hat v=
\frac{u}{\sqrt{u\cdot u}}.
\]

Notice we do **not need to multiply back by \(m\)**.

Scaling a vector by positive scalar does not change direction.

This handles extremely large and tiny finite components much better than naïvely squaring the original vector.

---

# 600.21 Introduce `UnitVec3`

This is where the Phase 6 theory becomes API design.

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
class UnitVec3T
{
public:
    constexpr Vec3T<T> value() const noexcept
    {
        return value_;
    }

    constexpr T x() const noexcept { return value_.x; }
    constexpr T y() const noexcept { return value_.y; }
    constexpr T z() const noexcept { return value_.z; }

private:
    explicit constexpr UnitVec3T(
        Vec3T<T> normalized) noexcept
        : value_{normalized}
    {
    }

    Vec3T<T> value_;

    template<std::floating_point U>
    friend std::optional<UnitVec3T<U>>
    tryNormalize(Vec3T<U>) noexcept;
};
```

The constructor is private.

Therefore arbitrary code cannot write:

```cpp
UnitVec3f{3,4,0};
```

and lie about the invariant.

---

# 600.22 Safe constructor

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
std::optional<UnitVec3T<T>>
tryNormalize(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    if (!isFinite(v))
        return std::nullopt;

    const T m =
        std::max({
            std::abs(v.x),
            std::abs(v.y),
            std::abs(v.z)
        });

    if (m == T(0))
        return std::nullopt;

    const Vec3T<T> scaled = v / m;

    const T scaledLength =
        std::sqrt(dot(scaled, scaled));

    if (!std::isfinite(scaledLength) ||
        scaledLength == T(0))
    {
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    return UnitVec3T<T>{
        scaled / scaledLength
    };
}
```

Now:

```cpp
auto dir = tryNormalize(v);

if (!dir)
{
    // No valid direction exists.
}
```

The caller must acknowledge the degeneracy.

---

# 600.23 Why not silently return zero?

Suppose:

```cpp
normalize(Vec3{0,0,0})
```

returns:

\[
(0,0,0).
\]

That avoids NaN.

But now a function claiming to return a unit vector returned length zero.

The invariant is broken.

Worse, later code may assume:

\[
u\cdot u=1.
\]

So returning zero can hide the bug more effectively than NaN.

Use explicit policies:

```cpp
tryNormalize(...)
normalizeOr(v, fallback)
normalizeChecked(...)
```

depending on the domain.

---

# 600.24 Approximate equality

Keep exact `==` semantically exact:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr bool operator==(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return
        a.x == b.x &&
        a.y == b.y &&
        a.z == b.z;
}
```

Then provide named closeness.

Scalar helper:

\[
|a-b|
\le
\max
\left(
\epsilon_a,
\epsilon_r\max(|a|,|b|)
\right).
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
bool almostEqualScalar(
    T a,
    T b,
    T absTol,
    T relTol) noexcept
{
    if (a == b)
        return true;

    if (!std::isfinite(a) ||
        !std::isfinite(b))
    {
        return false;
    }

    const T diff =
        std::abs(a - b);

    const T scale =
        std::max(
            std::abs(a),
            std::abs(b));

    return diff <=
        std::max(
            absTol,
            relTol * scale);
}
```

Then componentwise vector form.

---

# 600.25 But geometrical distance may be better

Sometimes the question is:

> Are these positions within 1 mm?

Then don't use arbitrary per-component epsilon.

Use:

\[
\boxed{
\|a-b\|^2\le(0.001)^2.
}
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
bool nearPosition(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b,
    T distanceTol) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> d = a - b;

    return lengthSquared(d)
        <= distanceTol * distanceTol;
}
```

Assuming numeric range is appropriate.

For world-scale extremes, use a robust distance/norm implementation.

The lesson is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{comparison policy belongs to the physical question}.
}
\]

---

# 600.26 Projection

For arbitrary nonzero target:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{proj}_b a
=
\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.
}
\]

Return optional because:

\[
b=0
\]

defines no projection direction.

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
std::optional<Vec3T<T>>
projectOnto(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    const T denom = dot(b, b);

    if (!std::isfinite(denom) ||
        denom == T(0))
    {
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    const T k =
        dot(a, b) / denom;

    return b * k;
}
```

For a unit axis:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{proj}_u a
=
(a\cdot u)u.
}
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>
projectOnto(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    UnitVec3T<T> u) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> axis = u.value();

    return axis * dot(a, axis);
}
```

This is an example of an invariant eliminating work.

---

# 600.27 Rejection

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{rej}_b a
=
a-\operatorname{proj}_b a.
}
\]

For unit axis:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>
rejectFrom(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    UnitVec3T<T> axis) noexcept
{
    return
        a - projectOnto(a, axis);
}
```

Real-life example: remove vertical velocity from a movement vector to get movement along a ground plane.

---

# 600.28 Reflection

For unit normal:

\[
\boxed{
R=I-2(I\cdot N)N.
}
\]

API:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>
reflect(
    Vec3T<T> incident,
    UnitVec3T<T> normal) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> n =
        normal.value();

    return incident -
        n * (T(2) * dot(incident, n));
}
```

Because the function requires `UnitVec3T`, it cannot accidentally use the simplified formula with a non-unit normal.

This is how **types can encode derivations**.

---

# 600.29 Refraction

Given normalized incident and normal plus:

\[
\eta=\frac{n_1}{n_2},
\]

we derived:

\[
k=
1-\eta^2
\left[
1-(I\cdot N)^2
\right].
\]

If:

\[
k<0,
\]

total internal reflection occurs.

So return optional:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
std::optional<UnitVec3T<T>>
refract(
    UnitVec3T<T> incident,
    UnitVec3T<T> normal,
    T eta) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> i =
        incident.value();

    const Vec3T<T> n =
        normal.value();

    const T d = dot(i, n);

    T k =
        T(1)
        - eta * eta *
          (T(1) - d * d);

    if (k < T(0))
        return std::nullopt;

    const Vec3T<T> result =
        eta * i
        -
        (eta * d +
         std::sqrt(k)) * n;

    return tryNormalize(result);
}
```

Production code may need a tiny-boundary policy around \(k=0\).

---

# 600.30 Robust angle

Naïve:

\[
\theta=
\arccos
\frac{a\cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}.
\]

More robust:

\[
\boxed{
\theta=
\operatorname{atan2}
(
\|a\times b\|,
a\cdot b
).
}
\]

For unit inputs:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
T angleBetween(
    UnitVec3T<T> a,
    UnitVec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> av = a.value();
    const Vec3T<T> bv = b.value();

    const T sinLike =
        length(cross(av, bv));

    const T cosLike =
        dot(av, bv);

    return std::atan2(
        sinLike,
        cosLike);
}
```

Range:

\[
[0,\pi].
\]

No `acos` domain clamp required.

---

# 600.31 Hadamard product

Componentwise product is still useful:

\[
a\odot b
=
(a_xb_x,a_yb_y,a_zb_z).
\]

For example RGB modulation or componentwise scale.

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>
hadamard(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return {
        a.x * b.x,
        a.y * b.y,
        a.z * b.z
    };
}
```

We named it because:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Hadamard}
\neq
\text{dot}
\neq
\text{cross}.
}
\]

---

# 600.32 A useful `min`/`max` layer

For bounding boxes:

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>
componentMin(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return {
        std::min(a.x, b.x),
        std::min(a.y, b.y),
        std::min(a.z, b.z)
    };
}
```

Likewise max.

These are not vector-space operations.

They are componentwise utility operations.

Naming that distinction is healthy.

---

# 600.33 `lerp`

Linear interpolation:

\[
\operatorname{lerp}(a,b,t)
=
(1-t)a+tb.
\]

```cpp
template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>
lerp(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b,
    T t) noexcept
{
    return
        a * (T(1) - t)
        + b * t;
}
```

For:

\[
0\le t\le1,
\]

this is a convex combination.

For:

\[
t<0
\]

or:

\[
t>1,
\]

it extrapolates.

Notice how Part 572 reappears directly in API code.

---

# 600.34 `lerp` of unit directions does not stay unit

Suppose:

\[
a=(1,0,0),
\]

\[
b=(0,1,0).
\]

At:

\[
t=0.5,
\]

lerp gives:

\[
(0.5,0.5,0).
\]

Length:

\[
\sqrt{0.5}
\neq1.
\]

Therefore:

```cpp
lerp(UnitVec3, UnitVec3)
```

should not naturally return `UnitVec3`.

It returns a raw vector unless explicitly renormalized.

Again:

\[
\boxed{
\text{return type follows mathematical invariant}.
}
\]

---

# 600.35 Point and vector should not necessarily be the same public type

Our core numeric type is `Vec3T`.

At the engine-semantic layer:

```cpp
struct LocalSpace {};
struct WorldSpace {};
struct ViewSpace {};
```

Define:

```cpp
template<class Space, std::floating_point T>
struct Vector3T
{
    Vec3T<T> value;
};

template<class Space, std::floating_point T>
struct Point3T
{
    Vec3T<T> value;
};
```

Now we can encode affine arithmetic.

---

# 600.36 Point minus point

\[
B-A
\]

returns displacement.

```cpp
template<class S, std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vector3T<S,T>
operator-(
    Point3T<S,T> b,
    Point3T<S,T> a) noexcept
{
    return {
        b.value - a.value
    };
}
```

---

# 600.37 Point plus vector

\[
P+v
\]

returns point.

```cpp
template<class S, std::floating_point T>
constexpr Point3T<S,T>
operator+(
    Point3T<S,T> p,
    Vector3T<S,T> v) noexcept
{
    return {
        p.value + v.value
    };
}
```

But we simply do not provide:

```cpp
Point3 + Point3
```

because the mathematical operation is not intrinsic.

---

# 600.38 Coordinate-space safety

Now this fails:

```cpp
Point3T<LocalSpace,float> local;
Point3T<WorldSpace,float> world;

auto x = world - local;
```

No matching operator.

The compiler catches:

\[
\boxed{
\text{coordinate-space mismatch}.
}
\]

There is zero extra runtime data from the empty tag types.

This is one of the strongest design improvements a graphics math layer can make.

---

# 600.39 Directions versus normals

Part 582 showed they transform differently.

Therefore an even stronger layer might have:

```cpp
template<class Space, class T>
struct Direction3T;

template<class Space, class T>
struct Normal3T;
```

A transform exposes different operations:

```cpp
transformPoint(...)
transformDirection(...)
transformNormal(...)
```

instead of one ambiguous:

```cpp
transform(Vec3)
```

This matters under nonuniform scale.

---

# 600.40 Do not make every semantic distinction the core `Vec3`

There is a danger in the opposite direction.

If we create:

```text
WorldUnitNormal3f
WorldUnitDirection3f
LocalUnitNormal3f
LocalVelocity3f
LocalForce3f
ViewDirection3f
...
```

the library can become unbearable.

So use layers:

```text
LOW LEVEL
Vec3f
    ↓
mathematical operations

SEMANTIC GEOMETRY
Point3<Space>
Direction3<Space>
Normal3<Space>

DOMAIN LAYER
Velocity
Force
Color
etc. where truly useful
```

The goal is not maximal type count.

The goal is protecting dangerous boundaries.

---

# 600.41 Storage representation versus compute representation

Our semantic Vec3 does not have to dictate GPU or SIMD format.

CPU core type:

```text
12-byte Vec3f
```

Bulk SIMD kernel might temporarily use:

```text
[x0 x1 x2 x3]
[y0 y1 y2 y3]
[z0 z1 z2 z3]
```

SoA.

GPU vertex representation might use:

```text
packed float3
compressed normal
```

Different representations can coexist.

The library should provide explicit conversion boundaries.

---

# 600.42 SIMD implementation is an optimization layer

Do **not** begin your vector library with intrinsics.

Begin with mathematical correctness.

Reference implementation:

```cpp
constexpr Vec3f operator+(
    Vec3f a,
    Vec3f b)
{
    return {
        a.x+b.x,
        a.y+b.y,
        a.z+b.z
    };
}
```

Then benchmark.

If a hotspot exists, optimized implementation may use:

```text
SIMD
SoA
AoSoA
batch transforms
```

The scalar implementation becomes your correctness oracle.

This is an extremely useful engineering pattern:

\[
\boxed{
\text{simple reference implementation}
\rightarrow
\text{optimized implementation}
\rightarrow
\text{cross-check tests}.
}
\]

---

# 600.43 A production library needs tests, not faith

For vector operations, tests should be divided into **identities**, **edge cases**, and **numerical contracts**.

Examples:

```cpp
TEST(Vec3, Addition)
{
    Vec3f a{1,2,3};
    Vec3f b{4,5,6};

    EXPECT_EQ(
        a + b,
        Vec3f(5,7,9));
}
```

Cross:

```cpp
TEST(Vec3, CrossBasis)
{
    EXPECT_EQ(
        cross(
            Vec3f::xAxis(),
            Vec3f::yAxis()),
        Vec3f::zAxis());
}
```

---

# 600.44 Property tests are stronger

Rather than only hard-coded inputs:

For random finite vectors \(a,b\), check:

\[
a+b=b+a
\]

approximately, acknowledging floating-point evaluation.

Check:

\[
a\times b\approx-(b\times a).
\]

Check:

\[
a\cdot(a\times b)\approx0.
\]

Check normalized vectors:

\[
\|\hat a\|\approx1.
\]

Check reflection:

\[
\|R\|\approx\|I\|
\]

for unit normal.

These tests validate structural mathematics rather than a handful of examples.

---

# 600.45 But floating point breaks some exact algebraic laws

Do not test:

\[
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)
\]

with exact equality and declare vector addition broken when it fails.

Floating-point addition is not associative.

Likewise distributivity can fail bitwise.

Your tests must distinguish:

\[
\boxed{
\text{mathematical law}
}
\]

from:

\[
\boxed{
\text{finite machine approximation}.
}
\]

---

# 600.46 Edge-case test matrix

A serious vector library should deliberately test values such as:

\[
0,
\]

\[
-0,
\]

very small subnormals,

very large finite floats,

\[
+\infty,
\]

\[
-\infty,
\]

NaN,

parallel vectors,

antiparallel vectors,

nearly parallel vectors,

orthogonal vectors.

These are not weird academic values.

They are exactly where numerical APIs expose weaknesses.

---

# 600.47 Manual execution trace

Let's run one vector through several functions.

Take:

\[
v=(3,4,0).
\]

### Squared length

\[
v\cdot v
=
3^2+4^2
=
25.
\]

### Length

\[
\sqrt{25}=5.
\]

### Normalize

\[
\hat v=
\left(
\frac35,\frac45,0
\right)
=
(0.6,0.8,0).
\]

Check:

\[
0.6^2+0.8^2
=
0.36+0.64
=
1.
\]

---

# 600.48 Projection trace

Project:

\[
a=(4,3,0)
\]

onto:

\[
b=(2,1,0).
\]

Dot:

\[
a\cdot b
=
8+3
=
11.
\]

Denominator:

\[
b\cdot b
=
4+1
=
5.
\]

Coefficient:

\[
\frac{11}{5}=2.2.
\]

Projection:

\[
2.2(2,1,0)
=
(4.4,2.2,0).
\]

Rejection:

\[
a-p
=
(-0.4,0.8,0).
\]

Check orthogonality:

\[
(-0.4)(2)+(0.8)(1)=0.
\]

Our code should reproduce this within floating-point tolerance.

---

# 600.49 Cross trace

Take:

\[
a=(1,0,0)
\]

and:

\[
b=(0,1,0).
\]

Cross:

\[
a\times b=(0,0,1).
\]

Swap:

\[
b\times a=(0,0,-1).
\]

That test simultaneously validates:

- coordinate formula;
- right-handed convention;
- antisymmetry.

---

# 600.50 Angle trace

Take unit:

\[
a=(1,0,0)
\]

and:

\[
b=(0,1,0).
\]

Cross magnitude:

\[
1.
\]

Dot:

\[
0.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\theta=
\operatorname{atan2}(1,0)
=
\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

Perfect.

---

# 600.51 Complexity

Every ordinary `Vec3` operation is fixed dimension.

So asymptotically:

\[
\boxed{O(1)}.
\]

But that statement is almost useless for performance engineering.

Actual costs differ:

```text
addition            ~3 scalar adds
scalar multiply     ~3 multiplies
dot                 ~3 multiplies + reduction
cross               ~6 multiplies + 3 subtracts
normalize           dot/norm + sqrt/divide
angle               dot + cross + norm + atan2
```

`atan2` is far more expensive than addition.

So "both are O(1)" does not mean equal cost.

---

# 600.52 Allocation

A correct basic Vec3 operation should allocate:

\[
\boxed{0\text{ heap bytes}.}
\]

This:

```cpp
Vec3f c = a + b;
```

should create a small value, typically registers/stack as required by optimization and ABI.

If basic vector addition causes dynamic allocation, your design has gone badly wrong.

---

# 600.53 Cache and bandwidth

For one vector, irrelevant.

For:

\[
10^7
\]

vectors, dominant.

A 12-byte position stream is roughly:

\[
120\text{ MB}
\]

for ten million positions.

Reading and writing several such streams can easily become memory-bandwidth dominated.

At scale, memory layout becomes as important as arithmetic.

That is why our library should not hide storage assumptions.

---

# 600.54 Thread safety

A Vec3 value itself has no global state.

Two threads operating on separate vectors are independent.

But:

```cpp
sharedVelocity += impulse;
```

from multiple threads without synchronization is a race.

The math type should not contain internal locks.

Synchronization belongs to the system owning shared state.

Tiny numeric values should remain cheap and composable.

---

# 600.55 Serialization

Never assume:

```cpp
file.write(
    reinterpret_cast<char*>(&v),
    sizeof(v));
```

defines a permanent portable format.

Questions include:

- float representation;
- endianness;
- padding;
- versioning;
- precision;
- platform ABI.

A file format should explicitly define components:

```text
x: IEEE binary32 little-endian
y: IEEE binary32 little-endian
z: IEEE binary32 little-endian
```

if that is the chosen format.

Object representation and serialization format are separate contracts.

---

# 600.56 GPU upload

Likewise, CPU:

```cpp
struct Vec3f
```

does not automatically match every GPU buffer layout.

The GPU-side format may expect specific:

- alignment;
- stride;
- packing.

Always define the buffer contract explicitly.

This is where many "math bugs" are actually memory-layout bugs.

---

# 600.57 Debug-build invariant checks

Useful debugging macro:

```cpp
#ifndef NDEBUG

#define ASSERT_FINITE_VEC3(v) \
    assert(isFinite(v))

#else

#define ASSERT_FINITE_VEC3(v) \
    ((void)0)

#endif
```

Then strategic boundaries:

```cpp
ASSERT_FINITE_VEC3(position);
ASSERT_FINITE_VEC3(velocity);
```

Do not necessarily put the check into every addition.

Catch corruption close to subsystem boundaries.

---

# 600.58 Production `Vec3` should be boring

This is important.

A high-quality foundational math type should not:

- allocate;
- log;
- touch global state;
- call virtual functions;
- hide expensive conversions;
- silently normalize;
- silently clamp NaNs;
- silently change coordinate spaces.

It should behave predictably.

Complex policies belong in named functions or higher-level semantic types.

---

# 600.59 What about fast-math?

Compilers can enable transformations that assume things such as:

- no NaNs;
- no infinities;
- reassociation allowed.

This may improve vector math throughput.

It can also invalidate debugging assumptions and bitwise determinism.

Therefore build policy matters.

A math library compiled under aggressive floating-point assumptions may behave differently from the reference semantics you expect.

Production engineering includes compiler configuration.

---

# 600.60 One sensible canonical header

Putting the core ideas together:

```cpp
#pragma once

#include <algorithm>
#include <cassert>
#include <cmath>
#include <concepts>
#include <cstddef>
#include <optional>
#include <type_traits>

namespace kairo::math
{

template<std::floating_point T>
struct Vec3T
{
    T x{};
    T y{};
    T z{};

    constexpr Vec3T() noexcept = default;

    constexpr Vec3T(
        T x_,
        T y_,
        T z_) noexcept
        : x{x_}, y{y_}, z{z_}
    {
    }

    explicit constexpr Vec3T(T s) noexcept
        : x{s}, y{s}, z{s}
    {
    }

    constexpr T& operator[](
        std::size_t i) noexcept
    {
        assert(i < 3);

        switch (i)
        {
            case 0: return x;
            case 1: return y;
            default: return z;
        }
    }

    constexpr T const& operator[](
        std::size_t i) const noexcept
    {
        assert(i < 3);

        switch (i)
        {
            case 0: return x;
            case 1: return y;
            default: return z;
        }
    }

    static constexpr Vec3T zero() noexcept
    {
        return {T(0), T(0), T(0)};
    }

    static constexpr Vec3T xAxis() noexcept
    {
        return {T(1), T(0), T(0)};
    }

    static constexpr Vec3T yAxis() noexcept
    {
        return {T(0), T(1), T(0)};
    }

    static constexpr Vec3T zAxis() noexcept
    {
        return {T(0), T(0), T(1)};
    }
};

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr bool operator==(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return
        a.x == b.x &&
        a.y == b.y &&
        a.z == b.z;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator-(
    Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return {-v.x, -v.y, -v.z};
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>& operator+=(
    Vec3T<T>& a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a.x += b.x;
    a.y += b.y;
    a.z += b.z;
    return a;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T>& operator-=(
    Vec3T<T>& a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a.x -= b.x;
    a.y -= b.y;
    a.z -= b.z;
    return a;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator+(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a += b;
    return a;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator-(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    a -= b;
    return a;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator*(
    Vec3T<T> v,
    T s) noexcept
{
    return {
        v.x * s,
        v.y * s,
        v.z * s
    };
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator*(
    T s,
    Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return v * s;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> operator/(
    Vec3T<T> v,
    T s) noexcept
{
    return {
        v.x / s,
        v.y / s,
        v.z / s
    };
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr T dot(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return
        a.x * b.x +
        a.y * b.y +
        a.z * b.z;
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> cross(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b) noexcept
{
    return {
        a.y * b.z - a.z * b.y,
        a.z * b.x - a.x * b.z,
        a.x * b.y - a.y * b.x
    };
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr T lengthSquared(
    Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return dot(v, v);
}

template<std::floating_point T>
T length(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return std::hypot(v.x, v.y, v.z);
}

template<std::floating_point T>
bool isFinite(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    return
        std::isfinite(v.x) &&
        std::isfinite(v.y) &&
        std::isfinite(v.z);
}

template<std::floating_point T>
class UnitVec3T
{
public:
    constexpr Vec3T<T>
    value() const noexcept
    {
        return value_;
    }

private:
    explicit constexpr UnitVec3T(
        Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
        : value_{v}
    {
    }

    Vec3T<T> value_;

    template<std::floating_point U>
    friend std::optional<UnitVec3T<U>>
    tryNormalize(Vec3T<U>) noexcept;
};

template<std::floating_point T>
std::optional<UnitVec3T<T>>
tryNormalize(Vec3T<T> v) noexcept
{
    if (!isFinite(v))
        return std::nullopt;

    const T scale = std::max({
        std::abs(v.x),
        std::abs(v.y),
        std::abs(v.z)
    });

    if (scale == T(0))
        return std::nullopt;

    Vec3T<T> u = v / scale;

    const T len =
        std::sqrt(dot(u, u));

    if (!std::isfinite(len) ||
        len == T(0))
    {
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    return UnitVec3T<T>{u / len};
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> projectOnto(
    Vec3T<T> v,
    UnitVec3T<T> axis) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> u = axis.value();

    return u * dot(v, u);
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> rejectFrom(
    Vec3T<T> v,
    UnitVec3T<T> axis) noexcept
{
    return v - projectOnto(v, axis);
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> reflect(
    Vec3T<T> incident,
    UnitVec3T<T> normal) noexcept
{
    const Vec3T<T> n =
        normal.value();

    return incident
        - n * (T(2) * dot(incident, n));
}

template<std::floating_point T>
constexpr Vec3T<T> lerp(
    Vec3T<T> a,
    Vec3T<T> b,
    T t) noexcept
{
    return
        a * (T(1) - t)
        + b * t;
}

using Vec3f = Vec3T<float>;
using Vec3d = Vec3T<double>;

static_assert(
    std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Vec3f>);

static_assert(
    std::is_standard_layout_v<Vec3f>);

} // namespace kairo::math
```

This is not the only valid production design.

It is a **defensible canonical baseline** whose decisions we can explain.

That is what matters.

---

# 600.61 What intentionally is NOT inside this header

Notice we did not dump everything imaginable into `Vec3`.

No:

```text
matrix transforms
quaternions
random generation
noise
color conversion
ray intersections
physics forces
serialization
GPU upload
```

Those belong to other layers.

A foundational type becomes worse when every subsystem attaches unrelated convenience functions to it.

Keep the primitive coherent.

---

# 600.62 Test the memory assumptions separately

For a build targeting a packed float3 ABI:

```cpp
static_assert(sizeof(float) == 4);
static_assert(sizeof(Vec3f) == 12);
static_assert(alignof(Vec3f) == alignof(float));
```

But if SIMD build uses a separate aligned compute type:

```cpp
struct alignas(16) SimdVec3
{
    float x, y, z, pad;
};
```

do not pretend it has the same external binary representation.

Explicit conversion:

```cpp
SimdVec3 load(Vec3f v);
Vec3f store(SimdVec3 v);
```

is clearer.

---

# 600.63 Scalar reference versus SIMD optimized implementation

Suppose later you write:

```cpp
SimdVec3 crossSimd(...);
```

Your test should compare:

\[
crossSimd(a,b)
\]

against:

\[
cross(a,b)
\]

over thousands/millions of representative random inputs.

The scalar implementation is the oracle.

If results differ slightly due to FMA/reordering, establish an explicit tolerance.

Optimization should have evidence.

---

# 600.64 Reconstruct the entire library from its mathematics

If you lose the code, you should be able to derive everything.

### Addition

Vector-space axiom:

\[
(x,y,z)+(a,b,c)
=
(x+a,y+b,z+c).
\]

### Dot

Euclidean inner product:

\[
xa+yb+zc.
\]

### Cross

Oriented 3D area:

\[
(yc-zb,\;za-xc,\;xb-ya).
\]

### Squared norm

\[
v\cdot v.
\]

### Normalize

\[
v/\|v\|.
\]

### Projection

\[
\frac{v\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.
\]

### Rejection

\[
v-\operatorname{proj}_b(v).
\]

### Reflection

\[
v-2\operatorname{proj}_n(v)
\]

for a unit normal.

### Angle

\[
\operatorname{atan2}
(
\|a\times b\|,
a\cdot b
).
\]

None of these need memorized C++.

The C++ merely represents the mathematics.

---

# 600.65 And reconstruct the safety from the failure modes

Why optional normalization?

Because:

\[
0
\]

has no direction.

Why `UnitVec3`?

Because many formulas simplify only if:

\[
\|u\|=1.
\]

Why finite checks?

Because NaN/Inf poison geometry.

Why exact `operator==` plus named approximation?

Because approximate equality is context-dependent and non-transitive.

Why space tags?

Because identical tuples in different bases can represent different geometric objects.

Why point/direction distinction?

Because:

\[
P-P=V
\]

and:

\[
P+V=P,
\]

not arbitrary vector-space point arithmetic.

Why packed versus aligned separation?

Because memory and compute have different optimization goals.

Every design decision should trace backward to a reason.

---

# 600.66 Interview attack tree

Suppose an interviewer asks:

> Implement Vec3.

Do not immediately dump three floats.

Start:

> I'll make it a small trivially-copyable value type with three floating components. Then I'll distinguish raw arithmetic from operations with geometric preconditions, such as normalization.

Then they ask:

> Why does normalization fail?

Because:

\[
v/\|v\|
\]

requires:

\[
\|v\|\neq0.
\]

Then:

> Why not return zero?

Because zero does not satisfy the unit-vector invariant.

Then:

> Why not always normalize inputs automatically?

Because it changes magnitude, costs a square root/division, hides caller bugs, and is wrong for displacement/velocity vectors where magnitude carries meaning.

Then:

> Why not `Vec3 * Vec3` for dot product?

Because componentwise multiplication is an equally plausible interpretation; named operations communicate intent.

Then:

> Why not `epsilon = 1e-5` everywhere?

Because floating-point error and meaningful physical tolerance depend on scale/domain.

Then:

> Why use 12 bytes instead of 16?

Because packed storage improves bandwidth; SIMD compute representation can be separate.

Then:

> Why not use one Vec3 for positions and directions?

You *can* at the numeric layer, but a stronger geometry layer should distinguish affine roles and coordinate spaces to prevent invalid arithmetic.

If you can follow that chain without memorized interview answers, you understand the library.

---

# 600.67 Debugging scenario 1 — object disappears

You find:

```text
position = (NaN, NaN, NaN)
```

Do not patch:

```cpp
if (!finite(position))
    position = {};
```

Trace backward.

Suppose:

```text
position
↑ velocity integration
↑ velocity
↑ collision response
↑ contact normal
↑ normalize(cross(edge1, edge2))
↑ degenerate triangle
```

The actual bug is a zero-area triangle producing no valid normal.

The vector library's `tryNormalize` helps expose that failure where it occurs.

That is better architecture.

---

# 600.68 Debugging scenario 2 — lighting breaks only after scaling

Geometry appears fine.

Lighting works until object gets:

```text
scale = (3,1,0.5)
```

Then highlights skew.

Raw Vec3 math is probably fine.

Check semantic operation:

Did code transform a normal using:

\[
A n
\]

instead of:

\[
A^{-T}n?
\]

This is not a Vec3 arithmetic bug.

It is a **normal semantics** bug.

A `Normal3` API can make the difference visible.

---

# 600.69 Debugging scenario 3 — physics works near origin, jitters far away

Near:

\[
(0,0,0)
\]

everything works.

At:

\[
(10^7,0,0)
\]

small motion vanishes.

Cause:

binary32 absolute spacing grows with magnitude.

Solutions might include:

- `Vec3d` authoritative positions;
- floating origin;
- region/local coordinates;
- camera-relative representation.

Again, not an addition formula bug.

It is representation precision.

---

# 600.70 Debugging scenario 4 — GPU vertices explode

CPU positions look valid.

First GPU vertex is correct.

Subsequent ones shift.

Investigate:

```text
CPU sizeof(Vec3) = 12
GPU expected stride = 16
```

or vice versa.

The numbers are fine.

The ABI/layout is not.

---

# 600.71 Real-life full engine trace

Suppose local spaceship vertex:

\[
P_L=(2,0,0).
\]

Its local normal:

\[
N_L=(0,1,0).
\]

Ship has world transform.

At semantic layer:

```cpp
Point3<LocalSpace> pLocal;
Normal3<LocalSpace> nLocal;
```

Transform:

```text
point:
Local → World
using affine transform including translation

normal:
Local → World
using inverse transpose
```

Now light position:

```cpp
Point3<WorldSpace> light;
```

Compute:

\[
L=
light-P_W.
\]

Because:

\[
Point-Point=Vector.
\]

Try normalize:

```cpp
auto lightDir = tryNormalize(L);
```

If success, compute:

\[
N_W\cdot L_W.
\]

Both are now:

```text
world-space
unit directions/normal
finite
```

A raw three-float library supplied the arithmetic.

The semantic layer guaranteed the geometry.

That is what a real engine vector stack should look like conceptually.

---

# 600.72 What "production-ready" really means here

It does **not** mean:

> this single header contains every feature every AAA engine will ever need.

It means the design is built around production concerns:

\[
\boxed{
\text{correct mathematical contracts}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{defined failure behavior}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{finite floating-point reality}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{cheap value semantics}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{memory-layout awareness}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{optimization boundaries}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{semantic space/invariant safety}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\text{testability/debuggability}.
}
\]

That is vastly different from a tutorial Vec3 with ten operators.

---

# 600.73 What not to put into the core type

A useful final rule is:

```text
If an operation depends only on the mathematical Vec3,
it can belong near Vec3.

If it depends on a semantic domain,
put it in that domain layer.
```

For example:

\[
dot(a,b)
\]

belongs to vector math.

But:

```cpp
applyGravity(Vec3 velocity)
```

belongs to physics.

Likewise:

```cpp
toSRGB(Vec3 color)
```

belongs to color processing.

And:

```cpp
transformNormal(...)
```

belongs with transformations/geometry semantics.

This prevents your math library from becoming a junk drawer.

a\cdot b

and:

a\wedge b
\]

inside one product.

```text
float x

float z
```

in memory.

**Why doesn't zero normalize?**

**Why isn't a normal merely another direction?**

Because its defining property is orthogonality to tangent space, so under general transforms it follows inverse-transpose behavior.

**Why doesn't approximate equality belong blindly in `operator==`?**

Because tolerance is domain-dependent and approximate comparison lacks clean equivalence properties such as transitivity.

**Why isn't 16-byte Vec3 always better than 12-byte Vec3?**

Because alignment/SIMD convenience competes against storage and bandwidth.

**Why is local `(1,0,0)` not necessarily the same geometric direction as world `(1,0,0)`?**

Because coordinates are coefficients relative to different bases.

**Why should unit vectors be a stronger type?**

Because the invariant:

\[

allows simpler formulas and catches invalid inputs at construction.

**Why should the core implementation remain simple?**

Because correctness, portability and testability come first; storage and SIMD optimizations can be specialized around measured workloads.

# PART 564 — RIGHT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS

## 564.1 What "right-handed" actually means

From Part 563, take an ordered independent basis:

\[
B=(b_1,b_2,b_3).
\]

Its orientation can be tested through the scalar triple product:

\[
H=(b_1\times b_2)\cdot b_3.
\]

Using the standard right-hand-oriented cross product, if:

\[
\boxed{H>0}
\]

the ordered basis is **right-handed**.

For an orthonormal basis, the magnitude must be exactly one mathematically:

\[
H=+1.
\]

For the standard Cartesian basis:

\[
e_x=(1,0,0),
\]

\[
e_y=(0,1,0),
\]

\[
e_z=(0,0,1),
\]

we have:

\[
e_x\times e_y=e_z.
\]

Therefore:

\[
(e_x\times e_y)\cdot e_z
=
e_z\cdot e_z
=
1.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{(e_x,e_y,e_z)\text{ is right-handed}.}
\]

---

# 564.2 The hand mnemonic is not the definition

You can use your right hand:

```text
index  → +X
middle → +Y
thumb  → +Z
```

depending on the physical mnemonic you prefer.

But the actual mathematical test is stronger:

\[
\boxed{
b_1\times b_2
\text{ points toward }b_3
}
\]

or equivalently:

\[
\boxed{
(b_1\times b_2)\cdot b_3>0.
}
\]

The hand gesture helps you remember the orientation relation.

It does not replace the relation.

---

# 564.3 Handedness belongs to an ordered basis

This matters.

Take the set:

\[
\{e_x,e_y,e_z\}.
\]

Now order it:

\[
(e_x,e_y,e_z).
\]

Right-handed.

Swap the first two:

\[
(e_y,e_x,e_z).
\]

Then:

\[
e_y\times e_x=-e_z.
\]

So:

\[
(e_y\times e_x)\cdot e_z=-1.
\]

That ordered basis is left-handed.

Same three geometric axes.

Different ordering.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\text{handedness is not merely a property of three unlabeled lines}.
}
\]

It depends on their ordered orientation.

---

# 564.4 Cyclic permutations preserve handedness

Start:

\[
(e_x,e_y,e_z).
\]

Cycle:

\[
(e_y,e_z,e_x).
\]

Check:

\[
e_y\times e_z=e_x.
\]

Still positive.

Cycle again:

\[
(e_z,e_x,e_y).
\]

And:

\[
e_z\times e_x=e_y.
\]

Still positive.

Thus cyclic permutations preserve orientation.

But swapping any single pair reverses it.

This mirrors the scalar triple product properties from Parts 548–549.

---

# 564.5 Right-handed does not mean "Y is up"

This misconception causes endless confusion.

Consider one right-handed system where:

\[
+Y
\]

is called "up."

You can also construct a perfectly valid right-handed system where:

\[
+Z
\]

is called "up."

Handedness says nothing by itself about which semantic role is assigned to an axis.

You need separate answers to questions such as:

\[
\text{Which axis is up?}
\]

\[
\text{Which axis is forward?}
\]

\[
\text{Which axis is right?}
\]

and:

\[
\text{What is their orientation order?}
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{up-axis convention}
\neq
\text{handedness}.
}
\]

---

# 564.6 Right-handed does not uniquely determine "forward"

Suppose world basis is standard:

\[
X=\text{right},
\qquad
Y=\text{up},
\qquad
Z=\text{some third axis}.
\]

The basis may be right-handed.

A camera system can nevertheless choose its *viewing direction* to be either \(+Z\) or \(-Z\), provided all camera-space conventions are built consistently.

So statements such as:

> right-handed means forward must be \(-Z\)

are too crude.

What may be true is that a **specific camera convention** uses:

\[
+X=\text{camera right},
\quad
+Y=\text{camera up},
\quad
-Z=\text{camera forward}.
\]

Then the positive third coordinate axis is actually camera **backward**:

\[
+Z=\text{backward}.
\]

The underlying ordered coordinate basis:

\[
(+X,+Y,+Z)
\]

can still be right-handed.

That distinction is essential.

---

# 564.7 Coordinates are not the physical arrows themselves

Suppose a point has coordinates:

\[
(2,3,5).
\]

Those numbers mean:

\[
P-O
=
2b_x+3b_y+5b_z.
\]

If the basis changes handedness, the same tuple can represent a different geometric displacement.

For example, define:

\[
b_x'=b_x,
\]

\[
b_y'=b_y,
\]

\[
b_z'=-b_z.
\]

Then tuple:

\[
(2,3,5)_{B'}
\]

represents:

\[
2b_x+3b_y-5b_z
\]

in the original basis.

Thus converting handedness is not:

> relabel the same numbers and hope.

You must understand which basis direction was reflected.

---

# 564.8 A handedness change requires orientation reversal

Can a pure rotation convert a right-handed frame into a left-handed frame?

No.

A rotation preserves orientation.

Imagine physically rotating your coordinate tripod.

No matter how you turn it, the X-Y-Z handed relationship remains the same.

To reverse handedness, you need an **orientation-reversing operation**, such as reflecting one axis:

\[
(x,y,z)
\mapsto
(x,y,-z).
\]

This corresponds to scaling one basis direction by \(-1\).

Its geometric effect is a mirror reflection.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{right-handed}\rightarrow\text{left-handed}
}
\]

cannot be accomplished by a proper rotation alone.

---

# 564.9 What happens to the cross product under a mirrored basis?

This is subtle.

Suppose original basis is right-handed:

\[
e_x\times e_y=e_z.
\]

Now define mirrored basis:

\[
e_x'=e_x,
\]

\[
e_y'=e_y,
\]

\[
e_z'=-e_z.
\]

Then physically:

\[
e_x'\times e_y'
=
e_z
=
-e_z'.
\]

So relative to the new ordered basis:

\[
\boxed{
e_x'\times e_y'=-e_z'.
}
\]

That is exactly the signature of a left-handed basis.

The geometric cross product did not "break."

The orientation of the basis changed.

---

# 564.10 Cross-product component formulas contain an orientation convention

The formula:

\[
a\times b
=
(
a_yb_z-a_zb_y,\;
a_zb_x-a_xb_z,\;
a_xb_y-a_yb_x
)
\]

is normally written relative to a positively oriented/right-handed orthonormal basis.

This matters enormously.

If you simply move the same symbolic component formula into a coordinate basis of opposite orientation while pretending it represents the same geometric cross product, you have silently changed an orientation convention.

In engine code, people often avoid this philosophical distinction by establishing one internal cross-product convention and explicitly converting coordinate spaces at boundaries.

That is usually saner.

---

# 564.11 Mesh normals and a right-handed frame

Suppose triangle vertices are:

\[
A,B,C.
\]

Edges:

\[
e_1=B-A,
\]

\[
e_2=C-A.
\]

Normal:

\[
N=e_1\times e_2.
\]

The output orientation depends on:

1. the vertex order;
2. the cross-product convention;
3. the coordinate-basis orientation.

Flip one of these orientation choices and the normal may reverse.

This is why "my normals point inward" can arise from several different mismatches.

---

# 564.12 Right-handed TBN example

Suppose:

\[
T=(1,0,0),
\]

\[
B=(0,1,0),
\]

\[
N=(0,0,1).
\]

Then:

\[
T\times B=N.
\]

So ordered tangent basis:

\[
(T,B,N)
\]

is right-handed.

If your shader reconstructs:

\[
B=N\times T,
\]

then:

\[
T\times(N\times T)=N
\]

for unit perpendicular \(T,N\), as shown in Part 563.

So this convention produces a positively oriented TBN frame.

Mirrored UVs may deliberately require a sign flip.

---

# PART 565 — LEFT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS

A left-handed basis is not "wrong geometry."

It is simply the opposite orientation class.

---

# 565.1 Mathematical definition

For ordered independent basis:

\[
B=(b_1,b_2,b_3),
\]

under our standard right-handed geometric cross product, define:

\[
H=(b_1\times b_2)\cdot b_3.
\]

If:

\[
\boxed{H<0},
\]

the basis is left-handed.

For an orthonormal left-handed frame:

\[
\boxed{H=-1.}
\]

---

# 565.2 Concrete construction

Start from standard right-handed:

\[
e_x=(1,0,0),
\]

\[
e_y=(0,1,0),
\]

\[
e_z=(0,0,1).
\]

Flip the third direction:

\[
f_x=e_x,
\]

\[
f_y=e_y,
\]

\[
f_z=-e_z.
\]

Then:

\[
f_x\times f_y
=
e_x\times e_y
=
e_z.
\]

But:

\[
f_z=-e_z.
\]

Therefore:

\[
f_x\times f_y=-f_z.
\]

And:

\[
(f_x\times f_y)\cdot f_z
=
e_z\cdot(-e_z)
=
-1.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
(f_x,f_y,f_z)
\text{ is left-handed}.
}
\]

---

# 565.3 The mirror analogy

Put your right hand and left hand in front of you.

They are mirror images.

You can rotate your right hand however you want, but you cannot make it coincide perfectly with your left hand without reflecting it.

That is the geometric intuition behind opposite handedness.

They are congruent under reflection but not under proper rotation.

This is also why the word **chirality** sometimes appears in mathematics and physics.

---

# 565.4 Metric geometry survives a handedness flip

Suppose transform:

\[
M(x,y,z)=(x,y,-z).
\]

Take vectors:

\[
a=(a_x,a_y,a_z),
\]

\[
b=(b_x,b_y,b_z).
\]

After reflection:

\[
a'=(a_x,a_y,-a_z),
\]

\[
b'=(b_x,b_y,-b_z).
\]

Dot:

\[
a'\cdot b'
=
a_xb_x+a_yb_y+(-a_z)(-b_z).
\]

Thus:

\[
=
a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
a'\cdot b'=a\cdot b.
}
\]

Therefore lengths are preserved:

\[
\|a'\|=\|a\|.
\]

Angles are preserved.

Distances are preserved.

What changes is **orientation**, not ordinary Euclidean metric structure.

That distinction is extremely important.

---

# 565.5 Why a mirrored object still has the same shape

A reflection preserves:

\[
\text{distance},
\]

\[
\text{angle},
\]

\[
\text{area magnitude},
\]

\[
\text{volume magnitude}.
\]

But it reverses signed orientation quantities.

For example, signed volume:

\[
(a\times b)\cdot c
\]

changes sign under an odd number of axis reflections.

So a mirrored mesh looks geometrically congruent, but its winding/orientation may reverse.

---

# 565.6 Converting coordinate tuples between a simple RH/LH pair

Suppose the two spaces differ only by Z reflection.

Then a point:

\[
P_R=(x,y,z)
\]

in right-handed coordinates corresponds to:

\[
\boxed{
P_L=(x,y,-z)
}
\]

in the reflected convention, assuming origins/scales and axis meanings otherwise match.

Similarly for ordinary direction vectors:

\[
D_L=(d_x,d_y,-d_z).
\]

But beware: normals, cross-derived orientations, triangle winding and transform matrices may require more thought because orientation-sensitive objects do not behave like arbitrary vectors under reflection.

---

# 565.7 Why triangle winding flips under a mirror

Consider triangle in XY plane:

\[
A=(0,0,0),
\]

\[
B=(1,0,1),
\]

\[
C=(0,1,0).
\]

Reflect Z.

Geometric orientation of the embedded triangle relative to the 3D basis changes.

More generally, any orientation-reversing transform changes the sign of oriented volume/area tests associated with the transformed frame.

This is why a handedness conversion may require reversing triangle index order if you want to preserve the intended concept of "front face."

For one triangle:

```cpp
i0, i1, i2
```

reversal can be:

```cpp
i0, i2, i1
```

which flips cross-product normal orientation.

---

# 565.8 Do not memorize graphics APIs as "the handedness"

A graphics API can support data and matrices built under many conventions.

An application, math library, camera system, asset format and projection setup may each adopt particular coordinate conventions.

So it is safer to document concrete facts:

```text
world +Y is up
world +Z is forward
basis orientation is left-handed
camera looks along ...
front-face winding is ...
matrix convention is ...
```

rather than using one vague label and assuming everything else follows from it.

That will save you enormous debugging time later.

---

# RIGHT VS LEFT: WHAT ACTUALLY CHANGES?

| Property | Handedness flip |
|---|---|
| Vector length | preserved |
| Dot product | preserved under reflection |
| Angle magnitude | preserved |
| Distance | preserved |
| Orthogonality | preserved |
| Triangle area magnitude | preserved |
| Volume magnitude | preserved |
| Signed orientation | reversed |
| Scalar triple-product sign | reversed |
| Winding interpretation | may reverse |
| Cross-product orientation relative to basis | reversed |

This is the distinction to own.

# PART 566 — ORIENTATION TESTS IN 2D USING SIGNED AREA

Now we turn handedness into a practical geometric predicate.

Given three 2D points:

\[
A,\quad B,\quad C,
\]

we want to answer:

> Does \(A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C\) make a left turn, right turn, or remain collinear?

This primitive is everywhere in computational geometry.

---

# 566.1 Build two edge vectors

Let:

\[
u=B-A
\]

and:

\[
v=C-A.
\]

In coordinates:

\[
u=(u_x,u_y),
\]

\[
v=(v_x,v_y).
\]

Embed them conceptually in the XY plane of 3D:

\[
(u_x,u_y,0),
\]

\[
(v_x,v_y,0).
\]

Their cross product has only Z component:

\[
u\times v
=
(0,0,u_xv_y-u_yv_x).
\]

Define the 2D cross scalar:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{cross2}(u,v)
=
u_xv_y-u_yv_x.
}
\]

This is the fundamental 2D orientation determinant.

---

# 566.2 Signed doubled triangle area

The magnitude of the 3D cross is parallelogram area:

\[
|u_xv_y-u_yv_x|.
\]

Triangle area is half:

\[
\boxed{
A_\triangle
=
\frac12
\left|
u_xv_y-u_yv_x
\right|.
}
\]

Therefore define signed doubled area:

\[
\boxed{
A_2(A,B,C)
=
(B_x-A_x)(C_y-A_y)
-
(B_y-A_y)(C_x-A_x).
}
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
A_{\triangle,\text{signed}}
=
\frac12 A_2.
}
\]

The factor \(1/2\) is irrelevant if we only care about sign, so orientation algorithms often use the doubled area directly.

---

# 566.3 Interpreting the sign

Under the conventional 2D orientation where \(+X\) points right and \(+Y\) points upward:

\[
A_2>0
\]

means:

\[
A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C
\]

is counterclockwise.

\[
A_2<0
\]

means clockwise.

\[
A_2=0
\]

means collinear.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{orient2D}(A,B,C)
=
\operatorname{sign}(A_2).
}
\]

---

# 566.4 Worked counterclockwise example

Take:

\[
A=(0,0),
\]

\[
B=(4,0),
\]

\[
C=(1,3).
\]

Then:

\[
B-A=(4,0),
\]

\[
C-A=(1,3).
\]

Compute:

\[
A_2
=
4(3)-0(1)
=
12.
\]

Positive.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
A,B,C\text{ are counterclockwise}.
}
\]

Actual triangle area:

\[
\frac{12}{2}=6.
\]

---

# 566.5 Reverse two vertices

Use:

\[
A,C,B.
\]

Now:

\[
C-A=(1,3),
\]

\[
B-A=(4,0).
\]

Cross scalar:

\[
1(0)-3(4)=-12.
\]

Same area magnitude.

Opposite orientation.

Exactly like cross anti-commutativity.

---

# 566.6 Collinearity

Take:

\[
A=(0,0),
\]

\[
B=(2,2),
\]

\[
C=(5,5).
\]

Then:

\[
B-A=(2,2),
\]

\[
C-A=(5,5).
\]

Compute:

\[
2(5)-2(5)=0.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
A,B,C\text{ are collinear}.
}
\]

The triangle has zero area.

---

# 566.7 Why orientation is translation invariant

Translate every point by vector \(t\):

\[
A'=A+t,
\]

\[
B'=B+t,
\]

\[
C'=C+t.
\]

Then:

\[
B'-A'
=
(B+t)-(A+t)
=
B-A.
\]

Similarly:

\[
C'-A'=C-A.
\]

So signed area does not change.

Thus orientation is a property of relative geometry, not absolute position.

---

# 566.8 Positive scaling versus reflection

Uniform scale \(s>0\):

\[
u\rightarrow su,
\qquad
v\rightarrow sv.
\]

Then:

\[
\operatorname{cross2}(su,sv)
=
s^2\operatorname{cross2}(u,v).
\]

Sign stays same.

But reflect X:

\[
(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y).
\]

The determinant changes sign.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{2D reflection reverses orientation}.
}
\]

This is the 2D analogue of handedness reversal in 3D.

---

# 566.9 Screen coordinates can reverse your intuition

Many screen-space coordinate conventions use Y increasing downward.

If:

\[
+X=\text{right},
\qquad
+Y=\text{down},
\]

then the screen basis has opposite orientation from conventional mathematical XY with Y up.

A triangle that *looks clockwise on the screen* can produce the sign you mentally associate with counterclockwise mathematical coordinates, depending on the convention.

So never say:

> positive determinant means visually counterclockwise

without specifying coordinate orientation.

The formula is objective.

The English label "clockwise" depends on how axes are drawn.

---

# 566.10 C++ implementation

```cpp
struct Vec2 {
    double x;
    double y;
};

[[nodiscard]]
constexpr double orient2D(
    Vec2 a,
    Vec2 b,
    Vec2 c) noexcept
{
    return
        (b.x - a.x) * (c.y - a.y)
      - (b.y - a.y) * (c.x - a.x);
}
```

Then conceptual classification:

```cpp
const double s = orient2D(a, b, c);

if (s > 0.0) {
    // Positive orientation.
}
else if (s < 0.0) {
    // Negative orientation.
}
else {
    // Collinear in exact arithmetic.
}
```

---

# 566.11 Why exact `== 0` becomes dangerous

For integer coordinates within a safe integer range, orientation can sometimes be evaluated exactly using sufficiently wide integer arithmetic.

For floating-point coordinates, near-collinear points may produce a tiny residual:

\[
1.2\times10^{-15}
\]

instead of zero.

But a universal epsilon is also problematic because the determinant scales like area.

If coordinates scale by \(s\):

\[
A_2\rightarrow s^2A_2.
\]

A tolerance meaningful for coordinates around \(1\) may be nonsense around \(10^9\).

Robust computational geometry often uses adaptive/exact orientation predicates when correctness of the sign is critical.

This becomes especially important in:

- convex hulls;
- triangulation;
- intersection algorithms;
- topology construction.

For gameplay approximations, a scale-aware tolerance may be sufficient.

---

# 566.12 Why orientation tests are predicates, not measurements

Sometimes we care about area magnitude.

Sometimes only sign matters.

If the algorithm asks:

> which side of directed edge \(AB\) does \(C\) lie on?

then:

\[
\operatorname{sign}
\left(
\operatorname{orient2D}(A,B,C)
\right)
\]

is the required information.

Computing:

\[
\sqrt{\cdot}
\]

or normalized distances would be unnecessary.

Good geometry algorithms compute the quantity actually needed.

---

# PART 567 — ORIENTATION TESTS IN 3D USING TRIPLE PRODUCTS

2D orientation used signed area.

In 3D, the corresponding primitive is **signed volume**.

---

# 567.1 Four points are needed

In 2D, three points can define orientation because:

\[
B-A,\ C-A
\]

are two vectors that can span the plane.

In 3D, three points define only a triangle plane.

To determine which side of that plane a fourth point occupies, we need:

\[
A,B,C,D.
\]

Construct:

\[
u=B-A,
\]

\[
v=C-A,
\]

\[
w=D-A.
\]

Then evaluate scalar triple product:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{orient3D}(A,B,C,D)
=
[(B-A)\times(C-A)]\cdot(D-A).
}
\]

Equivalent cyclic arrangement:

\[
(B-A)\cdot[(C-A)\times(D-A)].
\]

The first form makes the plane-side interpretation clearer.

---

# 567.2 Interpret it geometrically

First:

\[
N=(B-A)\times(C-A).
\]

This is an oriented normal to triangle plane \(ABC\).

Then:

\[
N\cdot(D-A)
\]

measures the signed component of \(D-A\) along that normal, multiplied by the base's parallelogram area.

Therefore:

\[
\operatorname{orient3D}>0
\]

means \(D\) lies on the positive-normal side of oriented plane \(ABC\).

Negative means the opposite side.

Zero means:

\[
D
\]

lies in the same plane as \(A,B,C\), or the base triangle itself is degenerate.

---

# 567.3 Signed tetrahedral volume

The scalar triple product equals parallelepiped signed volume.

The tetrahedron with vertices:

\[
A,B,C,D
\]

has one-sixth that volume.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{tet,signed}}
=
\frac16
\operatorname{orient3D}(A,B,C,D).
}
\]

The factor \(1/6\) is irrelevant for a sign predicate.

---

# 567.4 Worked example

Take:

\[
A=(0,0,0),
\]

\[
B=(1,0,0),
\]

\[
C=(0,1,0),
\]

\[
D=(0,0,2).
\]

Then:

\[
B-A=e_x,
\]

\[
C-A=e_y.
\]

Cross:

\[
e_x\times e_y=e_z.
\]

Dot with:

\[
D-A=(0,0,2).
\]

Result:

\[
2.
\]

Therefore \(D\) lies on the positive side of oriented triangle \(ABC\).

Tetrahedron volume:

\[
\frac{2}{6}
=
\frac13.
\]

---

# 567.5 Move \(D\) below the plane

Take:

\[
D=(0,0,-2).
\]

Then:

\[
e_z\cdot(0,0,-2)=-2.
\]

Same volume magnitude.

Opposite orientation.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{orient3D sign tells plane side}.
}
\]

---

# 567.6 Reverse triangle winding

Swap:

\[
B,C.
\]

Then base normal becomes:

\[
(C-A)\times(B-A)
=
-
[(B-A)\times(C-A)].
\]

So every orient3D result changes sign.

The geometric position of \(D\) did not change.

The **orientation of the reference plane** changed.

This is exactly the same logic as reversing triangle normals.

---

# 567.7 Coplanarity

If:

\[
\operatorname{orient3D}=0,
\]

then the four points have zero signed tetrahedron volume.

For nondegenerate \(ABC\), this means \(D\) lies in their plane.

So orient3D is also a coplanarity predicate.

---

# 567.8 Scale behavior

If all coordinates are scaled uniformly by \(s\), each displacement scales by \(s\).

Cross:

\[
s^2.
\]

Dot with third displacement:

\[
s^3.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{orient3D}
\text{ scales cubically}.
}
\]

Again, this makes fixed absolute epsilons dangerous.

---

# 567.9 C++ implementation

```cpp
[[nodiscard]]
double orient3D(
    Vec3d a,
    Vec3d b,
    Vec3d c,
    Vec3d d) noexcept
{
    return dot(
        cross(b - a, c - a),
        d - a
    );
}
```

Conceptually:

```text
triangle ABC
      ↓
oriented normal-area vector
      ↓
dot against D-A
      ↓
signed volume / side test
```

---

# 567.10 Why robust orientation predicates matter so much

Imagine building a tetrahedralization or deciding whether triangles intersect.

A wrong sign can change algorithmic topology:

```text
point classified above plane
instead of below plane
```

may cause an edge to be inserted on the wrong side.

Unlike a small shading error, this can corrupt the entire combinatorial structure.

This is why computational geometry distinguishes between approximate numeric quantities and robust **predicate signs**.

---

# ORIENTATION UNIFICATION

At this point 2D and 3D should look like the same idea at different dimensions.

In 2D:

\[
\boxed{
\det(B-A,C-A)
}
\]

gives signed area and turn orientation.

In 3D:

\[
\boxed{
\det(B-A,C-A,D-A)
}
\]

gives signed volume and side orientation.

This pattern generalizes through determinants.

The determinant Part later will make that structure explicit.
