# PART 583 — LINEAR FUNCTIONALS

Part 581 introduced covectors.

Now we formalize the actual thing they do.

---

# 583.1 What is a function?

A function takes input and returns output:

\[
f:X\rightarrow Y.
\]

Example:

\[
f(x)=x^2.
\]

A **functional** is a function whose output is a scalar.

For vector space V:

\[
f:V\rightarrow\mathbb R.
\]

A **linear functional** additionally obeys linearity.

---

# 583.2 Formal definition

A function:

\[
f:V\rightarrow\mathbb R
\]

is linear if:

\[
\boxed{
f(av+bw)
=
af(v)+bf(w)
}
\]

for every vectors:

\[
v,w
\]

and scalars:

\[
a,b.
\]

This combines additivity:

\[
f(v+w)=f(v)+f(w)
\]

and homogeneity:

\[
f(av)=af(v).
\]

---

# 583.3 Example: coordinate extraction

In:

\[
\mathbb R^3,
\]

define:

\[
f_x(x,y,z)=x.
\]

Then:

\[
f_x(av+bw)
\]

extracts X of the combination.

Because X coordinates combine linearly:

\[
=
a f_x(v)+b f_x(w).
\]

So coordinate extraction is a linear functional.

This is the dual basis idea from 581.

---

# 583.4 Example: dot with fixed vector

Fix:

\[
n.
\]

Define:

\[
f(v)=n\cdot v.
\]

Then:

\[
f(av+bw)
=
n\cdot(av+bw).
\]

Dot-product distributivity:

\[
=
a(n\cdot v)+b(n\cdot w).
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
v\mapsto n\cdot v
}
\]

is a linear functional.

This is why every fixed normal can be used as a linear measuring rule.

---

# 583.5 Plane as a functional's kernel

Define:

\[
f(v)=n\cdot v.
\]

Now consider all vectors satisfying:

\[
f(v)=0.
\]

That is:

\[
n\cdot v=0.
\]

These are exactly vectors perpendicular to n.

In 3D they form a plane through the origin.

This set is called the **kernel**:

\[
\boxed{
\ker f=
\{v\mid f(v)=0\}.
}
\]

So one nonzero linear functional naturally defines a plane of vectors it annihilates.

---

# 583.6 "Annihilate" is not mystical vocabulary

If:

\[
f(v)=0,
\]

we say f annihilates v.

For a surface normal/covector n:

\[
n(t)=0
\]

for tangent t.

So the normal covector **annihilates tangent directions**.

This is an extremely clean way to define a surface normal:

\[
\boxed{
\text{normal covector = measurement rule that returns zero on every tangent direction}.
}
\]

Now the inverse-transpose law from Part 582 becomes conceptually natural.

---

# 583.7 Real-life example: elevation function

Suppose coordinates represent displacement:

\[
v=(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z).
\]

Define:

\[
f(v)=\Delta z.
\]

Then all horizontal displacements satisfy:

\[
f(v)=0.
\]

The kernel is the horizontal plane.

If:

\[
f(v)>0,
\]

movement goes upward.

If:

\[
f(v)<0,
\]

downward.

A linear functional divides vector space into:

```text
positive side
zero hyperplane
negative side
```

This is exactly how plane equations and half-space tests work.

---

# 583.8 Every linear functional in finite-dimensional coordinates

In ordinary finite-dimensional coordinates, a linear functional on:

\[
\mathbb R^n
\]

can be represented:

\[
\boxed{
f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=
a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n.
}
\]

For 3D:

\[
\boxed{
f(x,y,z)
=
ax+by+cz.
}
\]

The coefficients:

\[
(a,b,c)
\]

are covector components.

This looks exactly like a dot product, but conceptually the object is a scalar-producing map.

---

# 583.9 Linear versus affine functional

Plane not through the origin:

\[
ax+by+cz+d=0.
\]

The map:

\[
f(x)=ax+by+cz+d
\]

is not linear if:

\[
d\neq0,
\]

because:

\[
f(0)=d\neq0.
\]

A linear map must send zero to zero.

Instead this is an **affine functional**.

This distinction matters in plane equations.

The normal part:

\[
ax+by+cz
\]

is linear.

The offset:

\[
d
\]

moves the plane away from the origin.

---

# 583.10 Why transformations of covectors are inverse

Suppose:

\[
v'=Av.
\]

We want the same physical scalar measurement:

\[
f(v)
\]

after changing vector coordinates.

Call new functional:

\[
f'.
\]

We require:

\[
f'(v')=f(v).
\]

Since:

\[
v=A^{-1}v',
\]

we get:

\[
f'(v')
=
f(A^{-1}v').
\]

So the new functional must compose with the **inverse** transformation.

That is the conceptual reason covectors transform contragrediently/oppositely to vectors.

In coordinate notation this becomes inverse transpose.

So Part 582 wasn't a weird graphics exception.

It is a manifestation of general dual-space mathematics.

---

# 583.11 Mastery gate 583

You need to own:

\[
\boxed{
f(av+bw)=af(v)+bf(w).
}
\]

You should be able to identify:

\[
f(x,y,z)=2x-y+5z
\]

as linear.

But:

\[
g(x,y,z)=2x-y+5z+3
\]

is affine, not linear.

You should understand:

\[
\ker f
\]

as the set of directions the functional measures as zero.

And you should connect:

\[
\boxed{
\text{surface tangent space}
=
\ker(\text{normal covector})
}
\]

at least conceptually.

---

# PART 584 — EXTERIOR-PRODUCT INTUITION

Now we return to a problem you first saw around the cross product.

---

# 584.1 Cross product gave us something useful—but suspicious

In 3D:

\[
a\times b
\]

produces a vector perpendicular to both.

Its magnitude equals parallelogram area.

Its sign/orientation comes from handedness.

That works beautifully in 3D.

But remember Part 547:

In 4D, two independent vectors do **not** determine a unique perpendicular direction.

So what did the pair \(a,b\) fundamentally represent?

Not necessarily a normal vector.

The truly intrinsic geometric object is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{the oriented parallelogram / plane element spanned by }a,b.
}
\]

Exterior algebra keeps that object directly instead of converting it into a perpendicular vector.

---

# 584.2 Think of two sticks holding a piece of cloth

Take two vectors:

\[
a,b.
\]

Place them tail-to-tail.

They span an oriented parallelogram:

```text
        a+b
         ●
        /|
       / |
      /  |
     /   |
    ●────●
   O      a

other side follows b
```

What information matters?

The spanned plane.

The area.

The orientation.

If the vectors become parallel, area collapses to zero.

This is precisely the information we want an algebraic object to encode.

That object will be a **bivector**.

---

# 584.3 A bivector is not "two vectors stored together"

This distinction matters.

The pair:

\[
(a,b)
\]

contains more information than their oriented area element.

For example, replace:

\[
a,b
\]

with another pair:

\[
c,d
\]

that spans the same oriented parallelogram.

Exterior algebra can represent those as the same bivector.

So the bivector represents the **oriented plane element**, not the specific generating pair.

---

# 584.4 Why not always use cross product?

Because cross product turns oriented area into a normal vector only due to special 3D structure.

Exterior product works naturally in:

\[
2D,\ 3D,\ 4D,\ \ldots
\]

without pretending every plane has one unique perpendicular vector.

In 4D, an oriented plane remains an oriented plane.

No fake `Vec4` normal is required.

---

# 584.5 Exterior algebra adds grades

Ordinary scalars are grade 0.

Vectors are grade 1.

Oriented plane elements/bivectors are grade 2.

Oriented volume elements/trivectors are grade 3.

Conceptually:

```text
grade 0 → scalar
grade 1 → directed line element
grade 2 → oriented area element
grade 3 → oriented volume element
...
```

This is extremely powerful because geometry itself naturally has dimensions.

Instead of forcing everything to be "another vector," exterior algebra lets each geometric object retain its dimensional grade.

---

# 584.6 Why this is useful in graphics thinking

A triangle patch naturally supplies two tangent directions:

\[
T_u,\ T_v.
\]

What do they fundamentally define?

Not merely a normal.

They define an oriented surface element.

Cross product in 3D gives:

\[
T_u\times T_v.
\]

Exterior algebra would instead retain:

\[
T_u\wedge T_v.
\]

The latter directly means:

\[
\boxed{
\text{oriented tangent-plane area element}.
}
\]

A normal can be derived from that later if the ambient dimension, metric, and orientation make such a conversion meaningful.

This is conceptually cleaner.

---

# 584.7 Degeneracy becomes natural

If:

\[
b=\lambda a,
\]

the two vectors span no area.

So their exterior product should be:

\[
0.
\]

That means:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b=0
}
\]

when they are linearly dependent.

Compare cross product:

\[
a\times b=0
\]

for parallel 3D vectors.

Exterior product generalizes that fact to arbitrary dimension.

---

# 584.8 Why Part 584 is before Part 585

Part 584's point is conceptual:

> The cross product was hiding a more fundamental object: oriented area.

Part 585 now gives the actual algebraic operation that constructs it.

---

# PART 585 — WEDGE PRODUCT AS ORIENTED AREA CONCEPT

The wedge product is written:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b.
}
\]

It takes two vectors and returns a bivector.

---

# 585.1 First defining property: antisymmetry

Swapping the vectors reverses orientation:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b
=
-(b\wedge a).
}
\]

This matches everything we learned about signed area.

If:

\[
a=b,
\]

then:

\[
a\wedge a
=
-(a\wedge a).
\]

Therefore:

\[
2(a\wedge a)=0.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge a=0.
}
\]

That immediately captures zero area from repeated direction.

---

# 585.2 Bilinearity

The wedge distributes:

\[
\boxed{
(a+b)\wedge c
=
a\wedge c+b\wedge c
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge(b+c)
=
a\wedge b+a\wedge c.
}
\]

Scalars pull out:

\[
(\lambda a)\wedge b
=
\lambda(a\wedge b).
\]

This means oriented area responds linearly to each edge vector.

Double one side of a parallelogram:

\[
\text{area doubles}.
\]

Correct.

---

# 585.3 Derive coordinate form in 2D

Let:

\[
a=a_xe_x+a_ye_y,
\]

\[
b=b_xe_x+b_ye_y.
\]

Then:

\[
a\wedge b
=
(a_xe_x+a_ye_y)
\wedge
(b_xe_x+b_ye_y).
\]

Expand:

\[
=
a_xb_x(e_x\wedge e_x)
+
a_xb_y(e_x\wedge e_y)
\]

\[
+
a_yb_x(e_y\wedge e_x)
+
a_yb_y(e_y\wedge e_y).
\]

But:

\[
e_x\wedge e_x=0,
\]

\[
e_y\wedge e_y=0,
\]

and:

\[
e_y\wedge e_x
=
-(e_x\wedge e_y).
\]

Therefore:

\[
a\wedge b
=
(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)
(e_x\wedge e_y).
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b
=
(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)e_x\wedge e_y.
}
\]

Recognize the coefficient?

It is exactly the signed 2D area determinant from Part 566.

So orientation tests were already computing the coefficient of a wedge product.

---

# 585.4 3D wedge product

Let:

\[
a=(a_x,a_y,a_z)
\]

and:

\[
b=(b_x,b_y,b_z).
\]

There are three independent coordinate planes:

\[
e_x\wedge e_y,
\]

\[
e_x\wedge e_z,
\]

\[
e_y\wedge e_z.
\]

Expanding gives:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b
=
(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)e_x\wedge e_y
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
+
(a_xb_z-a_zb_x)e_x\wedge e_z
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
+
(a_yb_z-a_zb_y)e_y\wedge e_z.
}
\]

These three coefficients describe how much oriented area lies in each coordinate plane.

---

# 585.5 Compare cross product components

Cross product:

\[
a\times b
=
(
a_yb_z-a_zb_y,\;
a_zb_x-a_xb_z,\;
a_xb_y-a_yb_x
).
\]

Wedge components are roughly:

```text
XY area
XZ area
YZ area
```

Cross components correspond to perpendicular axes:

```text
X normal ↔ YZ area
Y normal ↔ ZX area
Z normal ↔ XY area
```

This is not coincidence.

In 3D, an oriented plane element can be mapped to its perpendicular pseudovector.

This mapping depends on the metric and orientation and is related to the **Hodge dual**.

You don't need Hodge-star machinery yet.

The important thing is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{cross product is essentially a 3D dual representation of the wedge product}.
}
\]

---

# 585.6 Why wedge product is more fundamental than cross product

In 4D, wedge of two vectors still works.

How many independent plane components exist?

Choose two distinct coordinate axes:

\[
\binom42=6.
\]

They are:

\[
e_1\wedge e_2,
\]

\[
e_1\wedge e_3,
\]

\[
e_1\wedge e_4,
\]

\[
e_2\wedge e_3,
\]

\[
e_2\wedge e_4,
\]

\[
e_3\wedge e_4.
\]

So a general 4D bivector has six components.

That exactly matches our dimensional argument from Part 547.

There is no reason to squash those six independent oriented-area components into four coordinates.

Exterior algebra simply stores the correct geometric object.

---

# 585.7 Magnitude

In Euclidean geometry, the magnitude of a simple bivector:

\[
a\wedge b
\]

corresponds to parallelogram area:

\[
\boxed{
\|a\wedge b\|
=
\|a\|\|b\|\sin\theta.
}
\]

Same area magnitude as:

\[
\|a\times b\|
\]

in 3D.

But the bivector represents the oriented plane directly.

---

# 585.8 Real surface example

Our spaceship triangle has edges:

\[
e_1=B-A,
\]

\[
e_2=C-A.
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
e_1\wedge e_2
}
\]

represents its oriented double-triangle-area plane element.

Its magnitude:

\[
\|e_1\wedge e_2\|
\]

is the parallelogram area.

Triangle area:

\[
\boxed{
A_\triangle
=
\frac12\|e_1\wedge e_2\|.
}
\]

If the triangle collapses to a line:

\[
e_1\wedge e_2=0.
\]

This is a dimension-independent way of expressing triangle degeneracy.

---

# 585.9 Wedge builds higher grades

Take three vectors:

\[
a,b,c.
\]

You can form:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b\wedge c.
}
\]

This represents an oriented volume element.

If the three vectors are linearly dependent:

\[
a\wedge b\wedge c=0.
\]

In 3D, its scalar magnitude corresponds to parallelepiped volume.

So:

```text
wedge 2 vectors → oriented area

wedge 3 vectors → oriented volume

wedge k vectors → oriented k-dimensional volume
```

This is a remarkably clean generalization of determinants, cross products and triple products.

---

# 585.10 Linear independence detector

A powerful fact:

\[
\boxed{
v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k=0
}
\]

iff the vectors are linearly dependent, assuming the usual exterior-algebra setting.

Why?

If one vector is a combination of the others, bilinearity plus antisymmetry causes repeated-direction terms, all of which vanish.

So wedge products naturally encode independence and oriented measure.

---

# 585.11 Mastery gate 585

You should be able to derive:

\[
a\wedge b
=
(a_xb_y-a_yb_x)e_x\wedge e_y
\]

in 2D from bilinearity and antisymmetry.

Then explain:

\[
a\wedge a=0
\]

and why:

\[
a\wedge b=0
\]

means no 2D area is spanned.

And you should be able to explain the relationship:

\[
\boxed{
\text{cross product}
\approx
\text{3D dual encoding of wedge-product area}.
}
\]

---

# PART 586 — GEOMETRIC-ALGEBRA MOTIVATION FOR GRAPHICS

Now: why invent an even larger algebra?

Because dot products, wedge products, complex numbers, cross products, reflections and rotations look like separate tricks—but they are related pieces of one geometric multiplication system.

That system is **geometric algebra**.

This Part is motivation, not a full geometric-algebra course.

---

# 586.1 The fragmentation problem

Look at what we have learned:

\[
a\cdot b
\]

gives scalar alignment.

\[
a\wedge b
\]

gives oriented area.

\[
a\times b
\]

gives a special 3D pseudovector.

Complex numbers rotate 2D.

Quaternions will rotate 3D.

Normals/covectors encode constraints.

Matrices transform coordinates.

This works.

But the toolbox feels fragmented.

Geometric algebra asks:

> Can we construct one algebraic product in which geometric relations such as length, angle, oriented plane, reflection and rotation appear naturally?

---

# 586.2 Geometric product

For vectors \(a,b\), geometric algebra defines a product:

\[
\boxed{
ab
=
a\cdot b
+
a\wedge b.
}
\]

Look carefully.

The result is not necessarily another vector.

It contains:

\[
\boxed{
\text{scalar part}
}
\]

plus:

\[
\boxed{
\text{bivector part}.
}
\]

So multiplying two vectors captures both:

\[
\cos\theta
\]

and:

\[
\sin\theta
\]

style geometric relationships simultaneously.

---

# 586.3 Parallel vectors

If \(a,b\) are parallel:

\[
a\wedge b=0.
\]

Therefore:

\[
ab=a\cdot b.
\]

Product is purely scalar.

That makes sense: two parallel vectors span no area.

---

# 586.4 Perpendicular vectors

If:

\[
a\cdot b=0,
\]

then:

\[
ab=a\wedge b.
\]

Product is purely bivector.

Two perpendicular vectors have no scalar alignment and span maximal area for their lengths.

Again the algebra matches geometry.

---

# 586.5 Recover dot and wedge from geometric product

Swap order:

\[
ba
=
b\cdot a+b\wedge a.
\]

Dot is symmetric:

\[
b\cdot a=a\cdot b.
\]

Wedge is antisymmetric:

\[
b\wedge a=-a\wedge b.
\]

Therefore:

\[
ab+ba
=
2a\cdot b.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
a\cdot b
=
\frac12(ab+ba).
}
\]

Subtract:

\[
ab-ba
=
2a\wedge b.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b
=
\frac12(ab-ba).
}
\]

So dot and wedge aren't unrelated operations inside geometric algebra.

They are the symmetric and antisymmetric portions of one product.

That is a beautiful structural insight.

---

# 586.6 Vector squared

Take:

\[
a^2=aa.
\]

Then:

\[
a\wedge a=0.
\]

Thus:

\[
a^2=a\cdot a.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
a^2=\|a\|^2
}
\]

in ordinary Euclidean signature.

A vector's square is its squared magnitude.

That gives vector inversion naturally:

For nonzero \(a\):

\[
a^{-1}
=
\frac{a}{a^2}
=
\frac{a}{\|a\|^2}.
\]

Because:

\[
a a^{-1}=1.
\]

This starts to make geometry algebraically compact.

---

# 586.7 The startling 2D connection to complex numbers

Let orthonormal basis:

\[
e_1,e_2.
\]

Define bivector:

\[
I=e_1e_2.
\]

Because they are perpendicular:

\[
e_1e_2=-e_2e_1.
\]

Now compute:

\[
I^2
=
e_1e_2e_1e_2.
\]

Swap middle:

\[
e_2e_1=-e_1e_2.
\]

Therefore:

\[
I^2
=
-e_1e_1e_2e_2.
\]

Since unit basis vectors square to 1:

\[
e_1^2=e_2^2=1.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
I^2=-1.
}
\]

That is exactly the defining algebraic behavior of:

\[
i^2=-1
\]

from complex numbers.

So the imaginary unit in 2D rotations can be interpreted geometrically as the **oriented unit plane element**.

That is a powerful connection to Part 503.

---

# 586.8 Rotations emerge from plane elements

Because:

\[
I^2=-1,
\]

the exponential:

\[
e^{I\theta}
\]

behaves like:

\[
\cos\theta+I\sin\theta.
\]

This is the same structure as complex rotation.

In geometric algebra, rotations are represented by objects called **rotors**.

Conceptually a rotor contains:

\[
\cos\frac\theta2
\]

plus an oriented-plane term involving:

\[
\sin\frac\theta2.
\]

And vectors are rotated through a sandwich-like operation.

This mirrors what quaternions later do in 3D.

Indeed, 3D rotation quaternions are deeply related to the even subalgebra of 3D geometric algebra.

That is why quaternion formulas can feel less arbitrary once geometric algebra is understood.

We will not replace the dedicated quaternion Parts 667+ here.

---

# 586.9 Reflections become fundamental

Reflection across a plane can also be expressed elegantly using geometric products.

Recall our earlier reflection formula:

\[
r
=
v-2(v\cdot n)n.
\]

Geometric algebra can encode reflection through compact sandwich products involving a unit normal.

Why is that important conceptually?

Because rotations can be understood as compositions of reflections.

This gives one algebraic framework for both transformations rather than unrelated formulas.

---

# 586.10 Why graphics engineers may care

Geometric algebra offers a unified language for:

\[
\text{projections},
\]

\[
\text{reflections},
\]

\[
\text{rotations},
\]

\[
\text{oriented subspaces},
\]

\[
\text{intersections in extended formulations},
\]

and other geometry.

It is especially conceptually attractive when a system constantly manipulates directions, planes, rotations, and geometric incidence relations.

---

# 586.11 Why most production graphics code still uses vectors/matrices/quaternions

A powerful abstraction does not automatically win ecosystem adoption.

Traditional graphics stacks have enormous investment in:

```text
Vec3
Mat4
Quat
dot
cross
```

GPUs, shading languages, file formats and APIs are built around them.

Matrices are universally understood.

Quaternions are compact and efficient for rotation.

So geometric algebra may offer conceptual unification but introduce:

- less familiar notation;
- different library ecosystems;
- more complex multivector representation;
- potentially unnecessary generality for routine tasks.

A graphics engineer should understand the idea without assuming every engine should be rewritten around GA.

---

# 586.12 Real benefit even if you never use a GA library

After this Part you should see:

\[
\boxed{
\text{dot product = scalar interaction}
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
\text{wedge product = oriented subspace interaction}.
}
\]

Cross products, complex rotations and quaternions stop looking like completely disconnected mathematical hacks.

That conceptual unification alone is useful.

---

# 586.13 Mastery gate 586

You should be able to derive:

\[
\boxed{
ab=a\cdot b+a\wedge b
}
\]

then:

\[
\boxed{
a\cdot b=\frac{ab+ba}{2}
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b=\frac{ab-ba}{2}.
}
\]

You should understand why:

\[
a^2=\|a\|^2.
\]

And derive for an orthonormal 2D basis:

\[
(e_1e_2)^2=-1.
\]

If you can explain why this links geometric plane orientation to complex-number rotation, you've understood the motivation.

---

# PART 587 — FLOATING-POINT VECTOR STORAGE IN C++

Now we abruptly leave abstract mathematics and touch memory.

This is intentional.

We have spent almost 90 Parts talking about what vectors **mean**.

Now:

> What actually exists inside RAM when an engine says `Vec3 position`?

This Part starts the implementation block leading into Vec2/Vec3/Vec4 design, alignment, SIMD and engine invariants. The following Parts explicitly cover those separately, so here we focus on **the foundational physical storage model**. Project_Sheldon_Master_Curricul…

---

# 587.1 Mathematics says

\[
v=(x,y,z).
\]

Computer memory does not store parentheses.

It stores bits.

A typical C++ representation might be:

```cpp
struct RawVec3
{
    float x;
    float y;
    float z;
};
```

Conceptually:

```text
RawVec3 object

+-----------+
| x float   |
+-----------+
| y float   |
+-----------+
| z float   |
+-----------+
```

But we need to understand what "float" and those boxes actually mean.

---

# 587.2 What is `float`?

C++ defines a floating-point type named:

```cpp
float
```

but C++ does not universally require it to be IEEE-754 binary32 on every imaginable implementation.

On mainstream desktop/mobile/GPU-oriented platforms it is overwhelmingly commonly:

\[
32\text{-bit IEEE-754 binary32}.
\]

An engine that depends on that can verify assumptions:

```cpp
#include <limits>

static_assert(sizeof(float) == 4);

static_assert(
    std::numeric_limits<float>::is_iec559
);
```

`is_iec559` is commonly used to detect IEC 60559/IEEE-style semantics, though platform-specific guarantees may still matter.

Never confuse:

\[
\boxed{
\text{common ABI fact}
}
\]

with:

\[
\boxed{
\text{universal C++ language guarantee}.
}
\]

---

# 587.3 Typical binary32 structure

A common IEEE binary32 value occupies:

\[
32\text{ bits}.
\]

Conceptually:

```text
1 sign bit
8 exponent bits
23 stored fraction bits
```

With normalized implicit leading significand bit, effective precision is roughly:

\[
24\text{ binary significant bits}.
\]

This is why a `Vec3` does not hold exact real numbers.

It holds three finite floating-point approximations.

So mathematical vector:

\[
(0.1,0.2,0.3)
\]

becomes:

```text
nearest representable binary float to 0.1
nearest representable binary float to 0.2
nearest representable binary float to 0.3
```

Every vector operation later inherits this finite representation.

---

# 587.4 Typical `Vec3` memory footprint

If:

```cpp
sizeof(float) == 4
```

then three raw floats require 12 bytes of member payload:

\[
3\times4=12.
\]

On many conventional ABIs:

```cpp
struct RawVec3
{
    float x;
    float y;
    float z;
};
```

will have:

```text
sizeof(RawVec3) = 12
alignof(RawVec3) = 4
```

But do not turn "often" into a language-law assumption.

C++ implementations may insert padding to satisfy object layout/alignment rules.

The object representation can include padding.

This is why later Parts 593–594 explicitly distinguish alignment and packed/aligned Vec3 designs.

---

# 587.5 Arrays give stronger contiguity intuition

For:

```cpp
float v[3];
```

array elements are contiguous.

Memory conceptually:

```text
address +0   → v[0]
address +4   → v[1]
address +8   → v[2]
```

assuming 4-byte floats.

There is no padding **between array elements**.

This fact makes arrays useful when you need guaranteed regular scalar strides.

---

# 587.6 Struct representation

For:

```cpp
struct Vec3
{
    float x;
    float y;
    float z;
};
```

the compiler lays out the members according to the type's object-layout rules and alignment requirements.

On ordinary platforms you might see:

```text
offset 0  x
offset 4  y
offset 8  z
sizeof 12
```

But later we may deliberately request stronger alignment:

```cpp
struct alignas(16) Vec3Aligned
{
    float x;
    float y;
    float z;
};
```

Now a likely layout is:

```text
offset 0   x
offset 4   y
offset 8   z
offset 12  padding
sizeof 16
```

Why intentionally waste 4 bytes?

Potentially to make loads, arrays, ABI compatibility or SIMD operations simpler.

Full trade-off belongs to Parts 593–595.

---

# 587.7 Arrays of Vec3 make padding matter more

Suppose:

```cpp
Vec3 positions[4];
```

If:

\[
sizeof(Vec3)=12,
\]

layout might be:

```text
position 0: bytes  0..11
position 1: bytes 12..23
position 2: bytes 24..35
position 3: bytes 36..47
```

Stride:

\[
12.
\]

If aligned Vec3 has:

\[
sizeof=16,
\]

then:

```text
position 0: bytes  0..15
position 1: bytes 16..31
position 2: bytes 32..47
position 3: bytes 48..63
```

Stride:

\[
16.
\]

This affects:

- total memory;
- cache usage;
- vectorized loads;
- GPU buffer layouts;
- serialization;
- binary interoperability.

So `sizeof(Vec3)` is not trivia.

It affects entire array architecture.

---

# 587.8 One million positions

Suppose one million vertices.

Packed 12-byte positions:

\[
12,000,000\text{ bytes}
\]

roughly 12 MB decimal.

16-byte stride:

\[
16,000,000\text{ bytes}.
\]

Difference:

\[
4,000,000\text{ bytes}.
\]

Four megabytes for just one million vectors.

Now add:

- normals;
- tangents;
- velocities;
- particle positions;
- instance data.

Alignment choices can materially affect memory bandwidth.

But 16-byte layout may also simplify SIMD/GPU paths.

This is why there is no universal "best Vec3 layout."

---

# 587.9 AoS versus SoA preview

Suppose four particle positions.

Array of structures:

```cpp
struct Vec3 { float x,y,z; };

Vec3 p[4];
```

Memory:

```text
x0 y0 z0 | x1 y1 z1 | x2 y2 z2 | x3 y3 z3
```

This is **Array of Structures**, AoS.

Alternative:

```cpp
float x[4];
float y[4];
float z[4];
```

Memory:

```text
x0 x1 x2 x3
y0 y1 y2 y3
z0 z1 z2 z3
```

This is **Structure of Arrays**, SoA.

If computation needs:

```text
all X components at once
```

SoA may map naturally to vectorized processing.

If code repeatedly processes:

```text
one complete position
```

AoS can be convenient.

We are not choosing yet.

The point is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{mathematical vector representation does not dictate physical memory layout}.
}
\]

---

# 587.10 CPU register representation need not match memory representation

Memory might store:

```text
12 bytes
```

for x,y,z.

CPU calculation may load them into:

```text
128-bit SIMD register
```

with a fourth unused lane.

For example conceptually:

```text
[x y z ?]
```

or:

```text
[x y z 0]
```

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{storage layout}
\neq
\text{execution register layout}.
}
\]

This distinction matters when people claim:

> Vec3 must be 16 bytes because SIMD.

Not necessarily.

You can have packed memory and widen during computation.

Whether that is beneficial depends on workload and architecture.

Part 595 will study SIMD explicitly.

---

# 587.11 Endianness still exists

Suppose one float uses four bytes.

The order of those bytes in memory depends on machine endianness.

Earlier Parts taught endianness.

A `Vec3` is therefore not merely:

```text
12 meaningful bytes
```

in some universally portable serialization format.

If you write raw object bytes to disk and read them on another platform, questions include:

- float representation;
- byte order;
- padding;
- alignment;
- ABI;
- versioning.

So robust serialization normally defines a binary format rather than dumping arbitrary C++ object representations blindly.

---

# 587.12 `memcpy` versus reinterpret-casting

Suppose you need the bits of a float.

Dangerous thinking:

```cpp
uint32_t bits =
    *reinterpret_cast<uint32_t*>(&f);
```

That can violate C++ aliasing/object-model rules.

Safer modern approaches include:

```cpp
#include <bit>

std::uint32_t bits =
    std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f);
```

assuming equal sizes.

Or `std::memcpy` for byte transfers.

This matters in graphics engines because low-level math code often sits close to:

- GPU buffers;
- serialization;
- SIMD;
- hashing;
- binary formats.

Low-level speed does not excuse undefined behavior.

---

# 587.13 Why raw `memcmp` is not vector equality

Suppose:

\[
+0.0f
\]

and:

\[
-0.0f.
\]

They compare numerically equal:

```cpp
+0.0f == -0.0f
```

is true under normal IEEE behavior.

But their bit patterns differ.

So raw byte equality can say:

```text
different
```

while floating-point comparison says:

```text
equal.
```

NaNs create even stranger semantics:

\[
NaN\neq NaN.
\]

Thus:

```cpp
memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof(Vec3))
```

is not generally the same semantic operation as:

```cpp
a == b
```

for floating vectors.

And approximate geometric equality is yet another operation, coming in Part 596.

---

# 587.14 Padding makes byte comparison worse

If a struct contains padding bytes, those bytes may hold unspecified values depending on how the object was created/assigned.

Two vectors with equal member values could potentially have different padding bit contents.

Therefore comparing entire object representations can produce false differences.

Likewise hashing raw struct bytes can accidentally hash meaningless padding.

This is why low-level object representation must be understood before binary tricks.

---

# 587.15 Ownership and lifetime

A simple vector value:

```cpp
struct Vec3
{
    float x, y, z;
};
```

typically owns its three scalar members directly.

No heap allocation.

No pointer ownership.

Construction creates one value object.

Copying copies component values.

Destruction usually has nothing to do.

This is ideal for a tiny math type.

You generally want:

```text
cheap copy
cheap move
trivial lifetime
no hidden allocation
```

unless there is a very unusual requirement.

That is why vector math types are typically value types.

---

# 587.16 Why no heap allocation?

Imagine:

```cpp
class Vec3
{
    float* data;
};
```

where every vector allocates three floats dynamically.

Now every position may require:

```text
allocation
pointer indirection
fragmentation
lifetime management
cache misses
```

for twelve bytes of actual numeric payload.

That would be disastrous for normal engine workloads.

Vectors are small fixed-size data.

They should normally live inline.

---

# 587.17 Thread safety

A `Vec3` value has no magical concurrency concerns if each thread owns its own object.

But shared mutation still races.

Example:

```cpp
sharedPosition.x += 1.0f;
```

from multiple threads without synchronization can be a data race.

"Vec3 is simple" does not make unsynchronized shared writes legal.

Math types should preferably be easy to use as immutable values or thread-local/data-partitioned values in parallel systems.

---

# 587.18 CPU cache intuition

Suppose cache line is commonly around 64 bytes on a particular CPU.

With packed 12-byte Vec3s, one cache line can contain portions of several vectors.

With 16-byte stride, exactly four vectors fit in 64 bytes.

Neither fact alone says which is faster.

Consider workload.

If you process:

```text
position + velocity + normal
```

stored in separate arrays, different cache patterns arise than one monolithic vertex struct.

Performance emerges from access patterns, not merely individual `sizeof`.

---

# 587.19 GPU buffer mismatch

Suppose CPU believes:

```text
Vec3 stride = 12
```

but shader/buffer layout expects:

```text
stride = 16
```

Then GPU might read:

```text
vertex 0 xyz correctly

vertex 1 x from previous padding/data

vertex 1 y/z shifted

everything after first element corrupted
```

This is a classic data-layout bug.

The math is perfect.

The memory contract is wrong.

Graphics engineers must debug both.

---

# 587.20 Real memory trace

Suppose:

```cpp
RawVec3 v{1.0f, 2.0f, 3.0f};
```

On a conventional platform with 32-bit IEEE little-endian floats, conceptual byte representation may resemble:

```text
1.0f bits = 0x3F800000
bytes     = 00 00 80 3F

2.0f bits = 0x40000000
bytes     = 00 00 00 40

3.0f bits = 0x40400000
bytes     = 00 00 40 40
```

So contiguous memory might look:

```text
00 00 80 3F | 00 00 00 40 | 00 00 40 40
     x              y              z
```

Again, that concrete byte sequence assumes a specific conventional platform and should not be treated as universal C++ behavior.

But this is what "the vector exists in memory" actually means.

---

# 587.21 Float precision propagates into vector geometry

Suppose position:

\[
P=(10^8,10^8,10^8)
\]

stored in 32-bit floats.

At that magnitude, the spacing between adjacent representable floats is much larger than around zero.

Adding:

\[
0.001
\]

may change nothing.

Then two nearby points:

\[
P
\]

and:

\[
P+(0.001,0,0)
\]

may collapse to identical stored values.

Now:

\[
B-A
\]

becomes zero.

That can destroy:

- normals;
- triangle areas;
- collision distances;
- tangent frames.

So vector storage precision is not only a memory issue.

It changes what geometry can exist numerically.

---

# 587.22 Why large-world engines care

Imagine a world coordinate measured in metres.

At origin:

\[
x\approx0,
\]

float gives extremely fine absolute spacing.

At:

\[
x=10^7,
\]

spacing becomes much coarser.

Your character can start jittering because centimetre or millimetre movement can no longer be represented accurately.

Solutions later may include:

```text
double-precision world positions
floating origin
camera-relative rendering
hierarchical coordinates
local cells
```

Again, representation affects architecture.

---

# 587.23 Float versus double vector storage

A `double` commonly uses 8 bytes.

So:

```cpp
struct DVec3
{
    double x, y, z;
};
```

has 24 bytes of scalar payload versus 12 for three 4-byte floats.

Double offers substantially more precision and exponent range but doubles bandwidth/storage for raw components.

Graphics often uses:

```text
double on CPU world simulation
float on GPU relative rendering
```

in large-world scenarios.

Whether this is appropriate depends on engine requirements.

---

# 587.24 `float` is usually enough for local graphics vectors

Normals:

\[
[-1,1]
\]

directions:

\[
[-1,1]
\]

UVs often modest ranges.

Camera-relative positions perhaps within kilometres rather than astronomical coordinates.

For these, binary32 may be entirely adequate.

The problem isn't:

> float is bad.

The engineering question is:

\[
\boxed{
\text{Does the numeric range and required resolution fit the chosen representation?}
}
\]

---

# 587.25 A baseline value type

Before Parts 588–590 design specialized vector APIs, the fundamental storage might look as simple as:

```cpp
struct Float3
{
    float x{};
    float y{};
    float z{};
};
```

This gives us three named component values.

No normalization invariant.

No semantic coordinate-space information.

No distinction between:

```text
position
normal
velocity
RGB colour
```

That's deliberately low-level.

Later Parts add API meaning.

---

# 587.26 Do not confuse storage type with semantic type

These may all physically contain:

```text
3 × float
```

but mean wildly different things:

```cpp
WorldPosition
WorldDirection
SurfaceNormal
Velocity
RGB
Scale3
AngularVelocity
```

The fact that they have identical memory representation does not mean every operation between them is valid.

For example:

```cpp
WorldPosition + SurfaceNormal
```

may compile with a generic raw Vec3 API yet have no sensible domain meaning.

Part 598–599 will address stronger invariants and coordinate-space distinction.

---

# 587.27 Mastery gate 587

You should be able to answer this chain without guessing:

A mathematical Vec3 is:

\[
(x,y,z).
\]

A typical machine Vec3 may be:

```text
three binary floating-point values
stored inline in a C++ object
```

with a common payload of:

\[
12\text{ bytes}
\]

when `float` is 4 bytes.

But actual `sizeof` and alignment are object-layout/ABI properties.

Padding may exist.

Array elements have regular contiguous layout.

Object memory representation is not automatically a portable file format.

Raw byte equality is not floating-point semantic equality.

A vector's stored precision constrains geometric precision.

And:

\[
\boxed{
\text{representation}
\rightarrow
\text{memory footprint}
\rightarrow
\text{bandwidth/cache behavior}
\rightarrow
\text{numeric precision}
\rightarrow
\text{actual engine behavior}.
}
\]

Now connect the entire block using our spaceship triangle.

We start with a triangle point.

In homogeneous clip coordinates:

\[
P_c=(X,Y,Z,W).
\]

Part 580 says:

\[
\boxed{
P_{\text{ndc}}
=
(X/W,Y/W,Z/W)
}
\]

gives a canonical projective coordinate suitable for later viewport/raster mapping.

Now consider the triangle surface.

Its tangent vectors transform as ordinary vectors.

Its surface normal is something different.

Part 581 says:

\[
\boxed{
\text{a normal behaves naturally as a covector-like measurement rule}
}
\]

because it measures tangent motion and returns zero:

\[
n(t)=0.
\]

Part 583 formalizes such measurement rules as linear functionals.

That lets Part 582 make complete sense:

\[
\boxed{
t'=At
}
\]

but:

\[
\boxed{
n'=A^{-T}n
}
\]

so:

\[
n'(t')=n(t).
\]

The normal still annihilates the transformed tangent plane.

Then Parts 584–585 ask something even deeper:

What was the surface itself?

Two tangent vectors:

\[
T_u,T_v
\]

define an oriented surface element:

\[
\boxed{
T_u\wedge T_v.
}
\]

The cross-product normal was merely a convenient 3D dual encoding of that oriented area.

Part 586 then shows that:

\[
\boxed{
a\cdot b
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
a\wedge b
}
\]

can be seen as complementary portions of one geometric product:

\[
\boxed{
ab=a\cdot b+a\wedge b.
}
\]

So alignment, area, reflections and rotations begin to fit inside one algebraic picture.

Finally Part 587 asks:

> Fine—but where does any of this actually live?

And the answer is:

```text
float x
float y
float z
```

or some related layout in real memory, with finite precision, alignment, cache and ABI constraints.

That transition is fundamental:

```text
projective geometry
      ↓
dual-space geometry
      ↓
surface orientation
      ↓
exterior algebra
      ↓
geometric algebra
      ↓
actual bits in RAM
```

That is what this curriculum is supposed to do: connect abstract math all the way down to the machine instead of leaving them as separate subjects.

# PART 553 — REFLECTION OF A DIRECTION ACROSS A NORMAL

## 553.1 The problem

Imagine an incoming ray striking a perfectly reflecting surface.

We know:

- the incoming direction;
- the surface orientation;
- we want the outgoing reflected direction.

The physically familiar law is:

\[
\boxed{
\theta_i=\theta_r
}
\]

where the two angles are measured relative to the surface normal.

But implementing reflection by explicitly calculating angles would be wasteful. Dot products and projection let us derive the reflected vector directly.

---

## 553.2 Fix the convention first

This matters enormously because reflection formulas often look "wrong" only because two codebases define their directions differently.

We will define:

\[
\hat n
\]

as a **unit surface normal**, and:

\[
\vec i
\]

as the **incident direction pointing in the direction the ray is travelling toward the surface**.

For a ray approaching the front side of the surface, usually:

\[
\vec i\cdot\hat n<0.
\]

For example, horizontal surface:

\[
\hat n=(0,1).
\]

A ray travelling down-right toward it might be:

\[
\vec i=
\left(
\frac1{\sqrt2},
-\frac1{\sqrt2}
\right).
\]

We seek reflected direction:

\[
\vec r.
\]

---

# 553.3 Decompose the incident vector

Part 538 taught us projection.

The component of \(\vec i\) along unit normal \(\hat n\) is:

\[
\operatorname{proj}_{\hat n}\vec i
=
(\vec i\cdot\hat n)\hat n.
\]

Call it:

\[
\vec i_n.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
\vec i_n
=
(\vec i\cdot\hat n)\hat n.
}
\]

The tangent component is the rejection:

\[
\vec i_t
=
\vec i-\vec i_n.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
\vec i
=
\vec i_t+\vec i_n.
}
\]

Picture:

```text
                     n
                     ↑
                     │
        reflected   /│
                  /  │
                /    │
──────────────●──────────── surface
               \    │
                \   │
                 \  │
                  \ ↓
                  incoming
```

Reflection keeps the tangent component and flips the normal component.

That is the entire operation.

---

# 553.4 Reflect by negating only the normal component

Incoming:

\[
\vec i
=
\vec i_t+\vec i_n.
\]

Reflected:

\[
\vec r
=
\vec i_t-\vec i_n.
\]

But:

\[
\vec i_t
=
\vec i-\vec i_n.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\vec r
=
(\vec i-\vec i_n)-\vec i_n.
\]

So:

\[
\vec r
=
\vec i-2\vec i_n.
\]

Substitute:

\[
\vec i_n
=
(\vec i\cdot\hat n)\hat n.
\]

We obtain:

\[
\boxed{
\vec r
=
\vec i
-
2(\vec i\cdot\hat n)\hat n
}
\]

when:

\[
\|\hat n\|=1.
\]

That is the reflection formula.

You now know why the factor **2** exists.

We are not merely removing the normal component once. We remove the original normal component and then add an equal component on the opposite side.

---

# 553.5 Non-unit normal formula

If \(n\) is not normalized, projection onto \(n\) is:

\[
\operatorname{proj}_n i
=
\frac{i\cdot n}{n\cdot n}n.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
r
=
i-
2
\frac{i\cdot n}{n\cdot n}n
}
\]

for nonzero \(n\).

This is mathematically valid.

Nevertheless, graphics pipelines often maintain unit normals because many other formulas become simpler.

---

# 553.6 Hand-worked example

Let:

\[
i=
\left(
\frac1{\sqrt2},
-\frac1{\sqrt2}
\right)
\]

and:

\[
n=(0,1).
\]

Dot:

\[
i\cdot n
=
-\frac1{\sqrt2}.
\]

Then:

\[
2(i\cdot n)n
=
2
\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
(0,1).
\]

So:

\[
=
\left(
0,-\sqrt2
\right).
\]

Now:

\[
r
=
\left(
\frac1{\sqrt2},
-\frac1{\sqrt2}
\right)
-
\left(
0,-\sqrt2
\right).
\]

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
r=
\left(
\frac1{\sqrt2},
\frac1{\sqrt2}
\right).
}
\]

The X/tangent component stayed unchanged.

The Y/normal component flipped sign.

Exactly what reflection should do.

---

# 553.7 Prove reflection preserves magnitude

For a perfect reflection:

\[
\|r\|=\|i\|.
\]

Let's prove it.

Let:

\[
d=i\cdot n
\]

with unit \(n\).

Then:

\[
r=i-2dn.
\]

Self-dot:

\[
r\cdot r
=
(i-2dn)\cdot(i-2dn).
\]

Expand:

\[
=
i\cdot i
-
4d(i\cdot n)
+
4d^2(n\cdot n).
\]

But:

\[
i\cdot n=d
\]

and:

\[
n\cdot n=1.
\]

Therefore:

\[
r\cdot r
=
i\cdot i
-
4d^2
+
4d^2.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
r\cdot r=i\cdot i.
}
\]

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
\|r\|=\|i\|.
}
\]

Reflection changes orientation, not vector magnitude.

---

# 553.8 Prove the normal component reverses

Dot reflected vector with \(n\):

\[
r\cdot n
=
[i-2(i\cdot n)n]\cdot n.
\]

Expand:

\[
=
i\cdot n
-
2(i\cdot n)(n\cdot n).
\]

Unit normal:

\[
n\cdot n=1.
\]

Therefore:

\[
r\cdot n
=
i\cdot n-2i\cdot n.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
r\cdot n
=
-(i\cdot n).
}
\]

The signed normal projection reverses perfectly.

That is the algebraic form of:

\[
\theta_i=\theta_r.
\]

---

# 553.9 Tangent component is unchanged

Projecting onto the normal accounts for the part that flips. The rejection from the normal is:

\[
i_t=i-(i\cdot n)n.
\]

For \(r\):

\[
r_t=r-(r\cdot n)n.
\]

Substitute:

\[
r=i-2dn
\]

and:

\[
r\cdot n=-d.
\]

Then:

\[
r_t
=
i-2dn+d n.
\]

Therefore:

\[
r_t=i-dn.
\]

But:

\[
i_t=i-dn.
\]

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
r_t=i_t.
}
\]

So reflection can be summarized exactly as:

\[
\boxed{
\text{tangent component unchanged,
normal component sign reversed}.
}
\]

---

# 553.10 Limiting cases

If \(i\) is tangent to the surface:

\[
i\cdot n=0.
\]

Then:

\[
r=i.
\]

No normal component exists to flip.

If \(i\) is directly opposite the normal:

\[
i=-n,
\]

then:

\[
r=-n-2(-1)n=n.
\]

It reverses completely.

Those two cases should always be sanity tests.

---

# 553.11 Reflection is an involution

An **involution** is an operation whose second application undoes the first.

Reflect \(i\) to obtain \(r\).

Then reflect \(r\) across the same plane.

Because the normal component has already been flipped, the second reflection flips it back.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
R_n(R_n(i))=i.
}
\]

This is useful when reasoning about reflection transformations later.

---

# 553.12 Reflection is linear for a fixed normal

For fixed unit \(n\):

\[
R_n(i)
=
i-2(i\cdot n)n.
\]

Since dotting with fixed \(n\) is linear:

\[
R_n(ai+bj)
=
aR_n(i)+bR_n(j).
\]

So reflection across a plane through the origin is a linear transformation.

Later, using matrices, it becomes a **Householder reflection**:

\[
R=I-2nn^T.
\]

Do not worry about matrix mechanics yet. The important point is that the formula you derived becomes an entire reflection matrix later.

---

# 553.13 Implementation

```cpp
[[nodiscard]]
constexpr Vec3 reflect(
    Vec3 incident,
    Vec3 unitNormal) noexcept
{
    return incident
         - unitNormal
         * (2.0f * dot(incident, unitNormal));
}
```

A more explicit API would make the invariant visible:

```cpp
Vec3 reflect(
    Vec3 incident,
    UnitVec3 normal);
```

If the normal is not unit, either normalize it first or use the denominator form.

---

# 553.14 Production failure modes

A zero normal defines no reflection plane. A non-unit normal passed to the simplified formula changes the result incorrectly. Mixing world-space incident direction with tangent-space normal is mathematically meaningless even though the code compiles.

Direction convention is another major source of bugs. Some shading code uses a vector **from the surface toward the viewer**, whereas `incident` here points **toward the surface**. Negating one convention changes the formula's apparent sign.

Always draw the arrows before blaming the algebra.

---

# PART 554 — REFRACTION GEOMETRY FROM SNELL'S LAW

Reflection stays in the original medium.

Refraction happens when a ray crosses from one medium into another and its propagation direction bends because the propagation speed changes.

Examples include:

\[
\text{air}\rightarrow\text{glass},
\]

\[
\text{air}\rightarrow\text{water},
\]

\[
\text{glass}\rightarrow\text{air}.
\]

The governing geometric law is **Snell's law**.

---

# 554.1 Index of refraction

Each optical medium has an index of refraction:

\[
n.
\]

Conceptually:

\[
n=\frac{c}{v}
\]

where:

- \(c\) is speed of light in vacuum;
- \(v\) is phase velocity of light in that medium.

The index is dimensionless.

For our geometry, we need two values:

\[
n_1
\]

for the incident medium and:

\[
n_2
\]

for the transmitted medium.

Define:

\[
\boxed{
\eta=\frac{n_1}{n_2}.
}
\]

---

# 554.2 Snell's law

If:

\[
\theta_i
\]

is the incident angle relative to the normal and:

\[
\theta_t
\]

is the transmitted/refracted angle, then:

\[
\boxed{
n_1\sin\theta_i
=
n_2\sin\theta_t.
}
\]

Thus:

\[
\sin\theta_t
=
\frac{n_1}{n_2}
\sin\theta_i.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\sin\theta_t=\eta\sin\theta_i.
}
\]

This equation determines how much the tangent component changes.

---

# 554.3 Direction convention

We need a precise convention again.

Let:

\[
I
\]

be a **unit incident vector pointing in the direction of travel toward the interface**.

Let:

\[
N
\]

be a unit normal pointing from medium 2 back toward medium 1.

For ordinary front-face incidence:

\[
I\cdot N\le0.
\]

Define:

\[
c_i=\cos\theta_i.
\]

Because of our arrow convention:

\[
\boxed{
c_i=-I\cdot N.
}
\]

For a ray directly into the surface:

\[
I=-N
\]

so:

\[
c_i=1.
\]

Correct.

---

# 554.4 Decompose the incident vector

The component along the normal is:

\[
(I\cdot N)N.
\]

Since:

\[
I\cdot N=-c_i,
\]

normal component is:

\[
-c_iN.
\]

Therefore incident vector can be written:

\[
\boxed{
I=I_t-c_iN
}
\]

where:

\[
I_t=I+c_iN
\]

is tangent to the surface.

Check:

\[
I_t\cdot N
=
I\cdot N+c_i
=
-c_i+c_i
=
0.
\]

So \(I_t\) lies in the interface tangent plane.

---

# 554.5 How large is the tangent component?

Because \(I\) is unit:

\[
\|I\|=1.
\]

The normal component magnitude is:

\[
c_i=\cos\theta_i.
\]

By Pythagoras:

\[
\|I_t\|^2+c_i^2=1.
\]

Thus:

\[
\|I_t\|
=
\sqrt{1-c_i^2}.
\]

And:

\[
\boxed{
\|I_t\|=\sin\theta_i.
}
\]

Excellent.

Snell tells us what the transmitted tangent magnitude must become:

\[
\sin\theta_t
=
\eta\sin\theta_i.
\]

Therefore the transmitted tangent vector is:

\[
\boxed{
T_t=\eta I_t.
}
\]

---

# 554.6 Determine the refracted normal component

The transmitted direction \(T\) should also be unit.

Let:

\[
c_t=\cos\theta_t.
\]

Then:

\[
c_t^2
=
1-\sin^2\theta_t.
\]

But:

\[
\sin\theta_t
=
\eta\sin\theta_i.
\]

Therefore:

\[
c_t^2
=
1-\eta^2\sin^2\theta_i.
\]

And:

\[
\sin^2\theta_i
=
1-c_i^2.
\]

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
c_t
=
\sqrt{
1-\eta^2(1-c_i^2)
}.
}
\]

The transmitted ray travels into medium 2, which is opposite \(N\), so its normal component is:

\[
-c_tN.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
T=T_t-c_tN.
}
\]

Substitute \(T_t=\eta I_t\):

\[
T
=
\eta(I+c_iN)-c_tN.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
T
=
\eta I+
(\eta c_i-c_t)N.
}
\]

That is the refracted-direction formula.

---

# 554.7 Common dot-product form

Since:

\[
c_i=-I\cdot N,
\]

let:

\[
d=I\cdot N.
\]

Then:

\[
c_i=-d.
\]

Define:

\[
k=
1-\eta^2(1-d^2).
\]

Then:

\[
c_t=\sqrt{k}.
\]

Substituting gives:

\[
\boxed{
T
=
\eta I
-
(\eta d+\sqrt{k})N
}
\]

where:

\[
\boxed{
k=
1-\eta^2(1-(I\cdot N)^2).
}
\]

This is the form commonly implemented in graphics math libraries.

---

# 554.8 Normal incidence test

Take:

\[
I=-N.
\]

Then:

\[
d=I\cdot N=-1.
\]

So:

\[
k=
1-\eta^2(1-1)
=
1.
\]

Then:

\[
T
=
\eta(-N)
-
[\eta(-1)+1]N.
\]

Simplify:

\[
=-\eta N+\eta N-N.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
T=-N=I.
}
\]

At normal incidence there is no bending.

Correct.

---

# 554.9 Same refractive index test

If:

\[
n_1=n_2,
\]

then:

\[
\eta=1.
\]

Snell says:

\[
\theta_t=\theta_i.
\]

The refracted direction should be identical to the incident direction.

Using the formula indeed gives:

\[
\boxed{T=I.}
\]

Another mandatory sanity test.

---

# 554.10 Bend toward versus away from normal

If medium 2 has **larger** refractive index:

\[
n_2>n_1.
\]

Then:

\[
\eta<1.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\sin\theta_t
<
\sin\theta_i.
\]

Within the usual \(0^\circ\)–\(90^\circ\) range:

\[
\theta_t<\theta_i.
\]

So the ray bends **toward the normal**.

Conversely, if:

\[
n_2<n_1,
\]

then:

\[
\eta>1
\]

and the ray bends **away from the normal**—until a critical point where transmission becomes impossible.

---

# 554.11 Total internal reflection

Look at:

\[
k=
1-\eta^2(1-c_i^2).
\]

For a real transmitted direction, we require:

\[
k\ge0.
\]

If:

\[
k<0,
\]

then:

\[
\sqrt{k}
\]

would require the square root of a negative real number.

Physically this means **no refracted ray exists**.

Instead, we get total internal reflection.

So:

\[
\boxed{
k<0
\Rightarrow
\text{total internal reflection}.
}
\]

---

# 554.12 Derive the critical angle

Snell:

\[
n_1\sin\theta_i
=
n_2\sin\theta_t.
\]

Maximum possible transmitted sine is:

\[
\sin\theta_t=1.
\]

Therefore at the critical angle:

\[
n_1\sin\theta_c=n_2.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
\sin\theta_c
=
\frac{n_2}{n_1}.
}
\]

This only produces a value below or equal to one when:

\[
n_1\ge n_2.
\]

Thus total internal reflection occurs when travelling from a **higher-index** medium toward a **lower-index** medium with sufficiently oblique incidence.

---

# 554.13 Worked example: air into glass

Use approximate:

\[
n_1=1,
\qquad
n_2=1.5.
\]

Then:

\[
\eta=\frac1{1.5}\approx0.6667.
\]

Suppose:

\[
\theta_i=45^\circ.
\]

Then:

\[
\sin\theta_t
=
0.6667
\sin45^\circ.
\]

\[
\approx
0.6667(0.7071)
\approx0.4714.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\theta_t
\approx
28.1^\circ.
\]

The transmitted angle is smaller.

The ray bent toward the normal.

---

# 554.14 Entering versus leaving a surface

A single geometric surface normally has one stored outward normal, but rays can strike from either side.

Suppose `outwardNormal` points from inside material to outside.

Then a ray has:

\[
frontFace
=
I\cdot outwardNormal<0.
\]

If entering:

\[
N=outwardNormal,
\qquad
\eta=\frac{n_{\text{outside}}}{n_{\text{inside}}}.
\]

If exiting:

\[
N=-outwardNormal,
\qquad
\eta=\frac{n_{\text{inside}}}{n_{\text{outside}}}.
\]

This reorients \(N\) so it always opposes the incident direction.

That enormously simplifies the refract formula.

---

# 554.15 C++ reference implementation

```cpp
[[nodiscard]]
std::optional<Vec3> refract(
    Vec3 unitIncident,
    Vec3 unitNormal,
    float eta) noexcept
{
    const float d =
        dot(unitIncident, unitNormal);

    const float k =
        1.0f
        - eta * eta
        * (1.0f - d * d);

    if (k < 0.0f) {
        // Total internal reflection.
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    return
        eta * unitIncident
        - (eta * d + std::sqrt(k))
        * unitNormal;
}
```

The function's contract should state that both input directions are normalized and that the normal has been oriented to oppose the incident ray.

---

# 554.16 Numerical edge near the critical angle

At the exact mathematical threshold:

\[
k=0.
\]

Floating-point evaluation might produce:

\[
k=-10^{-8}
\]

for a case theoretically just transmissive, or:

\[
+10^{-8}
\]

for a case theoretically just beyond critical.

So production code needs a clear policy. A tiny negative value may be clamped to zero if it is attributable to rounding, whereas a meaningfully negative value represents real total internal reflection.

Do not blindly write:

```cpp
sqrt(max(k, 0.0f))
```

unless the caller separately knows whether it needs to distinguish TIR from numerical boundary error.

---

# 554.17 Snell only determines direction

Another important distinction:

Snell's law tells us the **transmitted direction**.

It does not tell us:

- what fraction of light reflects;
- what fraction transmits;
- polarization behavior;
- spectral dispersion;
- absorption.

Those are additional optical phenomena.

Later shading sections introduce Fresnel terms and physically based material models.

So refraction direction alone is not a complete glass shader.

---

# PART 555 — HALF-VECTOR CONSTRUCTION IN SHADING

Reflection gives us a mirror direction.

But many shading models prefer a different geometric object:

\[
\boxed{\text{the direction halfway between light and view directions}.}
\]

That is the **half vector**.

---

# 555.1 Fix shading direction conventions

At a surface point \(P\), define unit vectors:

\[
L
\]

pointing **from the surface toward the light**, and:

\[
V
\]

pointing **from the surface toward the viewer/camera**.

This is crucial.

The physical incoming light propagation direction is:

\[
-L.
\]

But shading formulas often store \(L\) pointing outward toward the light because that makes:

\[
N\cdot L
\]

convenient.

Given unit \(L,V\), define:

\[
\boxed{
H=
\frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}
}
\]

provided:

\[
L\neq -V.
\]

This is the half vector.

---

# 555.2 Why does adding directions produce the bisector?

Suppose \(L,V\) are unit.

Let:

\[
S=L+V.
\]

We want to show \(S\) forms equal angles with both.

Compute:

\[
S\cdot L
=
(L+V)\cdot L.
\]

Expand:

\[
=L\cdot L+V\cdot L.
\]

Because \(L\) is unit:

\[
L\cdot L=1.
\]

So:

\[
S\cdot L
=
1+L\cdot V.
\]

Similarly:

\[
S\cdot V
=
L\cdot V+V\cdot V
=
L\cdot V+1.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
S\cdot L=S\cdot V.
}
\]

Since \(L,V\) have equal magnitude, \(S\) forms the same cosine angle with both.

Thus its normalized form \(H\) is their angular bisector.

---

# 555.3 Derive the half-angle relation

Let angle between \(L\) and \(V\) be:

\[
\theta.
\]

Then:

\[
L\cdot V=\cos\theta
\]

because both are unit.

Now:

\[
\|L+V\|^2
=
(L+V)\cdot(L+V).
\]

Expand:

\[
=
1+2L\cdot V+1.
\]

Thus:

\[
=
2+2\cos\theta.
\]

Using:

\[
1+\cos\theta
=
2\cos^2\frac\theta2,
\]

we get:

\[
2+2\cos\theta
=
4\cos^2\frac\theta2.
\]

Hence:

\[
\boxed{
\|L+V\|
=
2\cos\frac\theta2
}
\]

for the principal range.

Now:

\[
L\cdot H
=
\frac{L\cdot(L+V)}
{\|L+V\|}.
\]

Numerator:

\[
1+\cos\theta
=
2\cos^2\frac\theta2.
\]

Denominator:

\[
2\cos\frac\theta2.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
L\cdot H
=
\cos\frac\theta2.
}
\]

Same for \(V\).

So \(H\) is literally halfway in angular space.

---

# 555.4 Why the half vector appears in specular reflection

The physical incoming light direction is:

\[
I=-L.
\]

Perfect reflection about unit normal \(N\) gives:

\[
R
=
-L
-
2((-L)\cdot N)N.
\]

Therefore:

\[
R
=
-L+2(L\cdot N)N.
\]

Under exact mirror reflection toward the viewer:

\[
R=V.
\]

Then:

\[
V
=
-L+2(L\cdot N)N.
\]

Move \(L\):

\[
L+V
=
2(L\cdot N)N.
\]

Therefore the sum \(L+V\) is parallel to \(N\).

So:

\[
\boxed{
H=N
}
\]

under perfect mirror alignment, assuming the front-facing hemisphere gives a positive scale.

This is the key shading interpretation:

> the surface normal produces perfect specular alignment when it matches the half vector between light and view directions.

---

# 555.5 Why use \(N\cdot H\)?

Suppose a micro-surface orientation were exactly:

\[
H.
\]

Then incoming light from \(L\) would reflect toward \(V\).

So microfacet shading models care strongly about how likely it is to find microscopic normals aligned with:

\[
H.
\]

This is why \(N\cdot H\) appears constantly in physically based shading.

The complete microfacet BRDF belongs much later. Here, the point is to understand **why the half vector is geometrically natural**.

---

# 555.6 Why \(L\) and \(V\) must be normalized first

Suppose directions are geometrically the same but magnitudes differ:

\[
L=(100,0),
\]

\[
V=(0,1).
\]

Then:

\[
L+V=(100,1),
\]

which points almost entirely along L.

That is not the angular bisector.

The sum bisects the angle only when the contributing direction vectors have equal magnitude—conventionally unit magnitude.

So:

\[
\boxed{
H=\operatorname{normalize}
(
\hat L+\hat V
).
}
\]

---

# 555.7 The antiparallel failure

If:

\[
L=-V,
\]

then:

\[
L+V=0.
\]

There is no unique half vector.

Geometrically, two opposite directions have infinitely many directions lying \(90^\circ\) from each.

No unique angular bisector plane direction exists.

So:

```cpp
normalize(L + V);
```

is invalid in this case.

A shading implementation must know whether such configurations are excluded by hemisphere tests or need a fallback.

---

# 555.8 C++ implementation

```cpp
[[nodiscard]]
std::optional<Vec3> halfVector(
    Vec3 unitLight,
    Vec3 unitView) noexcept
{
    const Vec3 sum =
        unitLight + unitView;

    return tryNormalize(sum);
}
```

A strongly typed version would accept unit-direction types.

The operation is cheap but includes normalization, hence a dot/square root or reciprocal-square-root path.

---

# 555.9 Half vector versus reflection vector

These are not the same thing.

\[
R
\]

is produced by reflecting the incoming propagation direction around the normal.

\[
H
\]

is generated from the light and view directions:

\[
H=\operatorname{normalize}(L+V).
\]

At perfect specular alignment:

\[
H=N.
\]

Meanwhile:

\[
R=V.
\]

Do not confuse:

```text
R = where reflected light travels

H = normal orientation that would reflect L into V
```

That distinction becomes critical in shading.

---

# PART 556 — TANGENT VECTORS ON A SURFACE

We now move from ray directions to surface-local geometry.

A surface in 3D generally has two independent directions along which you can move **while remaining locally on the surface**.

Those are tangent directions.

---

# 556.1 What does "tangent" actually mean?

Consider standing on a surface.

A displacement straight away from it leaves the surface.

A tangent displacement moves sideways along it.

At a point \(P\), a tangent vector represents an infinitesimal/first-order movement that stays on the surface.

For a flat plane, this is easy.

If plane normal is:

\[
N,
\]

then vector \(T\) lies in the plane exactly when:

\[
\boxed{
T\cdot N=0.
}
\]

So every vector orthogonal to the normal is tangent to the plane.

---

# 556.2 There is usually not one tangent

A smooth two-dimensional surface embedded in 3D has a **two-dimensional tangent plane**.

Therefore infinitely many tangent vectors exist.

If \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are independent tangent directions, then any:

\[
aT_1+bT_2
\]

is also tangent.

So when an engine stores a field named:

```cpp
Vec3 tangent;
```

it does not mean:

> the mathematically unique tangent direction.

There generally isn't one.

It means the engine has selected **one preferred tangent direction**, often because texture coordinates provide a natural choice.

---

# 556.3 Triangle example

For triangle points:

\[
P_0,P_1,P_2,
\]

construct edges:

\[
E_1=P_1-P_0,
\]

\[
E_2=P_2-P_0.
\]

Both lie in the triangle plane.

So both are tangent vectors to the flat triangle surface.

Their cross product:

\[
N=E_1\times E_2
\]

is normal to that plane.

Thus:

\[
N\cdot E_1=0,
\]

\[
N\cdot E_2=0.
\]

This is the fundamental tangent-plane relationship.

---

# 556.4 Curved surface example: sphere

Consider a sphere centered at \(C\) with radius \(r\).

For surface point \(P\):

\[
\|P-C\|=r.
\]

The radial direction:

\[
N=P-C
\]

points normal to the sphere.

Why must a tangent direction \(T\) satisfy:

\[
(P-C)\cdot T=0?
\]

Consider a tiny attempted displacement:

\[
P' = P+\varepsilon T.
\]

Then:

\[
P'-C
=
(P-C)+\varepsilon T.
\]

Squared radius:

\[
\|(P-C)+\varepsilon T\|^2.
\]

Expand:

\[
=
\|P-C\|^2
+
2\varepsilon(P-C)\cdot T
+
\varepsilon^2\|T\|^2.
\]

Original squared radius is:

\[
r^2.
\]

For the displacement to stay on the sphere **to first order**, the term proportional to \(\varepsilon\) must vanish:

\[
2(P-C)\cdot T=0.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
(P-C)\cdot T=0.
}
\]

So tangent directions are perpendicular to the radial normal.

This is already the local differential geometry idea without requiring us to fully teach calculus yet.

---

# 556.5 Parameterized surfaces

A surface can be described by two parameters:

\[
P(u,v).
\]

Changing \(u\) slightly moves along one surface direction.

Changing \(v\) slightly moves along another.

The corresponding differential directions are:

\[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial u},
\qquad
\frac{\partial P}{\partial v}.
\]

These are tangent vectors.

Full derivative theory belongs in Phase 9, so for now treat them conceptually as:

> directions of surface change caused by changing one parameter while holding the other fixed.

Texture mapping gives us a practical instance of this idea.

---

# 556.6 Texture tangent

A mesh vertex may have 2D UV coordinates:

\[
(u,v).
\]

The **texture tangent** \(T\) usually represents the 3D direction corresponding locally to increasing \(u\).

The bitangent \(B\), Part 558, corresponds locally to increasing \(v\).

So:

```text
T → surface direction of increasing texture U
B → surface direction of increasing texture V
N → away from the surface
```

These form a local surface frame.

This is why normal maps can store directions in a 2D texture's local coordinate system.

---

# 556.7 Tangent magnitude can contain information

Mathematically a tangent vector does not have to be unit length.

For a parameterized surface:

\[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial u}
\]

can have magnitude representing:

> how much physical distance changes for one unit change in \(u\).

If texture coordinates are stretched, this derivative may be large.

Therefore normalizing a tangent removes scale information.

For shading frames, engines often want only the direction and normalize it. For differential geometry or texture-footprint calculations, that magnitude may matter.

Do not equate:

\[
\text{tangent vector}
\]

with:

\[
\text{unit tangent direction}.
\]

---

# 556.8 Construct a tangent from a normal when no preferred U exists

Suppose only a unit normal \(N\) is known.

We need *some* tangent direction.

Choose any vector \(A\) not parallel to \(N\), then remove its normal component:

\[
T'
=
A-(A\cdot N)N.
\]

This is rejection from Part 539.

Then:

\[
T=
\frac{T'}{\|T'\|}
\]

if \(T'\neq0\).

Why is it tangent?

\[
T'\cdot N
=
A\cdot N-(A\cdot N)(N\cdot N).
\]

For unit \(N\):

\[
= A\cdot N-A\cdot N=0.
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{
T\cdot N=0.
}
\]

This provides a valid tangent.

Part 560 will teach constructing an entire orthonormal basis from one direction systematically; we are only using the local surface interpretation here.

---

# 556.9 Robust helper-axis choice

If you choose:

\[
A=(1,0,0)
\]

but:

\[
N\approx(1,0,0),
\]

then rejection:

\[
A-(A\cdot N)N
\]

becomes nearly zero.

Normalizing it becomes unstable.

So a robust algorithm chooses an auxiliary axis poorly aligned with \(N\).

Conceptually, choose the coordinate axis corresponding to a small absolute component of \(N\), because that axis cannot be close to parallel with \(N\).

This is a general numerical rule:

\[
\boxed{
\text{do not construct perpendicular directions from nearly parallel seeds}.
}
\]

---

# PART 557 — NORMAL VECTORS ON A SURFACE

The tangent plane tells us all directions along the surface.

A **normal vector** points perpendicular to that tangent plane.

---

# 557.1 Formal local definition

At surface point \(P\), let tangent plane be:

\[
T_P.
\]

A nonzero vector \(N\) is normal if:

\[
\boxed{
N\cdot T=0
}
\]

for every tangent vector \(T\in T_P\).

For a 2D surface embedded in 3D, the tangent plane is 2D and its perpendicular complement is 1D.

Therefore normals occur along one axis:

\[
N
\]

or:

\[
-N.
\]

The geometry alone gives a normal line.

An **orientation convention** chooses which side is positive.

---

# 557.2 Triangle geometric normal

For triangle:

\[
P_0,P_1,P_2,
\]

construct:

\[
E_1=P_1-P_0,
\]

\[
E_2=P_2-P_0.
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
N_g=E_1\times E_2.
}
\]

The cross product is perpendicular to both edges, therefore perpendicular to the triangle plane.

So it is a valid geometric normal.

---

# 557.3 But the raw cross product is not a unit normal

From Part 545:

\[
\|E_1\times E_2\|
\]

equals parallelogram area.

Triangle area is:

\[
\frac12\|E_1\times E_2\|.
\]

Therefore the raw triangle normal has magnitude:

\[
\boxed{
\|N_g\|
=
2A_\triangle.
}
\]

That magnitude contains useful geometric information.

To obtain only orientation:

\[
\boxed{
\hat N_g
=
\frac{E_1\times E_2}
{\|E_1\times E_2\|}.
}
\]

Only valid for nondegenerate triangles.

---

# 557.4 Why a degenerate triangle has no stable normal

If vertices are collinear:

\[
E_1\times E_2=0.
\]

The triangle has zero area.

There is no uniquely defined triangle plane.

Therefore:

\[
\operatorname{normalize}(E_1\times E_2)
\]

is undefined.

Again, zero cross is not an irritating numerical corner case.

It represents a real geometric loss of information.

---

# 557.5 Plane equation from a normal

Given point \(P_0\) on a plane and normal \(N\), any point \(X\) in the plane has displacement:

\[
X-P_0
\]

tangent to the plane.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
N\cdot(X-P_0)=0.
}
\]

Expand:

\[
N\cdot X-N\cdot P_0=0.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
N\cdot X=d
}
\]

where:

\[
d=N\cdot P_0.
\]

This is the seed of plane equations used throughout collision, clipping, frustum tests, and ray intersection.

---

# 557.6 Normals are not inherently unit length

A vector only needs to satisfy perpendicularity to be normal.

If:

\[
N
\]

is normal, then for any nonzero scalar \(c\):

\[
cN
\]

is also normal.

Because:

\[
(cN)\cdot T
=
c(N\cdot T)
=
0.
\]

So "normal" describes geometric orientation, not length.

A **unit normal** adds the invariant:

\[
\|N\|=1.
\]

Shading formulas commonly assume unit normals.

---

# 557.7 Geometric normals versus shading normals

This distinction is essential.

A **geometric normal** follows directly from actual surface geometry.

For a triangle:

\[
N_g
\propto
(P_1-P_0)\times(P_2-P_0).
\]

A **shading normal** may be different.

For smooth shading, meshes often store a normal at each vertex. These normals may be averaged or artist-authored to make a faceted polygonal surface appear smooth.

Thus a fragment on a triangle can use a shading normal that is **not exactly perpendicular to that triangle's geometric plane**.

That is intentional.

So:

\[
\boxed{
\text{geometric normal}
\neq
\text{shading normal}
}
\]

in general.

---

# 557.8 Why interpolated normals need renormalization

Suppose two unit vertex normals:

\[
N_0,
N_1.
\]

Linear interpolation:

\[
N(t)
=
(1-t)N_0+tN_1.
\]

Even though each endpoint has length one, the interior generally does not.

Example:

\[
N_0=(1,0),
\]

\[
N_1=(0,1).
\]

At:

\[
t=\frac12,
\]

we get:

\[
N=
\left(
\frac12,\frac12
\right).
\]

Magnitude:

\[
\sqrt{\frac14+\frac14}
=
\frac1{\sqrt2}.
\]

Not 1.

So shading normally performs:

\[
\boxed{
\hat N=
\operatorname{normalize}(N_{\text{interpolated}}).
}
\]

This is one of the most common normalization operations in raster graphics.

---

# 557.9 Normal direction and winding

For triangle:

\[
N=(P_1-P_0)\times(P_2-P_0).
\]

Swap \(P_1,P_2\):

\[
N'=(P_2-P_0)\times(P_1-P_0).
\]

Cross anti-commutativity gives:

\[
N'=-N.
\]

Therefore winding determines orientation.

A mesh's notion of "outward" normal must remain consistent with its vertex-order convention.

---

# 557.10 A normal is not generally transformed like an ordinary direction

This is important enough to warn about now, but Part 582 is dedicated to proving it.

Under rotation or uniform scale, treating a normal like an ordinary direction appears to work.

Under nonuniform scale or shear, that can break perpendicularity.

Why?

Because the defining property of a normal is not merely:

> an arrow pointing somewhere.

It is:

\[
\boxed{
N\cdot T=0
\quad
\text{for every tangent }T.
}
\]

After transforming the surface tangents, the transformed normal must remain perpendicular to them.

Transforming it with the same matrix does not generally preserve that relation under nonuniform scaling.

Full inverse-transpose/covector derivation waits until Part 582.

For now remember:

\[
\boxed{
\text{normal semantics are stronger than ordinary direction semantics}.
}
\]

---

# 557.11 Surface normal of a sphere

Sphere centered at \(C\):

\[
\|P-C\|=r.
\]

The radial vector:

\[
P-C
\]

is perpendicular to the tangent plane.

Therefore unit outward normal is:

\[
\boxed{
N=
\frac{P-C}{r}
}
\]

or equivalently:

\[
\operatorname{normalize}(P-C).
\]

This is why ray tracers can compute sphere normals so cheaply.

---

# PART 558 — BITANGENT VECTORS

A surface tangent plane is two-dimensional.

One tangent \(T\) does not span it completely.

We need a second independent tangent direction.

In rendering this is usually called the **bitangent**:

\[
B.
\]

You may also encounter the older term **binormal**, though "bitangent" is often more descriptive because the vector is tangent to the surface rather than normal to something.

---

# 558.1 Desired TBN frame

We want three local directions:

\[
T
\]

tangent,

\[
B
\]

bitangent,

\[
N
\]

normal.

For an ideal orthonormal tangent frame:

\[
T\cdot N=0,
\]

\[
B\cdot N=0,
\]

\[
T\cdot B=0,
\]

and:

\[
\|T\|=\|B\|=\|N\|=1.
\]

Part 559 is specifically about orthonormal bases, so we will not turn this into its full theory yet.

But this is the target surface-frame structure.

---

# 558.2 Construct bitangent from normal and tangent

Suppose \(N,T\) are unit and perpendicular.

Then:

\[
\boxed{
B=N\times T
}
\]

is perpendicular to both.

Cross magnitude:

\[
\|N\times T\|
=
\|N\|
\|T\|
\sin90^\circ
=
1.
\]

So \(B\) is automatically unit.

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
B=N\times T
}
\]

constructs the third axis of one particular handed frame.

But swapping the cross order gives:

\[
T\times N=-B.
\]

So the exact convention matters.

There is no universal law saying every engine must use `cross(N,T)` rather than `cross(T,N)`.

---

# 558.3 Why bitangent is tangent to the surface

Because:

\[
B=N\times T,
\]

we know:

\[
B\cdot N=0.
\]

Anything perpendicular to surface normal lies in the tangent plane.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
B\text{ is itself tangent}.
}
\]

Hence the name **bitangent**: the second chosen tangent direction.

---

# 558.4 UV geometry gives a preferred tangent and bitangent

Suppose triangle positions:

\[
P_0,P_1,P_2
\]

have texture coordinates:

\[
UV_0=(u_0,v_0),
\]

\[
UV_1=(u_1,v_1),
\]

\[
UV_2=(u_2,v_2).
\]

Define spatial edges:

\[
E_1=P_1-P_0,
\]

\[
E_2=P_2-P_0.
\]

Define UV differences:

\[
\Delta UV_1=
(\Delta u_1,\Delta v_1)
\]

with:

\[
\Delta u_1=u_1-u_0,
\qquad
\Delta v_1=v_1-v_0,
\]

and similarly:

\[
\Delta UV_2=
(\Delta u_2,\Delta v_2).
\]

Locally we want:

\[
T
\]

to correspond to increasing \(u\), and:

\[
B
\]

to increasing \(v\).

---

# 558.5 Derive the tangent-space edge equations

A UV displacement:

\[
(\Delta u,\Delta v)
\]

corresponds approximately across the triangle to 3D displacement:

\[
\Delta u\,T+\Delta v\,B.
\]

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{
E_1
=
\Delta u_1 T+
\Delta v_1 B
}
\]

and:

\[
\boxed{
E_2
=
\Delta u_2 T+
\Delta v_2 B.
}
\]

This is a two-equation system whose unknowns are the 3D vectors \(T,B\).

The scalar coefficients come from UV differences.

---

# 558.6 Solve for \(T\)

Multiply the first equation by:

\[
\Delta v_2:
\]

\[
\Delta v_2E_1
=
\Delta u_1\Delta v_2T
+
\Delta v_1\Delta v_2B.
\]

Multiply the second by:

\[
\Delta v_1:
\]

\[
\Delta v_1E_2
=
\Delta u_2\Delta v_1T
+
\Delta v_2\Delta v_1B.
\]

Subtract.

The \(B\) terms cancel:

\[
\Delta v_2E_1-\Delta v_1E_2
=
(\Delta u_1\Delta v_2-
\Delta u_2\Delta v_1)T.
\]

Define:

\[
\boxed{
D=
\Delta u_1\Delta v_2
-
\Delta u_2\Delta v_1.
}
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
T
=
\frac{
\Delta v_2E_1-\Delta v_1E_2
}{
D
}.
}
\]

---

# 558.7 Solve for \(B\)

Multiply the second edge equation by:

\[
\Delta u_1
\]

and the first by:

\[
\Delta u_2.
\]

Subtract to eliminate \(T\).

Result:

\[
\boxed{
B
=
\frac{
-\Delta u_2E_1+
\Delta u_1E_2
}{
D
}.
}
\]

Equivalently:

\[
\boxed{
B
=
\frac{
\Delta u_1E_2-\Delta u_2E_1
}{
D
}.
}
\]

This is the standard tangent/bitangent construction derived from the triangle's spatial and UV edges.

---

# 558.8 Worked UV example

Take:

\[
P_0=(0,0,0),
\]

\[
P_1=(2,0,0),
\]

\[
P_2=(0,3,0).
\]

UV coordinates:

\[
UV_0=(0,0),
\]

\[
UV_1=(1,0),
\]

\[
UV_2=(0,1).
\]

Then:

\[
E_1=(2,0,0),
\]

\[
E_2=(0,3,0).
\]

UV differences:

\[
\Delta u_1=1,
\quad
\Delta v_1=0,
\]

\[
\Delta u_2=0,
\quad
\Delta v_2=1.
\]

Therefore:

\[
D=(1)(1)-(0)(0)=1.
\]

Tangent:

\[
T
=
1E_1-0E_2.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
T=(2,0,0).
}
\]

Bitangent:

\[
B
=
1E_2-0E_1.
\]

Thus:

\[
\boxed{
B=(0,3,0).
}
\]

Notice they are not unit.

Their magnitudes encode how physical geometry stretches relative to UV parameter distance.

Normalize them for a direction-only shading frame:

\[
\hat T=(1,0,0),
\]

\[
\hat B=(0,1,0).
\]

Normal:

\[
\hat N=(0,0,1).
\]

---

# 558.9 What does \(D=0\) mean?

Recall:

\[
D
=
\Delta u_1\Delta v_2
-
\Delta u_2\Delta v_1.
\]

This is the signed 2D area scale of the UV triangle.

If:

\[
D=0,
\]

then the UV edges are linearly dependent.

The UV triangle has collapsed to a line or point.

Therefore the texture coordinates do not contain enough two-dimensional information to distinguish U from V directions.

So dividing by \(D\) is impossible because:

\[
\boxed{
\text{a valid tangent frame cannot be recovered uniquely from degenerate UVs}.
}
\]

Again, division by zero corresponds to real geometric degeneracy.

---

# 558.10 Mirrored UVs

\(D\) can be negative.

That means the UV parameterization has reversed orientation relative to the triangle geometry.

In practice, mirrored UV islands are common.

This creates a tangent-frame handedness flip.

Therefore storing only \(T,N\) is sometimes insufficient unless you also know whether the corresponding \(B\) should be:

\[
N\times T
\]

or:

\[
-(N\times T).
\]

A common representation is conceptually:

```cpp
struct Tangent {
    Vec3 direction;
    float handedness;
};
```

with:

\[
handedness\in\{-1,+1\}.
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
B
=
handedness\,
(N\times T)
}
\]

for the chosen convention.

Different asset pipelines may encode this sign differently, so the convention must be documented.

---

# 558.11 Derive the handedness sign

Suppose we already computed a raw UV bitangent:

\[
B_{\text{raw}}.
\]

And we have cleaned unit:

\[
N,T.
\]

Candidate frame bitangent:

\[
B_c=N\times T.
\]

Compare it to raw UV bitangent:

\[
B_c\cdot B_{\text{raw}}.
\]

If positive, they point to the same hemisphere.

If negative, they oppose.

So:

\[
\boxed{
s=
\operatorname{sign}
[
(N\times T)\cdot B_{\text{raw}}
].
}
\]

Then:

\[
\boxed{
B=s(N\times T).
}
\]

This lets us compress the third frame direction into one sign when \(N\) and \(T\) are already available.

---

# 558.12 Why tangent often needs orthogonalization against the normal

The tangent accumulated from neighboring triangles or interpolated from vertices may not satisfy exactly:

\[
T\cdot N=0.
\]

Remove its normal component:

\[
T'
=
T-(T\cdot N)N
\]

assuming unit \(N\).

Then normalize:

\[
\hat T
=
\frac{T'}{\|T'\|}.
\]

This is exactly the rejection operation from Part 539.

After that:

\[
B=s(N\times\hat T).
\]

This construction produces a clean local frame if the inputs are nondegenerate.

You will recognize the deeper generalized procedure in Parts 559–561.

---

# 558.13 Why tangent space matters for normal mapping

Suppose a normal map stores local direction:

\[
n_t=
(n_x,n_y,n_z).
\]

Those numbers are coordinates relative to the local surface basis:

\[
T,B,N.
\]

Therefore the corresponding world-space vector is reconstructed by:

\[
\boxed{
n_w
=
n_xT+n_yB+n_zN.
}
\]

This is exactly Part 514's basis-coordinate interpretation.

The texture's RGB-ish vector is not automatically world-space.

It is a coordinate tuple relative to the tangent frame.

So tangent-space normal mapping is fundamentally:

\[
\boxed{
\text{basis reconstruction}.
}
\]

That connection is extremely important.

---

# 558.14 A full tangent-frame implementation skeleton

```cpp
struct TangentFrame {
    Vec3 tangent;
    Vec3 bitangent;
    Vec3 normal;
};

[[nodiscard]]
std::optional<TangentFrame>
buildTangentFrame(
    Vec3 normal,
    Vec3 rawTangent,
    Vec3 rawBitangent) noexcept
{
    auto nOpt = tryNormalize(normal);

    if (!nOpt) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    const Vec3 n = *nOpt;

    // Remove normal contamination from tangent.
    Vec3 t =
        rawTangent
        - n * dot(rawTangent, n);

    auto tOpt = tryNormalize(t);

    if (!tOpt) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }

    t = *tOpt;

    const Vec3 candidateB =
        cross(n, t);

    const float sign =
        dot(candidateB, rawBitangent) < 0.0f
        ? -1.0f
        : 1.0f;

    const Vec3 b =
        candidateB * sign;

    return TangentFrame{
        t,
        b,
        n
    };
}
```

This is a canonical/reference construction, not a claim about any specific engine repository.
